polities.gov: Hereditary monarchy, Valois house
polities.head: King; Charles VI to Henry III
polities.cap: Paris; the court moved among the Loire châteaux
polities.rel: Catholic; Huguenot minority after 1550
polities.pop: About 15 million by 1500, the largest in Latin Christendom
polities.econ: Grain, wine, cloth; royal revenue from the taille
polities.now: The crown is recovering from the Hundred Years' War and building the standing army and permanent taxation that make it the strongest monarchy in Europe. From 1562 the Wars of Religion divide the kingdom into Catholic and Huguenot camps.
polities.how: Charles VII expelled the English by 1453; Louis XI absorbed Burgundy's French lands in 1477; the Italian Wars from 1494 pitted the Valois against the Habsburgs for sixty years.
polities.next: Henry III's murder in 1589 passes the crown to the Protestant Henry of Navarre, who converts and ends the wars with the Edict of Nantes in 1598.

polities.gov: Absolute monarchy, Bourbon house; the Estates-General last met in 1614
polities.head: King; Henry IV, Louis XIII, Louis XIV, Louis XV, Louis XVI
polities.cap: Paris; the court at Versailles from 1682
polities.rel: Catholic; Protestant worship outlawed 1685
polities.econ: Europe's largest agricultural economy; Atlantic sugar and slave trade through Nantes and Bordeaux
polities.now: The most powerful state in Europe by population and army, governed from Versailles by a king who rules without a parliament. The treasury is the weak point: war debt from 1740 onward exceeds what a tax system exempting nobles and clergy can raise.
polities.how: Richelieu and Mazarin broke the nobility's independent power; Louis XIV fought four wars and took Alsace, Franche-Comté and the northern fortress line.
polities.next: Bankruptcy forces Louis XVI to call the Estates-General in 1789, and the Revolution follows within months.

polities.gov: Constitutional monarchy 1791, republic from September 1792, Directory from 1795
polities.head: Louis XVI to 1792; the Convention; the five Directors
polities.rel: Church lands nationalised 1789; clergy made state employees; dechristianisation 1793
polities.econ: War economy; assignat paper money collapses in 1796
polities.now: The Revolution has abolished feudal dues and noble privilege, executed the king, and is fighting most of Europe. The Terror of 1793 to 1794 killed about 17,000 by guillotine; the Directory that followed depends on the army.
polities.how: A fiscal crisis became a constitutional one when the Third Estate declared itself the National Assembly in June 1789; war with Austria from 1792 radicalised the republic.
polities.next: Bonaparte's coup of November 1799 ends the Directory; he crowns himself emperor in 1804.

polities.gov: Consulate to 1804, then hereditary empire under Napoleon
polities.head: Napoleon Bonaparte, First Consul then Emperor
polities.rel: Concordat with Rome 1801 restores the Church under state control
polities.pop: About 30 million in France proper; 44 million with annexed lands by 1812
polities.econ: Continental System bars British goods from 1806; the Civil Code of 1804 standardises property law
polities.now: France rules directly or through satellite kingdoms from Spain to Poland after defeating Austria, Prussia and Russia between 1805 and 1807. The empire rests on conscription and victory, and the Russian campaign of 1812 destroys the army that sustained it.
polities.how: Napoleon took power in 1799, made peace with the Church, and used the revolutionary army's size and the corps system to beat every coalition until 1812.
polities.next: Defeat at Leipzig in 1813 and the allied entry into Paris in 1814 restore the Bourbons; the Hundred Days end at Waterloo in June 1815.

polities.gov: Constitutional monarchy with a narrow franchise; Bourbon to 1830, then Orléans
polities.head: Louis XVIII, Charles X, Louis-Philippe
polities.rel: Catholic established; religious toleration kept
polities.econ: Early industrialisation in textiles and coal; railways from the 1830s; Algeria invaded 1830
polities.now: The monarchy restored by the allies governs through a charter and a parliament elected by fewer than 250,000 voters. Charles X's attempt to rule by decree produced the July Revolution of 1830 and a more liberal king, Louis-Philippe, whose regime rests on bankers and officials.
polities.how: The allies restored the Bourbons in 1814 and 1815 on condition of a charter; the Algiers expedition of 1830 began the French empire in Africa.
polities.next: Economic crisis and a banned reform banquet bring down Louis-Philippe in February 1848.

polities.gov: Republic 1848 to 1852; plebiscitary empire under Napoleon III from 1852
polities.head: Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte, president then emperor
polities.rel: Catholic; the state backs the Church in education
polities.econ: Railways, Crédit Mobilier banking, free trade treaty with Britain 1860
polities.now: Napoleon III rules through universal male suffrage and controlled elections, builds railways and modern Paris, and fights in Crimea, Italy and Mexico. The regime liberalises after 1860 as its foreign ventures fail.
polities.how: The republic of 1848 elected Louis-Napoléon president; he seized full power by coup in December 1851 and restored the empire a year later.
polities.next: Defeat and capture at Sedan in September 1870 end the empire; Paris proclaims the Third Republic the same week.

polities.gov: Parliamentary republic; weak presidency, strong Chamber of Deputies
polities.head: President of the Republic; power with the prime minister and Chamber
polities.rel: Church and state separated by law in 1905
polities.econ: Second colonial empire after Britain's; iron and steel in Lorraine; 1.4 million dead in 1914 to 1918
polities.now: A republic of frequent cabinets and durable institutions, it survived the Commune, the Dreyfus affair and the First World War, and holds an empire from Indochina to West Africa. After 1919 it seeks security against a larger Germany through alliances and the Maginot Line.
polities.how: The Commune of 1871 was crushed; republicans secured the regime by 1879; the Dreyfus affair of the 1890s split the country and ended with the separation of Church and state.
polities.next: Germany defeats France in six weeks in 1940; the Third Republic votes itself out of existence in July.

polities.gov: Authoritarian 'French State' under Pétain in the unoccupied zone; German occupation of the rest
polities.head: Marshal Philippe Pétain; de Gaulle's Free French from London
polities.rel: Catholic favoured by Vichy
polities.econ: Occupation costs and labour conscription to Germany
polities.now: The armistice of June 1940 left Germany the north and coast and gave Pétain the south, which collaborated, passed its own anti-Jewish laws and was occupied in turn in November 1942.
polities.how: The army collapsed in May and June 1940; parliament granted Pétain full powers on 10 July.
polities.next: Allied landings in June 1944 and the liberation of Paris in August restore a republic under de Gaulle's provisional government.

polities.gov: Parliamentary republic; 21 governments in 12 years
polities.head: President, largely ceremonial; prime ministers
polities.rel: Secular state
polities.econ: Postwar reconstruction with Marshall aid; the Monnet Plan; founding member of the European Coal and Steel Community in 1951
polities.now: A republic rebuilding fast at home while losing its empire abroad: defeat at Dien Bien Phu in 1954 ends Indochina, and the Algerian war from the same year consumes the state.
polities.how: Voters rejected a return to the Third Republic in 1945; de Gaulle resigned in 1946 over the weak executive the new constitution created.
polities.next: An army revolt in Algiers in May 1958 brings de Gaulle back; the Fifth Republic's constitution passes by referendum in September.

polities.gov: Semi-presidential republic; president directly elected since 1965
polities.head: President; de Gaulle, Pompidou, Giscard, Mitterrand, Chirac, Sarkozy, Hollande, Macron
polities.rel: Secular; Catholic heritage, Europe's largest Muslim minority
polities.econ: Seventh-largest economy; nuclear power, aerospace, luxury goods, agriculture; euro from 1999
polities.now: A strong presidency designed by de Gaulle, a nuclear deterrent, a permanent Security Council seat and a central place in the European Union. Algeria was given up in 1962; influence in francophone Africa has been shrinking since the 2010s.
polities.how: De Gaulle took power in 1958 to end the Algerian crisis and wrote a constitution around the executive; the Franco-German pairing drove European integration from the 1963 treaty onward.
polities.next: The open questions are the pension and debt burden, the strength of the far right, and whether the French-German engine of the EU still runs.

polities.gov: Hereditary monarchy with Parliament's consent needed for taxation
polities.head: King or queen; Lancaster, York, then Tudor from 1485
polities.rel: Catholic until the 1530s; Church of England under the crown from 1534
polities.econ: Wool and cloth exports; a small navy until Henry VIII
polities.now: A middling kingdom that has lost its French lands, fought a dynastic civil war, and under the Tudors broken with Rome. Elizabeth's long reign builds a Protestant identity, a navy that defeated the Armada in 1588, and the first trading companies.
polities.how: The Wars of the Roses ended at Bosworth in 1485; Henry VIII's divorce produced the royal supremacy over the Church; Mary's Catholic restoration lasted five years.
polities.next: James VI of Scotland inherits in 1603, joining the two crowns under one king.

polities.gov: Monarchy in conflict with Parliament; republic 1649 to 1660; constitutional settlement from 1689
polities.head: James I, Charles I, Cromwell as Lord Protector, Charles II, James II, William III and Mary, Anne
polities.rel: Church of England; Puritan ascendancy in the 1650s; toleration for Protestant dissenters from 1689
polities.econ: Atlantic colonies, the East India Company, the Bank of England from 1694
polities.now: The century decides who governs: Parliament won the Civil War and executed the king in 1649, restored the monarchy in 1660, and in 1688 replaced James II with William of Orange on terms that made the crown dependent on Parliament for money and law.
polities.how: Charles I's attempt to rule without Parliament from 1629 and to impose a prayer book on Scotland produced the wars of 1642 to 1651.
polities.next: The Act of Union with Scotland in 1707 creates Great Britain.

polities.gov: Hereditary monarchy, Stewart house, with a one-chamber Parliament
polities.head: King or queen; shared with England after 1603
polities.rel: Catholic until 1560; Presbyterian Church of Scotland after
polities.econ: Cattle, wool, fishing; the Darien scheme of 1698 bankrupts investors
polities.now: An independent kingdom sharing a monarch with England since 1603 and increasingly its wars; the Darien disaster and English trade barriers push its elite toward union.
polities.how: The Reformation of 1560 under Knox made Scotland Presbyterian; Mary Queen of Scots lost the throne in 1567 and her head in 1587.
polities.next: The Act of Union of 1707 merges the parliaments into one at Westminster.

polities.gov: Constitutional monarchy; cabinet government under a prime minister from the 1720s
polities.head: Anne, George I, George II, George III; prime ministers from Walpole to Pitt
polities.rel: Church of England; Catholics barred from office
polities.econ: First industrial economy: coal, iron, cotton; the national debt funds a navy that wins the Seven Years' War
polities.now: A fiscal-military state that beat France for North America and India by 1763, lost the thirteen colonies by 1783, and is industrialising faster than any rival while fighting revolutionary France.
polities.how: The union of 1707 and the Hanoverian succession of 1714 settled the constitution; Walpole built cabinet government; the Bank and the funded debt let Britain outspend France.
polities.next: Union with Ireland in 1801 creates the United Kingdom; the war with Napoleon runs to 1815.

polities.t: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland
polities.gov: Constitutional monarchy; franchise widened by the Reform Acts of 1832, 1867 and 1884
polities.head: George III to George V; prime ministers Peel, Palmerston, Gladstone, Disraeli, Salisbury, Asquith
polities.cap: London, the largest city in the world
polities.rel: Church of England; Catholic emancipation 1829
polities.econ: The workshop of the world until the 1880s; the pound on gold; the largest merchant fleet and navy
polities.now: The leading industrial, naval and financial power, ruling a quarter of the world's land and people by 1900. Germany and the United States have overtaken it in industry; its answer is the Entente with France and Russia and the dreadnought race.
polities.how: Victory in 1815, free trade from 1846, and the Royal Navy's command of the seas made Britain the arbiter of the century; the Irish famine and Home Rule question ran through its politics throughout.
polities.next: War with Germany in August 1914 costs about 900,000 dead and the financial primacy that passed to New York.
polities.wk: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland

polities.gov: Constitutional monarchy; universal suffrage by 1928; coalition government in both wars
polities.head: George V, Edward VIII, George VI; Lloyd George, Baldwin, MacDonald, Chamberlain, Churchill
polities.rel: Church of England established; Church of Scotland Presbyterian
polities.econ: Left the gold standard in 1931; depressed heavy industry in the north; Lend-Lease from 1941
polities.now: Victor in two world wars at the price of its financial independence and the beginning of the end of empire: the Irish Free State left in 1922, India's independence is conceded in principle, and the United States holds the debt.
polities.how: The First World War mobilised the whole economy; the Depression broke the gold standard; appeasement failed at Munich in 1938 and Churchill led the war from May 1940.
polities.next: Attlee's Labour government builds the welfare state from 1945 and grants India independence in 1947.

polities.gov: Constitutional monarchy; parliamentary democracy; devolved assemblies in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland since 1999
polities.head: Elizabeth II 1952 to 2022; Charles III; prime ministers Attlee, Thatcher, Blair and others
polities.rel: Church of England established; majority report no religion since 2021
polities.econ: Sixth-largest economy; finance, services, pharmaceuticals; North Sea oil from the 1970s; left the European Union in 2020
polities.now: A nuclear power with a permanent Security Council seat and a global financial centre, having given up the empire between 1947 and 1980 and the EU in 2020. The union itself is in question in Scotland and Northern Ireland.
polities.how: Suez in 1956 marked the limit of independent action; entry to the European Community in 1973 and Thatcher's reforms from 1979 reshaped the economy; the Good Friday Agreement of 1998 ended the Northern Ireland conflict.
polities.next: The open questions are productivity, the post-Brexit relationship with Europe, and whether the union holds.

polities.gov: Parliamentary republic since 1949; dominion from 1922
polities.head: President (ceremonial); Taoiseach heads the government
polities.rel: Catholic majority; Church influence has fallen sharply since the 1990s
polities.econ: From the poorest in western Europe to among the richest per head: EU membership 1973, low corporate tax, American technology and pharmaceutical investment
polities.now: A small open economy inside the EU and the euro, transformed since the 1990s, with the question of unification with Northern Ireland raised by Brexit.
polities.how: The Free State of 1922 followed the War of Independence; de Valera's 1937 constitution and the 1949 republic completed the break; neutrality held through the Second World War.
polities.next: Housing costs, dependence on a few multinationals, and the northern question shape the next decade.

polities.gov: Two crowns under one dynasty from 1479; separate laws and parliaments
polities.head: Isabella of Castile and Ferdinand of Aragon; Charles I (Charles V) from 1516
polities.cap: No fixed capital; Toledo, Valladolid, Seville for the Indies trade
polities.rel: Catholic; Jews expelled 1492; Muslims forced to convert from 1502
polities.econ: Merino wool, Seville's monopoly on American trade from 1503
polities.now: The union of Castile and Aragon has taken Granada, expelled the Jews, sent Columbus west and inherited the Habsburg lands with Charles V, making the Spanish crown the centre of a European and American empire.
polities.how: The marriage of 1469 joined the crowns; the conquest of Granada in 1492 ended Muslim rule; the Habsburg marriage alliance brought the Netherlands and the imperial title.
polities.next: Cortés and Pizarro deliver Mexico and Peru; American silver from 1545 funds a century of European war.

polities.gov: Composite monarchy under the Habsburgs; councils in Madrid governed each realm separately
polities.head: Charles V, Philip II, Philip III, Philip IV, Charles II
polities.rel: Catholic; the Inquisition; Moriscos expelled 1609
polities.pop: About 8 million in Spain; 10 million more in the American viceroyalties
polities.econ: American silver through Seville; royal bankruptcies in 1557, 1575, 1596, 1607, 1627, 1647
polities.now: The first global empire, from Manila to Antwerp, at war somewhere every year: against the Dutch revolt from 1568, England, France and the Ottomans. Silver pays the armies and the crown defaults anyway; Portugal left in 1640 and the Dutch won recognition in 1648.
polities.how: Charles V's inheritance combined Spain, the Netherlands, Austria and the Indies; Philip II moved the capital to Madrid and lost the Armada in 1588.
polities.next: Charles II dies childless in 1700, and the War of the Spanish Succession passes the crown to the French Bourbons.

polities.gov: Absolute monarchy on the French model; the Aragonese parliaments abolished after 1714
polities.head: Philip V, Ferdinand VI, Charles III, Charles IV
polities.rel: Catholic; Jesuits expelled 1767
polities.econ: Reformed colonial trade after 1765; Cádiz replaces Seville; Mexican silver output peaks
polities.now: A reformed monarchy that recovered administrative control of its empire under Charles III and then became a French client under Charles IV, losing its fleet at Trafalgar in 1805.
polities.how: The succession war of 1701 to 1714 cost Spain its European possessions outside the peninsula and gave the Bourbons a centralised state.
polities.next: Napoleon's seizure of the throne in 1808 begins the Peninsular War and the independence of Spanish America.

polities.t: Spain in the age of revolutions
polities.gov: Constitutional monarchy under the 1812 and later constitutions, interrupted by absolutism, pronunciamientos and a short republic in 1873
polities.head: Ferdinand VII, Isabella II, Amadeo I, the First Republic
polities.rel: Catholic; Church lands sold off from 1836
polities.econ: Loss of the American colonies by 1825; late and partial industrialisation in Catalonia and the Basque country
polities.now: A country that lost its continental American empire in fifteen years and has spent the rest of the century in civil wars between liberals and Carlists, with the army deciding governments.
polities.how: The war against Napoleon produced the liberal constitution of 1812; Ferdinand VII revoked it, and the pattern of coup and counter-coup set in.
polities.next: The Bourbon restoration of 1874 brings a managed two-party system that lasts until 1923.

polities.t: Restoration Spain and the Second Republic
polities.gov: Constitutional monarchy with managed elections to 1923; Primo de Rivera's dictatorship 1923 to 1930; republic from 1931
polities.head: Alfonso XII, Alfonso XIII; presidents of the republic from 1931
polities.rel: Catholic; the republic's anticlerical laws of 1931 to 1933
polities.econ: Cuba and the Philippines lost to the United States in 1898; neutral and profitable in 1914 to 1918
polities.now: The defeat of 1898 ended the overseas empire and discredited the political system; the Second Republic of 1931 tries land reform, regional autonomy and secularisation against a hostile army and Church.
polities.how: The restoration settlement rotated two parties by fixed elections; Morocco's Rif war and labour unrest brought the dictatorship; the king left in 1931.
polities.next: A military rising in July 1936 begins a three-year civil war that Franco wins.

polities.gov: Military dictatorship; single party; Franco as head of state for life
polities.head: Francisco Franco
polities.rel: Catholic church restored as a pillar of the regime
polities.econ: Autarky to 1959, then rapid growth with tourism and foreign investment
polities.now: Franco's regime won the civil war with German and Italian help, stayed out of the Second World War, was isolated after it, and was rehabilitated by the United States in 1953 for its bases. Growth from 1960 created the middle class that would inherit the state.
polities.how: The rising of July 1936 and three years of war killed about 500,000; repression continued into the 1940s.
polities.next: Franco dies in November 1975; King Juan Carlos and Adolfo Suárez steer a negotiated transition to democracy by 1978.

polities.gov: Parliamentary constitutional monarchy; constitution of 1978; seventeen autonomous communities
polities.head: Juan Carlos I to 2014, Felipe VI; prime ministers
polities.rel: Secular state; Catholic heritage
polities.econ: Fourth-largest eurozone economy; tourism, cars, renewables; joined the European Community in 1986
polities.now: A consolidated democracy and EU member with the Catalan question unresolved after the 2017 independence attempt, and unemployment that stays high in every downturn.
polities.how: The transition of 1976 to 1978, a failed coup in 1981, and accession to NATO and the EC anchored the new regime.
polities.next: Demography, regional finance and housing are the standing problems; Catalonia's status the political one.

polities.t: Kingdom of Portugal, the Avis dynasty
polities.gov: Hereditary monarchy with a Cortes
polities.head: John I to Sebastian and Henry
polities.rel: Catholic; Jews forcibly converted 1497
polities.econ: Sea route to India from 1498; pepper, African gold and slaves; Lisbon the spice market of Europe
polities.now: A small kingdom that mapped the Atlantic and Indian Ocean coasts, took Ceuta in 1415, reached India in 1498 and holds a chain of fortified ports from Mozambique to Macau.
polities.how: Henry the Navigator's voyages, the papal division of 1494 with Spain, and Vasco da Gama's route built a sea empire on a small population.
polities.next: King Sebastian's death in Morocco in 1578 leaves no heir; Philip II of Spain takes the crown in 1580.

polities.gov: Personal union with Spain; separate laws and offices
polities.head: Philip II, III and IV of Spain as kings of Portugal
polities.rel: Catholic
polities.econ: The Dutch seize Portuguese posts in Asia and Brazil's sugar coast in the 1630s
polities.now: Sixty years as a Habsburg possession that drew Portugal into Spain's wars and cost it Hormuz, Malacca and northern Brazil to the Dutch.
polities.how: Philip II claimed the crown by inheritance and arms in 1580.
polities.next: A noble revolt in December 1640 restores an independent king, John IV of Braganza.

polities.t: Kingdom of Portugal, the Braganza dynasty
polities.gov: Absolute monarchy; the marquis of Pombal governs for Joseph I from 1750 to 1777
polities.head: John IV to John VI
polities.cap: Lisbon; the court in Rio de Janeiro from 1808 to 1821
polities.rel: Catholic; Jesuits expelled 1759
polities.econ: Brazilian gold from the 1690s and the Methuen treaty of 1703 tie Portugal to British trade
polities.now: A kingdom living on Brazil's gold and the British alliance; Pombal rebuilt Lisbon after the 1755 earthquake and centralised the state; the royal family fled to Brazil ahead of Napoleon in 1807.
polities.how: Independence was secured by 1668; Brazilian gold funded the monarchy; Britain's navy protected it.
polities.next: The liberal revolution of 1820 recalls the king; Brazil declares independence in 1822.

polities.gov: Constitutional monarchy after civil war between liberals and absolutists; rotating parties from 1851
polities.head: Pedro IV, Maria II, Luís I, Carlos I, Manuel II
polities.rel: Catholic
polities.econ: Small, agrarian; the African colonies claimed in the scramble; the British ultimatum of 1890 humiliates the crown
polities.now: A weak constitutional monarchy that lost Brazil, fought a civil war over the constitution, and holds Angola and Mozambique on paper more than in fact.
polities.how: The liberal victory of 1834 ended absolutism; the regenerators and progressives alternated in office; the 1890 ultimatum and debt default in 1892 undermined the monarchy.
polities.next: The king is assassinated in 1908; a republican revolution follows in October 1910.

polities.t: First Republic and the Estado Novo
polities.gov: Unstable parliamentary republic to 1926; military rule, then Salazar's corporatist dictatorship from 1933
polities.head: Presidents; António de Oliveira Salazar, prime minister 1932 to 1968; Marcelo Caetano to 1974
polities.rel: Catholic; the republic anticlerical, Salazar's state aligned with the Church
polities.econ: Poor and agrarian; emigration to France and Brazil; colonial wars from 1961 consume the budget
polities.now: Western Europe's longest dictatorship, neutral in the Second World War, a NATO founder, and from 1961 fighting three colonial wars in Angola, Guinea and Mozambique that it cannot win.
polities.how: Sixteen years of republican chaos ended in the coup of 1926; Salazar, a finance professor, built a regime of order, censorship and balanced budgets.
polities.next: Junior officers overthrow the regime on 25 April 1974; the colonies are independent within eighteen months.

polities.gov: Semi-presidential parliamentary republic; constitution of 1976
polities.head: President; prime minister
polities.rel: Catholic majority; secular state
polities.econ: EU member since 1986; tourism, services, cork and wine; bailed out in 2011, recovered after 2015
polities.now: A democracy consolidated after the Carnation Revolution and anchored by the EU, with low wages by western European standards and a population that emigrates in every downturn.
polities.how: The revolution of 1974, decolonisation in 1975, and the constitution of 1976 settled the regime; EC accession in 1986 settled its direction.
polities.next: Housing, wages and demography are the standing problems.

polities.gov: Elective monarchy over some 300 princes, bishops and free cities; the Imperial Diet; Habsburg emperors from 1438
polities.head: Emperor Sigismund, Frederick III, Maximilian I
polities.cap: No capital; the emperor's court moved; Diets at Worms, Augsburg, Regensburg
polities.rel: Catholic; Hussite Bohemia in revolt from 1419
polities.econ: Augsburg and Nuremberg banking and metals; the Fuggers finance the emperors
polities.now: A legal framework holding together the German lands, Bohemia, the Low Countries and northern Italy, with real power in the territorial princes. Maximilian's reforms of 1495 created an imperial court and a common peace.
polities.how: The Golden Bull of 1356 fixed the seven electors; the Habsburgs held the title from 1438 and married into Burgundy and Spain.
polities.next: Luther's challenge in 1517 divides the Empire by confession, and the arbitration the emperor provided breaks down.

polities.t: Holy Roman Empire, divided by confession
polities.gov: Elective monarchy; princes choose their territory's religion under the Peace of Augsburg of 1555
polities.head: Charles V, Ferdinand I, Maximilian II, Rudolf II, Matthias, Ferdinand II, Ferdinand III
polities.cap: Vienna and Prague for the Habsburg court
polities.rel: Catholic and Lutheran by territory; Calvinist princes outside the 1555 settlement
polities.pop: About 20 million before 1618; a fifth to a third dead by 1648
polities.econ: The Thirty Years' War devastates the German lands; Swedish and French armies live off the country
polities.now: The Reformation split the princes into confessional camps that no imperial institution could arbitrate, and the Bohemian revolt of 1618 became a thirty-year European war fought on German soil.
polities.how: Charles V failed to crush the Lutheran princes; Augsburg in 1555 froze a division that Calvinism and Habsburg recovery then unfroze.
polities.next: The Peace of Westphalia in 1648 fixes German fragmentation in law and makes it a European interest.

polities.gov: A loose federation of some 300 sovereign estates under a Habsburg emperor; the Diet permanent at Regensburg from 1663
polities.head: Leopold I, Joseph I, Charles VI
polities.rel: Catholic, Lutheran and Calvinist territories under the 1648 guarantee
polities.econ: Recovery from the war; Brandenburg-Prussia and Saxony rise as the strongest princes
polities.now: The Empire survives as a frame rather than a state: France and Sweden guarantee its constitution, the princes make their own alliances, and the emperor's real power lies in his Austrian, Bohemian and Hungarian lands.
polities.how: Westphalia gave the estates sovereignty in all but name; Leopold I held off the Ottomans at Vienna in 1683 and won Hungary.
polities.next: Prussia's rise under Frederick the Great from 1740 makes the Empire a dualism of Austria and Prussia until Napoleon dissolves it in 1806.

polities.gov: Habsburg hereditary monarchy; constitutional from 1867 as the Dual Monarchy of Austria-Hungary
polities.head: Leopold I to Franz Joseph (1848 to 1916) and Charles I
polities.cap: Vienna; Budapest the Hungarian capital after 1867
polities.rel: Catholic; Protestants and Jews emancipated by the 1860s; Orthodox and Muslim subjects in the south
polities.econ: Agrarian with industrial Bohemia and Vienna; the Danube; the Compromise of 1867 created a customs union of two states
polities.now: A dynastic state ruling Germans, Hungarians, Czechs, Poles, Croats, Slovenes, Italians, Romanians and others. After losing the German question to Prussia in 1866 it compromised with Hungary, turned toward the Balkans, and annexed Bosnia in 1908.
polities.how: The Habsburgs held off the Ottomans at Vienna in 1683, took Hungary, survived Napoleon under Metternich's system, and crushed the 1848 revolutions with Russian help.
polities.next: The assassination of Franz Ferdinand in June 1914 produces the ultimatum to Serbia; the monarchy dissolves into successor states in November 1918.

polities.gov: Parliamentary republic to 1934, then the authoritarian 'corporate state' of Dollfuss and Schuschnigg
polities.head: Presidents; chancellors Seipel, Dollfuss, Schuschnigg
polities.rel: Catholic
polities.econ: A capital city without an empire; hyperinflation 1922, League loan, bank collapse of Creditanstalt in 1931
polities.now: The German-speaking remnant of the Habsburg monarchy, forbidden to join Germany by the peace treaty, split between socialist Vienna and the Catholic countryside, and after the 1934 civil war a one-party state resisting Hitler.
polities.how: The monarchy's collapse left a state most of whose citizens wanted union with Germany; the 1934 fighting ended parliamentary rule.
polities.next: German troops enter in March 1938 and Austria is annexed as the Ostmark.

polities.gov: Federal parliamentary republic; permanent neutrality declared 1955
polities.head: Federal president; chancellor
polities.rel: Catholic majority; secular state
polities.econ: Prosperous, with Vienna as a seat of UN agencies and OPEC; EU member since 1995
polities.now: Restored in 1945 under four-power occupation and independent by the State Treaty of 1955 on condition of neutrality; a stable, wealthy EU member whose politics turn on immigration.
polities.how: The Moscow Declaration of 1943 treated Austria as Hitler's first victim; the grand coalition of the two main parties governed for most of the postwar decades.
polities.next: Neutrality's meaning inside the EU and the far right's strength are the live questions.

polities.gov: Hohenzollern electorate of Brandenburg joined to the duchy of Prussia from 1618; the estates subdued after 1653
polities.head: Electors of Brandenburg; Frederick William, the Great Elector, 1640 to 1688
polities.rel: Lutheran, with a Calvinist dynasty from 1613; Huguenot refugees welcomed 1685
polities.econ: Poor sandy soil; the state's wealth is its army and administration
polities.now: A scattered Hohenzollern inheritance from the Rhine to the Niemen, which the Great Elector turned into a militarised state with a standing army of 30,000 and a tax system to pay it.
polities.how: Brandenburg gained Prussia by inheritance in 1618 and eastern Pomerania at Westphalia; the Great Elector's victories over Sweden made the army the state's core.
polities.next: The elector crowns himself King in Prussia in 1701.

polities.gov: Absolute monarchy built on the army and a professional bureaucracy
polities.head: Frederick I, Frederick William I, Frederick II (the Great), Frederick William II and III
polities.rel: Lutheran and Calvinist; religious toleration as state policy
polities.econ: The army takes most of the budget; Silesia's textiles and mines after 1742
polities.now: A kingdom that took Silesia from Austria in 1740, survived the Seven Years' War against three empires, partitioned Poland, and after collapsing before Napoleon in 1806 rebuilt itself through the Stein-Hardenberg reforms.
polities.how: Frederick William I built the army and the civil service; Frederick II used them to make Prussia a great power.
polities.next: The Congress of Vienna gives Prussia the Rhineland and the task of guarding the west against France.

polities.gov: Monarchy with a constitution from 1850; Bismarck governs without a budget from 1862
polities.head: Frederick William III and IV, William I; Otto von Bismarck minister-president from 1862
polities.rel: Protestant union church; Catholic Rhineland
polities.econ: The Zollverein from 1834 unites the German economy under Prussian leadership; Ruhr coal and steel; railways
polities.now: The strongest German state after Austria, leading the customs union, and from 1862 under a minister who settles the German question by three wars: Denmark 1864, Austria 1866, France 1870.
polities.how: The Vienna settlement gave Prussia the Rhineland's industry; the 1848 revolution failed to unify Germany by assembly; Bismarck did it by Prussian arms.
polities.next: The German Empire is proclaimed at Versailles in January 1871 with the Prussian king as emperor.

polities.gov: Federal constitutional monarchy of 25 states; the Reichstag elected by universal male suffrage but the chancellor answerable to the Kaiser
polities.head: William I, Frederick III, William II; chancellors Bismarck to 1890, then Caprivi, Hohenlohe, Bülow, Bethmann Hollweg
polities.rel: Protestant majority; Catholic third; Jews about one per cent
polities.econ: Overtook Britain in steel by 1893 and in industry by 1914; chemicals, electricals, the largest Social Democratic party in the world
polities.now: The strongest economy and army on the continent, with a constitution that gave the army and the Kaiser control of foreign policy and left the Reichstag the budget. Bismarck's alliances kept France isolated until 1890; after his dismissal the Franco-Russian alliance and the naval race with Britain followed.
polities.how: Three wars united Germany under Prussia; Bismarck's constitution and alliance system held the settlement for twenty years.
polities.next: Defeat in November 1918 ends the monarchy; the republic signs the Treaty of Versailles.

polities.gov: Parliamentary democracy with proportional representation and a directly elected president holding emergency powers
polities.head: Presidents Ebert and Hindenburg; chancellors Stresemann, Brüning and others
polities.rel: Protestant majority, Catholic third
polities.econ: Hyperinflation 1923; recovery on American loans 1924 to 1929; six million unemployed by 1932
polities.now: A republic born of defeat, burdened with reparations, which stabilised after 1924 and was broken by the Depression. From 1930 it is governed by presidential decree while the Nazis and Communists win the streets and the votes.
polities.how: The revolution of November 1918 and the treaty of 1919 fixed the republic's enemies; American credit sustained the good years; the crash of 1929 called the loans in.
polities.next: Hindenburg appoints Hitler chancellor on 30 January 1933.

polities.gov: One-party dictatorship; the Führer principle; the Enabling Act of March 1933
polities.head: Adolf Hitler, chancellor and from 1934 Führer
polities.rel: Churches subordinated; Jews stripped of citizenship 1935; the Holocaust from 1941
polities.pop: About 69 million in 1939; 80 million with Austria and the Sudetenland
polities.econ: Rearmament and autarky; forced labour and plunder in occupied Europe
polities.now: A regime that rebuilt the army in violation of Versailles, annexed Austria and Czechoslovakia, invaded Poland in 1939, conquered most of Europe by 1941, and murdered six million Jews. The war it chose in the east destroyed it.
polities.how: The Depression and conservative miscalculation gave Hitler the chancellorship; the Reichstag fire and the Enabling Act gave him the state.
polities.next: Unconditional surrender in May 1945; four-power occupation; two German states from 1949.

polities.gov: Parliamentary federal democracy under the Basic Law of 1949; a chancellor answerable to the Bundestag
polities.head: Chancellors Adenauer, Erhard, Kiesinger, Brandt, Schmidt, Kohl
polities.rel: Catholic and Protestant in roughly equal numbers
polities.econ: The economic miracle of the 1950s; the Deutsche Mark; founding member of the European Communities; export industry
polities.now: The western two-thirds of Germany, bound into NATO and the European Community by Adenauer, reconciled with France, and from Brandt's Ostpolitik in 1970 dealing with the East on the basis of the division it did not accept in law.
polities.how: The western occupation zones merged in 1949; the Marshall Plan and currency reform of 1948 launched the recovery; rearmament and NATO membership came in 1955.
polities.next: The Berlin Wall opens in November 1989; the East joins the Federal Republic in October 1990.

polities.gov: One-party communist state under the Socialist Unity Party
polities.head: Walter Ulbricht, Erich Honecker
polities.rel: Protestant tradition; churches tolerated and watched
polities.econ: The most industrialised Soviet-bloc economy, falling behind the West; the Wall from 1961 stops emigration
polities.now: The Soviet zone made a state in 1949, which built the Berlin Wall in 1961 to stop a third of its people leaving, and depends on Soviet troops and West German credits.
polities.how: The Soviet occupation installed a communist regime; the 1953 rising was crushed by Soviet tanks.
polities.next: Mass demonstrations in autumn 1989 and the opening of the Wall end the regime; unification follows in October 1990.

polities.gov: Parliamentary federal democracy; sixteen states
polities.head: Chancellors Kohl, Schröder, Merkel (2005 to 2021), Scholz, Merz
polities.rel: Christian plurality, large non-religious share in the east, Muslim minority
polities.econ: Europe's largest economy; cars, machinery, chemicals; the euro from 1999; dependence on Russian gas until 2022
polities.now: The united Germany is the EU's central power and reluctant leader: it paid for unification, anchored the euro, took in a million refugees in 2015, and after Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022 declared a turning point in defence spending.
polities.how: Unification in 1990 was agreed by four outside powers; Kohl traded the Deutsche Mark for the euro as the price of French consent.
polities.next: The old question, a country too large for Europe to balance and too small to lead it alone, is being answered in defence budgets and European debt.

polities.gov: Aristocratic republic; the Great Council of patrician families elects a doge for life
polities.head: Doge; the Council of Ten holds security
polities.rel: Catholic, with the state firmly above the Church
polities.pop: About 150,000 in the city; 1.5 million in its mainland and overseas territories
polities.econ: Spice and silk trade with the Levant, the Arsenal shipyard, glass, printing
polities.now: The richest trading republic of the Mediterranean, holding a mainland state in the Veneto and islands from Crete to the Ionian Sea, in a long retreat before the Ottomans and the Portuguese spice route.
polities.how: Venice built its empire on the Byzantine trade and the Fourth Crusade of 1204; the League of Cambrai nearly destroyed it in 1509.
polities.next: Loss of Crete in 1669 and the Morea in 1718 end the eastern empire; Napoleon abolishes the republic in 1797.

polities.gov: Elective theocratic monarchy; the pope as temporal sovereign
polities.head: The pope, elected by the cardinals
polities.rel: Catholic
polities.econ: Pilgrims, church revenues from all of Catholic Europe, a backward agrarian hinterland
polities.now: A middle-sized Italian state ruled by the pope, whose spiritual authority over Catholic Europe far exceeds his armies. Napoleon annexed it in 1809; the Congress of Vienna restored it.
polities.how: Popes consolidated central Italy from the fifteenth century; the Renaissance papacy rebuilt Rome; the Reformation halved Rome's obedience.
polities.next: Italian unification takes most of the state in 1860 and Rome itself in 1870; the Lateran Treaty of 1929 creates Vatican City.

polities.gov: Kingdoms under Aragonese, then Spanish, Austrian and Bourbon rule; viceroys for absentee kings until 1734
polities.head: Spanish Habsburg viceroys to 1707; Bourbon kings from 1734
polities.rel: Catholic
polities.pop: About 4 million in Naples, 1.5 million in Sicily around 1750
polities.econ: Grain, silk, olive oil; a feudal countryside and one of Europe's largest cities
polities.now: The south of Italy, a possession of foreign crowns for three centuries, with Naples the largest city in Italy and a landed baronage that outlasts every ruler.
polities.how: Aragon took Sicily in 1282 and Naples in 1442; Spain ruled both through viceroys until the succession war gave them to Austria, then to a Bourbon prince in 1734.
polities.next: The Bourbons are restored in 1815 as the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies and overthrown by Garibaldi in 1860.

polities.gov: Republic dominated by the Medici to 1530; Medici grand duchy from 1569; Habsburg-Lorraine from 1737
polities.head: Cosimo and Lorenzo de' Medici; the grand dukes
polities.rel: Catholic
polities.econ: Banking, wool and silk; the Medici bank the largest in Europe in the fifteenth century
polities.now: The city of the Renaissance, governed by a banking family that became a ducal dynasty; under the Lorraine grand dukes after 1737 it is the best-administered state in Italy.
polities.how: Medici money bought the republic; Charles V's siege of 1530 ended it; Leopold of Lorraine abolished torture and the death penalty in 1786.
polities.next: Annexed by Piedmont in 1860 in the unification of Italy.

polities.gov: Visconti then Sforza duchy; Spanish rule 1535 to 1706; Austrian rule from 1714
polities.head: Dukes of Milan; Spanish and Austrian governors
polities.rel: Catholic
polities.econ: The richest agriculture in Italy; silk; Austrian reforms of the eighteenth century
polities.now: The gateway between the Alps and Italy, fought over by France and Spain in the Italian Wars and held by Spain then Austria for three centuries.
polities.how: The Sforza dukes lost it to France and Spain in the wars after 1494; the Spanish succession war transferred it to Austria.
polities.next: Austrian rule ends in 1859 when France and Piedmont win at Solferino.

polities.gov: Oligarchic republic; a doge elected for two years after 1528
polities.head: Doge; the Bank of Saint George
polities.rel: Catholic
polities.econ: Bankers to the Spanish crown; Corsica held until 1768
polities.now: Venice's old rival, which lost its eastern trade and became the financier of Habsburg Spain under Andrea Doria's constitution of 1528.
polities.how: Doria took Genoa into the Spanish alliance; Genoese bankers moved Spanish silver across Europe for a century.
polities.next: Napoleon turns the republic into the Ligurian Republic in 1797; Vienna gives Genoa to Piedmont in 1815.

polities.t: Savoy, later the Kingdom of Sardinia
polities.gov: Duchy of Savoy; royal title from 1720; constitutional monarchy from 1848
polities.head: Dukes of Savoy; kings Victor Amadeus II to Victor Emmanuel II; Cavour prime minister 1852 to 1861
polities.rel: Catholic
polities.econ: Alpine passes, silk, the first Italian railways; Cavour's free-trade reforms
polities.now: An Alpine duchy that became a kingdom in 1720 and under Cavour the one Italian state with a constitution, an army and a foreign policy, which it used to unify Italy.
polities.how: Savoy traded its mountain position between France and the Habsburgs for territory for three centuries; the 1848 constitution survived where others fell.
polities.next: With French help it defeats Austria in 1859 and annexes the peninsula; the Kingdom of Italy is proclaimed in March 1861.

polities.gov: Constitutional monarchy under the Piedmontese statute; narrow franchise widened to near-universal male suffrage in 1912
polities.head: Victor Emmanuel II, Umberto I, Victor Emmanuel III; prime ministers Cavour, Crispi, Giolitti
polities.rel: Catholic; the pope refuses to recognise the state until 1929
polities.econ: Industrial north, agrarian south; mass emigration to the Americas; late colonial acquisitions in Eritrea, Somalia and Libya
polities.now: A united state whose north and south remain two countries, which took Rome in 1870, lost to Ethiopia at Adwa in 1896, conquered Libya in 1911, and entered the First World War in 1915 for territory it mostly received.
polities.how: Cavour's diplomacy and Garibaldi's expedition unified the peninsula in 1860 and 1861.
polities.next: Mussolini's March on Rome in October 1922 brings the Fascists to power with the king's consent.

polities.gov: One-party dictatorship under the monarchy; Mussolini as Duce
polities.head: Benito Mussolini; Victor Emmanuel III as king
polities.rel: Catholic; the Lateran Treaty of 1929 settles the Roman question
polities.econ: Corporatist economy; conquest of Ethiopia 1935 to 1936; sanctions; dependence on Germany
polities.now: The first fascist regime, which crushed opposition by 1926, conquered Ethiopia, intervened in Spain, allied with Hitler in 1939, and entered the war in June 1940 without the means to fight it.
polities.how: Postwar disorder and elite fear of socialism opened the door; the Matteotti murder of 1924 and the laws of 1925 closed it.
polities.next: Mussolini is dismissed in July 1943 after the Allied landing in Sicily; a referendum abolishes the monarchy in 1946.

polities.gov: Parliamentary republic; frequent governments, stable institutions
polities.head: President; prime minister
polities.rel: Catholic majority; secular state
polities.econ: Third-largest eurozone economy; machinery, fashion, food; public debt among the highest in the EU; the north-south gap persists
polities.now: A founding member of NATO and the European Community that has had about seventy governments since 1946, destroyed its old party system in the corruption trials of 1992, and has had the slowest growth in the eurozone since the euro.
polities.how: The referendum of 1946 chose the republic; Christian Democracy governed to 1992; the euro removed devaluation as a policy tool.
polities.next: Debt, demography and migration across the Mediterranean are the standing questions.

polities.gov: Seventeen provinces under the Spanish Habsburgs, each with its own estates; a governor-general in Brussels
polities.head: Charles V, then Philip II of Spain; governors Margaret of Parma, Alba, Parma
polities.rel: Catholic by law; Calvinism spreading from the 1560s
polities.pop: About 3 million, the most urbanised region in Europe
polities.econ: Antwerp the commercial capital of northern Europe until 1585
polities.now: The richest provinces of the Spanish crown, in open revolt from 1568 against taxation and religious persecution; by 1600 the north has broken away and Antwerp has fallen to Spain.
polities.how: Philip II's centralisation and the Inquisition provoked the revolt; Alba's repression spread it; the north's river barrier and sea power held it.
polities.next: The Twelve Years' Truce of 1609 recognises the Dutch Republic in practice; Westphalia in 1648 does so in law.

polities.gov: Confederation of seven provinces under the States General; the stadtholder of the House of Orange as military chief, with periods of no stadtholder
polities.head: Stadtholders Maurice, Frederick Henry, William III; grand pensionaries Oldenbarnevelt and De Witt
polities.cap: The Hague for government; Amsterdam for money
polities.rel: Calvinist public church; toleration in practice for Catholics, Jews and dissenters
polities.econ: The richest economy per head in Europe: the Baltic trade, the East India Company from 1602, the Amsterdam exchange and bank
polities.now: A merchant republic that fought Spain to independence, built the largest fleet and the first joint-stock empire, and in the eighteenth century lives on its capital as Britain overtakes it.
polities.how: The revolt secured the north by 1600; the Golden Age ran to the French invasion of 1672; the Orangist-republican quarrel continued throughout.
polities.next: French armies install the Batavian Republic in 1795; a kingdom under the House of Orange follows in 1815.

polities.gov: Constitutional monarchy since 1815; parliamentary government since 1848; coalition politics
polities.head: Kings and queens of the House of Orange-Nassau; prime minister
polities.cap: Amsterdam, with government at The Hague
polities.rel: Historically Calvinist and Catholic in pillars; majority non-religious today
polities.econ: Trading and financial economy; Rotterdam the largest port in Europe; natural gas; EU founding member
polities.now: A kingdom that held the East Indies until 1949, stayed neutral in the First World War and was occupied in the Second, and since 1945 has been among the most open economies in the world.
polities.how: The Congress of Vienna created the kingdom with Belgium, which left in 1830; the constitution of 1848 made ministers answerable to parliament.
polities.next: Housing, nitrogen limits on farming, and migration dominate current politics.

polities.gov: Habsburg province governed from Vienna through a governor in Brussels; the provincial estates kept their privileges
polities.head: Charles VI, Maria Theresa, Joseph II; governors in Brussels
polities.rel: Catholic
polities.econ: Flemish textiles; the Scheldt closed to trade by the Dutch
polities.now: The southern Netherlands, transferred from Spain to Austria in 1714, prosperous and conservative, in revolt in 1789 against Joseph II's reforms.
polities.how: The Spanish succession war gave the provinces to Austria; the barrier fortresses were garrisoned by the Dutch.
polities.next: France annexes the provinces in 1795; they are joined to the Netherlands in 1815 and become Belgium in 1830.

polities.gov: Constitutional monarchy; federal state of Flanders, Wallonia and Brussels since 1993
polities.head: Leopold I to Philippe; prime minister
polities.cap: Brussels, also the seat of the EU institutions and NATO
polities.rel: Catholic tradition; secular state
polities.econ: The first industrial economy on the continent; the Congo as the king's personal possession 1885 to 1908, then a colony to 1960
polities.now: Created by revolution in 1830 and neutral by treaty, invaded by Germany in 1914 and 1940, and since 1945 the host of the European institutions, with a language divide that has driven six state reforms.
polities.how: The revolt against Dutch rule won great-power recognition in 1839; Leopold II's Congo regime killed millions; the Flemish movement reshaped the state after 1945.
polities.next: The Flemish-Walloon divide and the cost of federal coalition-building are the standing problems.

polities.gov: Grand duchy since 1815; constitutional monarchy; parliamentary government
polities.head: Grand duke; prime minister
polities.rel: Catholic tradition
polities.econ: Steel until the 1970s, then banking and funds; the richest country per head in the EU
polities.now: A fortress city-state passed among Spain, Austria, France and the Netherlands, independent since 1867, and a founder of the European institutions it now hosts in part.
polities.how: The Congress of Vienna made it a grand duchy in personal union with the Dutch king; the London treaty of 1867 neutralised and demilitarised it.
polities.next: Its finance-centre model depends on EU tax rules it does not control.

polities.gov: Confederation of cantons; federal state since 1848 with direct democracy by referendum
polities.head: Federal Council of seven, with a rotating president
polities.rel: Catholic and Protestant cantons since the Reformation
polities.econ: Banking, pharmaceuticals, machinery, watches; among the richest countries per head
polities.now: A confederation that fought off the Habsburgs, split by Zwingli's and Calvin's Reformation, declared permanent neutrality in 1815, and became a federal republic in 1848 after a short civil war.
polities.how: The Swiss pike squares dominated European battlefields around 1500; the cantons stayed out of the Thirty Years' War; Napoleon's Helvetic Republic of 1798 was short-lived.
polities.next: The relationship with the EU, which it has refused to join, is renegotiated by treaty every few years.

polities.gov: Personal union of Denmark, Norway and Sweden under one monarch, with separate councils
polities.head: Margaret I's successors; Christian II
polities.rel: Catholic
polities.pop: About 1.5 million across the three kingdoms
polities.econ: Baltic herring, the Sound tolls, Hanseatic trade
polities.now: A dynastic union of the three Scandinavian crowns, dominated by Denmark and resented in Sweden, whose nobles revolt repeatedly.
polities.how: Margaret I joined the crowns in 1397 against the Hanseatic League's power.
polities.next: The Stockholm Bloodbath of 1520 provokes Gustav Vasa's revolt; Sweden leaves in 1523.

polities.gov: Elective monarchy until 1660, then hereditary absolute monarchy by law
polities.head: Christian III, Christian IV, Frederick III and successors
polities.rel: Lutheran state church from 1536
polities.pop: About 1.5 million in Denmark and Norway together in 1700
polities.econ: Sound tolls on Baltic shipping; Norwegian timber and fish; colonies in the Caribbean and India
polities.now: A twin kingdom controlling the entrance to the Baltic, Lutheran since 1536, absolutist after the 1660 coup, and on the losing side against Sweden and then Britain, which bombarded Copenhagen in 1807.
polities.how: Christian III imposed the Reformation; Christian IV's wars against Sweden failed; the king and burghers overthrew the nobility's power in 1660.
polities.next: The Treaty of Kiel in 1814 transfers Norway to Sweden; Denmark keeps Iceland, the Faroes and Greenland.

polities.gov: Constitutional monarchy since 1849; parliamentary democracy
polities.head: Monarch; prime minister
polities.rel: Lutheran state church; largely secular society
polities.econ: Agriculture and shipping, then pharmaceuticals and wind power; EU member since 1973 outside the euro
polities.now: A small kingdom that lost Norway in 1814 and Schleswig-Holstein to Prussia in 1864, stayed neutral in 1914, was occupied in 1940, and built one of the world's most complete welfare states.
polities.how: The defeat of 1864 turned Denmark inward; cooperative agriculture and the folk high schools shaped its society.
polities.next: Greenland's status and the welfare state's immigration politics are the live questions.

polities.gov: Constitutional monarchy; parliamentary democracy
polities.head: Monarch; prime minister
polities.rel: Lutheran tradition
polities.econ: Shipping, fish, hydropower; North Sea oil and gas from 1970 and a sovereign fund above a trillion dollars
polities.now: Independent of Sweden since 1905, occupied by Germany from 1940 to 1945, a NATO founder, twice a refuser of EU membership, and the richest country in Scandinavia on oil.
polities.how: The union with Sweden ended by referendum in 1905; the 1814 constitution written at Eidsvoll survived both unions.
polities.next: Managing the oil fund and the end of oil is the long question.

polities.gov: Hereditary monarchy from 1544; absolutism under Charles XI; the Age of Liberty's parliamentary rule 1719 to 1772
polities.head: Gustav Vasa, Gustavus Adolphus, Christina, Charles XI, Charles XII, Gustav III
polities.rel: Lutheran state church
polities.econ: Copper and iron from Falun and Bergslagen; the Baltic empire's tolls
polities.now: A poor northern kingdom that became a great power under Gustavus Adolphus in the Thirty Years' War, held the Baltic coast for a century, and lost it to Russia under Charles XII.
polities.how: Gustav Vasa founded the dynasty and the Lutheran state; Gustavus Adolphus's army and Swedish iron made the empire; Poltava in 1709 broke it.
polities.next: Finland is lost to Russia in 1809; Norway is gained from Denmark in 1814.

polities.gov: Constitutional monarchy; parliamentary democracy; the Social Democrats governed for most of the twentieth century
polities.head: Monarch; prime minister
polities.rel: Lutheran tradition; largely secular
polities.econ: Timber, iron, engineering, Volvo, Ericsson, IKEA; EU member since 1995 outside the euro
polities.now: A neutral for two centuries that built the model welfare state, joined the EU in 1995 and NATO in 2024 after Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
polities.how: The loss of Finland in 1809 ended Sweden's wars; Bernadotte's dynasty and the 1814 union with Norway followed; industrialisation came late and fast.
polities.next: Integration of a large immigrant population and the new NATO commitment are the current tests.

polities.gov: Parliamentary republic since 1919
polities.head: President; prime minister
polities.rel: Lutheran tradition
polities.econ: Forestry, then engineering and Nokia; EU member since 1995, euro since 1999
polities.now: Independent from Russia since December 1917, after a civil war in 1918, two wars with the Soviet Union in 1939 to 1944, and a Cold War of enforced neutrality, Finland joined NATO in 2023.
polities.how: A Swedish province for six centuries and a Russian grand duchy for one, Finland took the chance of the Russian revolution; the Winter War preserved its independence at the price of Karelia.
polities.next: Its 1,300-kilometre border with Russia is now NATO's longest.

polities.gov: Personal union, then the Commonwealth of 1569: an elective monarchy under a parliament of nobles where one deputy's veto could dissolve a session
polities.head: Jagiellon kings to 1572; elected kings including Báthory, Sigismund III, Sobieski, Poniatowski
polities.rel: Catholic majority; Orthodox, Protestant and Jewish communities with legal toleration from 1573
polities.pop: About 11 million in 1650, the largest state in Europe by area
polities.econ: Grain exports down the Vistula to Danzig; the nobility's serf estates
polities.now: A vast noble republic with an elected king and a paralysed parliament, which defeated the Teutonic Knights in 1410, saved Vienna from the Ottomans in 1683, and is partitioned by Russia, Prussia and Austria in 1772, 1793 and 1795.
polities.how: The union of 1386 joined the crowns; the Lublin union of 1569 made one state; the liberum veto and foreign-sponsored elections hollowed it out after 1652.
polities.next: The third partition of 1795 removes Poland from the map until 1918.

polities.gov: Parliamentary republic to 1926; Piłsudski's authoritarian rule after his coup
polities.head: Józef Piłsudski, in power 1926 to 1935; presidents and colonels after
polities.rel: Catholic majority; a third of the population Ukrainian, Jewish, Belarusian or German
polities.econ: Agrarian; Gdynia built as a port; the Depression severe
polities.now: Restored in 1918 and enlarged by the war with Soviet Russia in 1920, Poland sits between a revisionist Germany and a Soviet Union that both want its land.
polities.how: The collapse of all three partitioning empires in 1918 recreated Poland; Piłsudski defeated the Red Army at Warsaw in 1920.
polities.next: Germany and the Soviet Union partition Poland in September 1939; about six million Poles die, half of them Jews.

polities.gov: One-party communist state under Soviet guarantee
polities.head: Bierut, Gomułka, Gierek, Jaruzelski
polities.rel: Catholic church kept its independence; Karol Wojtyła elected pope in 1978
polities.econ: Heavy industry; coal; collectivisation abandoned; hard-currency debt crisis after 1976
polities.now: Shifted 200 kilometres west by the Allies in 1945, communist by Soviet imposition, Poland kept its Church and private farms and produced the revolts of 1956, 1970, 1976 and the Solidarity union of 1980.
polities.how: The Red Army's arrival and the Yalta settlement installed the regime; martial law in December 1981 suppressed Solidarity without ending it.
polities.next: Round-table talks and the election of June 1989 end communist rule; Poland joins NATO in 1999 and the EU in 2004.

polities.gov: Parliamentary republic with a directly elected president
polities.head: President; prime minister
polities.rel: Catholic majority
polities.econ: The fastest-growing large economy in Europe since 1990; EU member since 2004; manufacturing, services, EU funds
polities.now: The success case of post-communist transition, now the EU's front-line state against Russia with the largest army in the union after 2022, and a politics divided between liberal and national-conservative camps.
polities.how: Shock therapy in 1990, NATO in 1999 and EU membership in 2004 set the path.
polities.next: Defence spending, the rule-of-law dispute with Brussels, and Ukraine's war next door shape the decade.

polities.gov: Crusading military order ruling Prussia under a grand master
polities.head: Grand master of the Teutonic Order
polities.rel: Catholic; the last grand master converted to Lutheranism in 1525
polities.econ: Grain and amber; Hanseatic towns Danzig and Elbing
polities.now: A crusader state in Prussia in decline after its defeat by Poland-Lithuania at Grunwald in 1410, losing West Prussia in 1466.
polities.how: The Order conquered the pagan Prussians in the thirteenth century; Lithuania's conversion removed its purpose.
polities.next: Albert of Hohenzollern secularises the Order's lands as the Duchy of Prussia in 1525, under Polish suzerainty.

polities.gov: Elective monarchy with a powerful noble diet
polities.head: Sigismund, Matthias Corvinus (1458 to 1490), the Jagiellon kings
polities.rel: Catholic
polities.econ: Gold and silver mines in Upper Hungary; cattle exports
polities.now: The strongest state in central Europe under Matthias Corvinus, with a professional Black Army and a Renaissance court, then weakened by noble reaction under the Jagiellons.
polities.how: Matthias built a standing army and taxed the nobles; his successors dismantled both.
polities.next: The Ottomans destroy the Hungarian army at Mohács in 1526; the kingdom is divided among Habsburgs, Ottomans and Transylvania for 160 years.

polities.gov: Kingdom without a king; Admiral Horthy as regent; limited parliamentary rule
polities.head: Miklós Horthy, regent 1920 to 1944
polities.rel: Catholic majority, Calvinist minority; anti-Jewish laws from 1938
polities.econ: Agrarian; lost two-thirds of its territory and population at Trianon in 1920
polities.now: A truncated state whose politics are built on revising the Treaty of Trianon, which took it into Hitler's alliance to recover land from Czechoslovakia, Romania and Yugoslavia.
polities.how: The Habsburg collapse, a Soviet republic under Béla Kun in 1919, and Romanian occupation produced the Horthy regime.
polities.next: Germany occupies Hungary in March 1944; about 440,000 Hungarian Jews are deported to Auschwitz; the Red Army takes Budapest in 1945.

polities.gov: One-party communist state
polities.head: Rákosi; János Kádár 1956 to 1988
polities.rel: Catholic majority; churches controlled
polities.econ: 'Goulash communism': the New Economic Mechanism of 1968 allowed market elements
polities.now: Communist by Soviet imposition, Hungary rose in October 1956 and was crushed by Soviet tanks; Kádár then bought consent with consumer goods and a limited market.
polities.how: The 1956 revolution killed about 2,500 and sent 200,000 into exile; Kádár's regime followed.
polities.next: Hungary opens its border with Austria in 1989, letting East Germans out; free elections follow in 1990.

polities.gov: Parliamentary republic; since 2010 an 'illiberal democracy' under Viktor Orbán's two-thirds majorities
polities.head: President; prime minister Orbán since 2010
polities.rel: Catholic and Calvinist tradition
polities.econ: German car plants; EU funds, partly frozen over rule-of-law disputes
polities.now: An EU and NATO member since 2004 and 1999 whose government has rewritten the constitution, captured the media and courts, and positioned itself between Brussels and Moscow.
polities.how: Orbán's Fidesz won a constitutional majority in 2010 after the socialists' collapse and has kept it.
polities.next: Whether the system outlasts its builder is the open question.

polities.gov: Parliamentary democracy 1918 to 1938; communist one-party state from 1948
polities.head: Masaryk, Beneš; Gottwald, Novotný
polities.rel: Catholic majority; strong secular tradition
polities.econ: The industrial core of the old Habsburg monarchy: Škoda, Bata, armaments
polities.now: The one east-central European democracy that lasted between the wars, abandoned at Munich in 1938, occupied in 1939, and taken by communist coup in February 1948.
polities.how: Masaryk's state was built from Czech and Slovak lands with large German and Hungarian minorities; the Sudeten crisis destroyed it.
polities.next: The Prague Spring of 1968 is crushed by Warsaw Pact invasion; the Velvet Revolution of 1989 ends communism; the state splits peacefully in 1993.

polities.gov: Parliamentary republic
polities.head: President; prime minister
polities.rel: Majority non-religious
polities.econ: Cars and engineering; EU member since 2004 outside the euro
polities.now: The western half of Czechoslovakia since the Velvet Divorce of 1993, among the most industrialised and least religious countries in Europe.
polities.how: The 1989 revolution under Havel and the 1992 agreement to separate from Slovakia produced the state.
polities.next: Energy independence from Russia and euro adoption are the pending decisions.

polities.gov: Parliamentary republic
polities.head: President; prime minister
polities.rel: Catholic majority
polities.econ: The world's largest car output per head; EU member since 2004, euro since 2009
polities.now: Independent since 1993, a clerical-fascist satellite in 1939 to 1945, and since 2004 an EU member whose politics swing between pro-Western and Russia-leaning populist governments.
polities.how: Slovak nationalism inside Czechoslovakia produced the 1993 separation.
polities.next: Its stance on Ukraine and the rule of law under Fico's governments is watched in Brussels.

polities.rx: ^grand duchy of moscow$|^white horde$|^golden horde$|^blue horde$
polities.gov: Grand princes of Moscow, tributaries of the Golden Horde until 1480; autocracy under Ivan III
polities.head: Vasily I, Vasily II, Ivan III (1462 to 1505), Vasily III
polities.rel: Orthodox; Moscow claims to be the Third Rome after Constantinople's fall in 1453
polities.econ: Furs, grain, the Volga trade
polities.now: The principality that collected the Russian lands, took Novgorod in 1478, stopped paying tribute to the Horde in 1480, and under Ivan III adopted the Byzantine double eagle and the claim to all Rus.
polities.how: Moscow's princes served the Mongols as tax collectors and used the position to absorb their rivals.
polities.next: Ivan IV is crowned tsar in 1547 and conquers the Volga khanates of Kazan and Astrakhan.

polities.gov: Autocracy; the Zemsky Sobor assembly occasionally called; serfdom fixed in law by 1649
polities.head: Ivan IV (the Terrible), the Time of Troubles, the Romanovs from 1613, Peter I from 1682
polities.rel: Orthodox; the Old Believer schism after the 1660s reforms
polities.econ: Furs from Siberia, conquered from 1582 to the Pacific by 1640; grain; Archangel the only port until Peter
polities.now: An expanding autocracy that reached the Pacific, survived the Time of Troubles and Polish occupation of Moscow in 1610 to 1612, bound its peasants to the land, and under Peter I is being forced into European form.
polities.how: Ivan IV's conquests and terror, the dynasty's failure in 1598, and the Romanov restoration of 1613 shaped the state; Peter's reforms began with the Azov campaigns of 1695.
polities.next: Victory over Sweden at Poltava in 1709 and the Treaty of Nystad in 1721 make Russia a European power; Peter proclaims the empire in 1721.

polities.gov: Autocracy; serfdom abolished 1861; a Duma with limited powers from 1906
polities.head: Peter I, Catherine II, Alexander I, Nicholas I, Alexander II, Alexander III, Nicholas II
polities.rel: Orthodox state church; Muslim, Catholic, Lutheran and Jewish subjects; the Pale of Settlement
polities.pop: About 20 million in 1750, 70 million in 1860, 170 million in 1914
polities.econ: Grain exports, state-driven industrialisation from the 1890s with French loans; the Trans-Siberian railway
polities.now: The largest state on earth, from Warsaw to Alaska at its peak, with a huge peasant army and a backward economy; it beat Napoleon, lost the Crimean War, freed the serfs, lost to Japan in 1905, and entered the First World War with a parliament it ignored.
polities.how: Peter and Catherine built the empire by war against Sweden, the Ottomans and Poland; the reforms of the 1860s followed defeat in Crimea; the 1905 revolution produced the Duma.
polities.next: The February Revolution of 1917 ends the monarchy; the Bolsheviks take power in October.

polities.gov: One-party communist state; the Politburo of the Communist Party rules; federal in form
polities.head: Lenin, Stalin (1924 to 1953), Khrushchev, Brezhnev, Andropov, Chernenko, Gorbachev
polities.rel: State atheism; churches persecuted, then tolerated after 1943
polities.econ: Five-year plans from 1928; forced collectivisation and famine 1932 to 1933; oil and gas exports from the 1970s
polities.now: The Bolshevik state that won the civil war, industrialised by terror under Stalin, bore the main weight of defeating Germany at a cost of about 27 million dead, and ran half of Europe and a nuclear arsenal through the Cold War.
polities.how: October 1917 and the civil war created it; Stalin's plans and purges built it; the war of 1941 to 1945 legitimised it.
polities.next: Gorbachev's reforms unravel the system; the union dissolves in December 1991 into fifteen states.

polities.gov: Presidential republic by constitution; in practice a personalised authoritarian system under Putin since 2000
polities.head: Boris Yeltsin 1991 to 1999; Vladimir Putin since 2000, with Medvedev as placeholder 2008 to 2012
polities.rel: Orthodox church allied with the state; Muslim minority of about 10 per cent
polities.econ: Oil and gas exports; sanctions since 2014 and 2022; a war economy from 2022
polities.now: The Soviet successor state, which collapsed economically in the 1990s, recovered on oil under Putin, fought in Chechnya, Georgia and Syria, seized Crimea in 2014 and invaded Ukraine in February 2022.
polities.how: The 1991 dissolution, the 1993 constitution written after Yeltsin shelled parliament, and the 1998 default shaped the state Putin inherited.
polities.next: The outcome of the Ukraine war and the succession to Putin are the questions.

polities.gov: Semi-presidential republic; parliamentary democracy under martial law since 2022
polities.head: President; Zelensky since 2019
polities.rel: Orthodox, split between Kyiv and Moscow jurisdictions; Greek Catholic west
polities.pop: About 44 million before 2022; millions displaced since
polities.econ: Grain, steel, IT; GDP fell about 30 per cent in 2022
polities.now: Independent since 1991, Ukraine chose Europe in the revolutions of 2004 and 2014, lost Crimea and part of the Donbas to Russia in 2014, and has fought a full-scale Russian invasion since February 2022.
polities.how: The Cossack hetmanate, partition between Poland and Russia, the famine of 1932 to 1933, and the independence vote of 1991 are the lineage.
polities.next: The war's settlement and EU accession, in negotiation since 2024, decide its place.

polities.gov: Constitutional monarchy to 1924 and 1935 to 1973 with interruptions; military junta 1967 to 1974; parliamentary republic since 1974
polities.head: Kings of the Bavarian then Danish houses; presidents since 1974; prime minister
polities.rel: Orthodox state church
polities.econ: Shipping, tourism, agriculture; EU member since 1981; bailed out three times after 2010
polities.now: Independent from the Ottomans since 1830, enlarged by the Balkan wars, defeated in Anatolia in 1922, occupied in 1941, torn by civil war to 1949, ruled by colonels 1967 to 1974, and since then an EU democracy that nearly left the euro in 2015.
polities.how: The war of independence won great-power support; the Megali Idea of recovering Byzantium ended at Smyrna in 1922 with a population exchange of 1.5 million.
polities.next: Debt, demography and the Turkish relationship over the Aegean remain.

polities.gov: Kingdom from 1882; core of Yugoslavia 1918 to 1992; parliamentary republic since 2006
polities.head: Obrenović and Karađorđević kings; Tito's Yugoslavia; Milošević; presidents since
polities.rel: Orthodox
polities.econ: Agriculture, metals, growing German and Chinese investment
polities.now: The state whose nationalism triggered 1914, which built and then broke Yugoslavia, fought the wars of the 1990s under Milošević, lost Kosovo in 1999, and now balances EU candidacy against ties to Russia and China.
polities.how: Autonomy from the Ottomans in 1830, independence in 1878, and the Black Hand's assassination of Franz Ferdinand in 1914 set the arc.
polities.next: Kosovo's recognition and EU accession are the unresolved items.

polities.gov: Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes from 1918; royal dictatorship 1929; communist federation under Tito from 1945
polities.head: Kings Alexander and Peter II; Josip Broz Tito 1945 to 1980
polities.rel: Orthodox, Catholic and Muslim by nation
polities.econ: Worker self-management from 1950; Western credits after the 1948 break with Stalin
polities.now: The South Slav state created in 1918, occupied and dismembered in 1941, remade by Tito's partisans as a federation that broke with Stalin in 1948 and led the Non-Aligned Movement.
polities.how: Serbian-Croatian conflict ran through the kingdom; the partisan war killed about a million; Tito's authority held the federation.
polities.next: Tito dies in 1980; the federation breaks up in wars from 1991 to 1999.

polities.gov: Kingdom 1881 to 1947; communist state under Ceaușescu's dictatorship to 1989; semi-presidential republic since
polities.head: Kings Carol I to Michael; Gheorghiu-Dej, Nicolae Ceaușescu; presidents since 1990
polities.rel: Orthodox
polities.econ: Oil at Ploiești, grain; EU member since 2007
polities.now: United from Wallachia and Moldavia in 1859, doubled in 1918 with Transylvania, allied to Hitler for Bessarabia, communist from 1947, and freed by the only violent revolution of 1989, in which Ceaușescu was shot.
polities.how: Independence came at the Congress of Berlin in 1878; the 1918 settlement created Greater Romania; the Red Army brought communism.
polities.next: EU funds, emigration and corruption are the standing issues.

polities.gov: Principality then kingdom 1878 to 1946; communist state to 1989; parliamentary republic since
polities.head: Tsars Ferdinand and Boris III; Todor Zhivkov 1954 to 1989; presidents and prime ministers since
polities.rel: Orthodox; Turkish Muslim minority
polities.econ: Agriculture, tourism, outsourcing; EU member since 2007, euro from 2026
polities.now: Liberated by Russia in 1878, on the losing side in both world wars for Macedonia, the Soviet bloc's most loyal member, and since 2007 the EU's poorest state with the steepest population decline in Europe.
polities.how: San Stefano and Berlin in 1878 fixed its grievance over Macedonia; the Red Army's arrival in 1944 fixed its alignment.
polities.next: Emigration and governance decide whether EU convergence continues.

polities.gov: Principality 1914, republic, Zog's monarchy 1928 to 1939, Italian occupation, Hoxha's communist state 1944 to 1991, parliamentary republic since
polities.head: King Zog; Enver Hoxha; presidents and prime ministers since 1992
polities.rel: Muslim majority, Orthodox and Catholic minorities; religion banned 1967 to 1990
polities.econ: Europe's poorest state under Hoxha's isolation; remittances, tourism, construction since
polities.now: Independent from the Ottomans in 1912, Hoxha's Albania broke with Yugoslavia, the Soviet Union and China in turn and sealed itself off with 170,000 bunkers; since 1991 it has been a NATO member and EU candidate.
polities.how: The partisans took power in 1944; Hoxha's Stalinism outlasted Stalin by four decades.
polities.next: EU accession talks and emigration define the decade.

polities.gov: Prince-bishopric, then principality and kingdom to 1918; part of Yugoslavia; independent republic since 2006
polities.head: Prince-bishops of the Petrović house; King Nikola; presidents since 2006
polities.rel: Orthodox
polities.econ: Tourism on the Adriatic; uses the euro without membership
polities.now: A mountain principality that held off the Ottomans for centuries, joined Yugoslavia in 1918, stayed with Serbia after 1992, and voted for independence in 2006; a NATO member since 2017.
polities.how: The Petrović prince-bishops united the clans; the Congress of Berlin recognised independence in 1878.
polities.next: EU accession, possibly first among the candidates, is the goal.

polities.gov: Austro-Hungarian occupation 1878, annexation 1908; Yugoslav republic; since 1995 a state of two entities under the Dayton constitution
polities.head: Three-member rotating presidency; international High Representative
polities.rel: Muslim Bosniaks, Orthodox Serbs, Catholic Croats
polities.econ: Weak; remittances, metals, hydropower
polities.now: The province whose annexation in 1908 and assassination in 1914 shaped Europe's century, and whose war of 1992 to 1995 killed about 100,000; the Dayton settlement froze it in a shared state its Serb entity contests.
polities.how: Ottoman rule to 1878, Habsburg rule to 1918, Yugoslavia to 1992, and a war ended by NATO bombing and Dayton.
polities.next: Secession talk in Republika Srpska and EU candidacy pull in opposite directions.

polities.gov: Parliamentary republic
polities.head: President; prime minister
polities.rel: Catholic
polities.econ: Tourism on the Adriatic; EU member since 2013, euro and Schengen since 2023
