polities.now: Independent since 1991 after a war with the Yugoslav army and Serb rebels that ended in 1995; an EU and NATO member since 2013 and 2009.
polities.how: Habsburg crownland, Yugoslav republic, and the fascist Ustaše state of 1941 to 1945 are its twentieth-century lineage.
polities.next: Depopulation and dependence on tourism are the standing problems.

polities.gov: Parliamentary republic
polities.head: President; prime minister
polities.rel: Catholic tradition
polities.econ: The richest of the former Yugoslav states; pharmaceuticals, cars; EU member since 2004, euro since 2007
polities.now: Left Yugoslavia after a ten-day war in 1991 and became the first former Yugoslav state in the EU and the euro.
polities.how: A Habsburg land for six centuries, it joined Yugoslavia in 1918 and left first.
polities.next: A stable small economy with ageing as its main constraint.

polities.gov: Parliamentary republic
polities.head: President; prime minister
polities.rel: Orthodox majority, Albanian Muslim quarter
polities.econ: Poor; textiles, remittances
polities.now: Independent from Yugoslavia in 1991 without war, blocked from NATO and the EU by Greece over its name until the Prespa agreement of 2018 renamed it North Macedonia; a NATO member since 2020.
polities.how: The territory three states fought over in 1912 and 1913 became a Yugoslav republic in 1944.
polities.next: EU accession remains blocked, now by Bulgaria over history and language.

polities.gov: Parliamentary republic 1918 to 1940 and since 1991; Soviet republic 1940 to 1991
polities.head: President; prime minister
polities.rel: Lutheran tradition; largely non-religious; Orthodox Russian minority
polities.econ: Digital government, technology, timber; EU and NATO member since 2004, euro since 2011
polities.now: Independent in 1918, annexed by the Soviet Union in 1940 under the Nazi-Soviet pact, restored in 1991, and since then the most digitised state in Europe and a NATO front line.
polities.how: The Singing Revolution of 1988 to 1991 ended Soviet rule without bloodshed.
polities.next: Its Russian-speaking quarter and border with Russia are the security questions.

polities.gov: Parliamentary republic 1918 to 1940 and since 1991; Soviet republic between
polities.head: President; prime minister
polities.rel: Lutheran and Catholic tradition; Orthodox Russian minority
polities.econ: Transit trade, timber, finance; EU and NATO since 2004, euro since 2014
polities.now: Independent in 1918, annexed in 1940, restored in 1991, with a Russian-speaking quarter and the Baltic's largest port at Riga.
polities.how: German-Baltic landlords, Russian rule, two independences.
polities.next: Integration of Russian speakers and NATO's eastern defence are the issues.

polities.gov: Parliamentary republic 1918 to 1940 and since 1990; authoritarian under Smetona 1926 to 1940; Soviet republic between
polities.head: President; prime minister
polities.rel: Catholic
polities.econ: Lasers, logistics, food; EU and NATO since 2004, euro since 2015
polities.now: Heir to the medieval grand duchy, independent in 1918, annexed in 1940, and the first Soviet republic to declare independence, in March 1990; a strong supporter of Ukraine and Taiwan.
polities.how: The Sąjūdis movement and the January 1991 killings at the Vilnius television tower ended Soviet rule.
polities.next: The Suwałki gap between Belarus and Kaliningrad is NATO's most exposed point.

polities.gov: Presidential dictatorship under Lukashenko since 1994
polities.head: Alexander Lukashenko
polities.rel: Orthodox majority
polities.econ: State-owned industry, potash, dependence on Russian energy and credit
polities.now: The Soviet republic that kept its system: Lukashenko has ruled since 1994, crushed the 2020 protests, and let Russia use Belarusian territory to invade Ukraine in 2022.
polities.how: Independence came with the Soviet dissolution; the 1994 election was the last free one.
polities.next: The state is bound to Russia's war outcome.

polities.gov: Parliamentary republic
polities.head: President; prime minister
polities.rel: Orthodox
polities.econ: Europe's poorest state; agriculture, wine, remittances
polities.now: Independent since 1991 with the breakaway Transnistria region held by Russian troops since 1992; an EU candidate since 2022 under a pro-European government.
polities.how: Bessarabia passed between Russia and Romania; the Soviet republic became a state in 1991 and lost its east bank at once.
polities.next: EU accession and Transnistria's status depend on the Ukraine war.

polities.gov: Parliamentary republic
polities.head: President; prime minister
polities.rel: Orthodox
polities.econ: Wine, tourism, transit; remittances
polities.now: Independent since 1991, Georgia lost Abkhazia and South Ossetia in the 1990s and fought a five-day war with Russia in 2008; its government has turned away from the EU path since 2022 against mass protests.
polities.how: A medieval kingdom, a Russian province from 1801, a Soviet republic, and the Rose Revolution of 2003.
polities.next: Whether it remains on a European course is in contest on the streets of Tbilisi.

polities.gov: Fragmented monarchies of Kartli, Kakheti and Imereti after 1490
polities.head: Bagrationi kings
polities.rel: Orthodox
polities.econ: Agriculture; tribute to Persia and the Ottomans
polities.now: The medieval Georgian kingdom has split into three, caught between Ottoman and Persian overlords, with Russia as the new protector from 1783.
polities.how: Mongol and Timurid invasions broke the unified kingdom of the twelfth century.
polities.next: Russia annexes Kartli-Kakheti in 1801 and the rest by 1810.

polities.gov: Parliamentary republic since 2018
polities.head: Prime minister; president ceremonial
polities.rel: Armenian Apostolic Church, the oldest state church
polities.econ: Mining, IT, remittances; dependent on Russia for security until 2023
polities.now: Independent since 1991, Armenia won Nagorno-Karabakh in the 1990s war and lost it in 2020 and 2023 to an Azerbaijan armed by Turkey and Israel; it is now moving away from Russia.
polities.how: The genocide of 1915, a Soviet republic, and the Karabakh conflict define its modern history.
polities.next: A peace treaty with Azerbaijan and the opening of borders with Turkey are in negotiation.

polities.gov: Presidential authoritarian state; the Aliyev family since 1993
polities.head: Ilham Aliyev, president since 2003
polities.rel: Shia Muslim majority, secular state
polities.econ: Oil and gas from the Caspian; pipelines to Turkey and Europe
polities.now: Oil-rich and authoritarian, Azerbaijan recovered Nagorno-Karabakh by force in 2020 and 2023 and expelled its Armenian population.
polities.how: Baku's oil boom of 1900, Soviet rule, and the Karabakh war shaped the state.
polities.next: Succession in the Aliyev family and the peace with Armenia.

polities.gov: Venetian possession 1489 to 1571; Ottoman to 1878; British to 1960; presidential republic since, divided since 1974
polities.head: President; the north under a Turkish Cypriot administration recognised only by Turkey
polities.cap: Nicosia, the last divided capital in Europe
polities.rel: Orthodox Greek majority; Muslim Turkish minority
polities.econ: Tourism, shipping, financial services; EU member since 2004
polities.now: An island ruled by Venice, the Ottomans and Britain, independent in 1960, invaded by Turkey in 1974 after a Greek-backed coup, and divided since, with the south in the EU.
polities.how: The 1960 power-sharing constitution broke down in 1963; the 1974 invasion partitioned the island.
polities.next: Reunification talks have failed repeatedly; gas finds offshore add a new dispute.

polities.gov: Knights of St John 1530 to 1798; British colony to 1964; parliamentary republic since 1974
polities.head: President; prime minister
polities.rel: Catholic
polities.econ: Tourism, financial services, online gaming; EU member since 2004
polities.now: The fortress island that held against the Ottomans in 1565 and the Axis in 1941 to 1942, British to 1964, and the EU's smallest member.
polities.how: Britain took it from Napoleon in 1800 and held it as the Mediterranean fleet's base.
polities.next: Rule-of-law scrutiny after a journalist's murder in 2017 continues.

polities.gov: Danish dependency; home rule 1904; sovereign kingdom in union with Denmark 1918; republic since 1944
polities.head: President; prime minister
polities.rel: Lutheran tradition
polities.econ: Fishing, aluminium, tourism, geothermal power; banking collapse in 2008
polities.now: Independent from Denmark since 1944, a NATO founder without an army, outside the EU, and recovered from the 2008 bank collapse that took down its three largest banks.
polities.how: Settled around 870, under Norway from 1262 and Denmark from 1380; the Althing of 930 is the oldest surviving parliament.
polities.next: Tourism's scale and the EU question recur.

polities.gov: Hereditary sultanate; the sultan commands a slave-recruited administration and the Janissary corps
polities.head: Mehmed II (the Conqueror), Bayezid II, Selim I, Suleiman I (the Magnificent, 1520 to 1566)
polities.rel: Sunni Islam; the sultan as caliph from 1517; Christians and Jews as protected tax-paying communities
polities.econ: Control of the Levant, Egyptian grain and the eastern trade routes; timar land grants fund the cavalry
polities.now: The strongest military state in Europe and the Middle East: it took Constantinople in 1453, Syria and Egypt in 1517, Belgrade in 1521, Hungary in 1526, and besieged Vienna in 1529. Suleiman's law code and navy under Barbarossa hold the Mediterranean.
polities.how: Recovered from Timur's defeat of 1402, the sultans built a standing army of converted Christian boys and a tax system that outmatched every neighbour.
polities.next: Lepanto in 1571 checks the navy; the long war with Austria and Persia strains the treasury; the empire holds but stops expanding.

polities.gov: Sultanate with power shifting to grand viziers, the harem and the Janissaries; provincial notables gain autonomy
polities.head: Selim II to Abdulhamid I; the Köprülü viziers 1656 to 1683
polities.rel: Sunni Islam; the millet system for Christians and Jews
polities.econ: Inflation from American silver after 1580; coffee; the Capitulations give European merchants privileges
polities.now: An empire that failed before Vienna in 1683, lost Hungary at Karlowitz in 1699 and the Crimea to Russia in 1783, and is governed in the provinces by local dynasts while the centre fights the Janissaries over reform.
polities.how: The Köprülüs restored order after 1656; the 1683 defeat began the Austrian and Russian advances that continued for two centuries.
polities.next: Selim III's reform army is overthrown by the Janissaries in 1807; Mahmud II destroys the corps in 1826.

polities.gov: Reforming autocracy (Tanzimat 1839 to 1876); constitution 1876, suspended 1878, restored by the Young Turks in 1908
polities.head: Selim III, Mahmud II, Abdülmecid, Abdülhamid II (1876 to 1909), Mehmed V; the Committee of Union and Progress from 1908
polities.rel: Sunni Islam; equality of non-Muslims declared 1856; Armenian massacres 1894 to 1896 and genocide 1915
polities.pop: About 25 million in 1900 before the Balkan losses
polities.econ: Foreign debt default 1875, European debt administration from 1881; the Baghdad railway; oil found in Mosul
polities.now: The 'sick man of Europe', losing Greece, Serbia, Egypt, Algeria, Tunisia, Bosnia, Libya and nearly all its Balkan lands between 1830 and 1913, while reformers rebuild the army and the law on European lines. The Young Turks take it into the First World War on Germany's side in 1914.
polities.how: Mahmud II broke the Janissaries; the Tanzimat decrees promised equal citizenship; the 1878 Congress of Berlin and the bankruptcy put the empire under European tutelage.
polities.next: Defeat in 1918, partition at Sèvres in 1920, and Mustafa Kemal's war of independence; the sultanate is abolished in November 1922.
polities.wk: Decline and modernization of the Ottoman Empire

polities.gov: Secular republic under Atatürk's one-party rule to 1946; multiparty with three military coups (1960, 1971, 1980); presidential system under Erdoğan since 2017
polities.head: Mustafa Kemal Atatürk 1923 to 1938; İnönü; Menderes; Özal; Recep Tayyip Erdoğan since 2003
polities.rel: Sunni Muslim majority, Alevi minority; secularism in the constitution, contested in practice
polities.econ: Manufacturing, construction, tourism, agriculture; NATO member since 1952; EU candidate since 1999, talks frozen
polities.now: Atatürk's republic abolished the caliphate, Latinised the alphabet and built a secular nationalist state; since 2003 Erdoğan has reversed the secular settlement and concentrated power, while Turkey plays Russia, NATO and the Middle East against each other.
polities.how: The war of independence to 1922 and the Lausanne treaty of 1923, with the population exchange with Greece, created the state; the army guarded Kemalism by coup until the 2016 attempt failed.
polities.next: Inflation, the Kurdish question, and the post-Erdoğan succession are the open items.

polities.gov: Military regime of slave-soldiers who rose to sultan; no hereditary succession
polities.head: Sultans Barsbay, Qaitbay, al-Ghawri
polities.rel: Sunni Islam; the Abbasid caliph kept at Cairo as a figurehead
polities.pop: About 4 million in Egypt and Syria, after plague losses
polities.econ: The spice trade between the Indian Ocean and Venice until the Portuguese route of 1498
polities.now: The regime that stopped the Mongols in 1260 and expelled the crusaders rules Egypt and Syria from Cairo, the largest city in the Islamic world, and lives on the transit trade the Portuguese are about to divert.
polities.how: Turkish and Circassian slave soldiers seized the sultanate in 1250 and recruited their successors from the same source.
polities.next: Selim I destroys the Mamluk army at Marj Dabiq and Ridaniya in 1516 and 1517; Egypt becomes an Ottoman province.

polities.t: Ottoman Egypt under the Mamluk beys
polities.gov: Ottoman province in name; Mamluk beys hold real power
polities.head: Ottoman governor; beys such as Ali Bey al-Kabir, who declared independence in 1768
polities.rel: Sunni Islam; Coptic Christian minority
polities.econ: Grain and the Red Sea coffee trade; Napoleon's invasion of 1798 to 1801
polities.now: A province where the Mamluk households have recovered control from the Ottoman governor; Bonaparte's expedition of 1798 and the British intervention that followed break their hold.
polities.how: The Ottoman conquest of 1517 kept the Mamluks as a military class, who outlasted the governors.
polities.next: Muhammad Ali, an Albanian officer, takes power in 1805 and massacres the beys in 1811.

polities.gov: Hereditary governorship under the Ottomans from 1841; the khedivate from 1867
polities.head: Muhammad Ali 1805 to 1848; Said; Ismail 1863 to 1879
polities.rel: Sunni Islam; Coptic minority
polities.econ: Cotton for Lancashire; the Suez Canal opened 1869; state bankruptcy in 1876
polities.now: A modernising dynasty that conquered Sudan, nearly took Constantinople in 1839, built the canal, and borrowed itself into a debt that European creditors are now collecting through control of the treasury.
polities.how: Muhammad Ali built a conscript army and state industries; Ismail's spending on Paris-style Cairo and the canal brought the bankruptcy and the Dual Control of 1876.
polities.next: The Urabi revolt against foreign control brings a British invasion in 1882 and an occupation that lasts seventy years.

polities.gov: Khedivate under British occupation; protectorate 1914; nominal independence 1922 as a kingdom with British troops at the Canal
polities.head: Khedives and kings Fuad I and Farouk; British consul-general Cromer 1883 to 1907
polities.rel: Sunni Islam; Coptic minority; the Muslim Brotherhood founded 1928
polities.econ: Cotton monoculture; the Canal the artery of the British Empire
polities.now: A kingdom whose politics turn on the British presence: the 1919 revolution won nominal independence, the 1936 treaty kept British troops at the Canal, and defeat in Palestine in 1948 discredited the monarchy.
polities.how: Britain occupied Egypt in 1882 to secure the Canal and the debt and stayed.
polities.next: The Free Officers under Nasser overthrow Farouk in July 1952.
polities.wk: History of Egypt under the British

polities.gov: Military-backed presidential republic since 1953; a year of Muslim Brotherhood government 2012 to 2013
polities.head: Nasser 1954 to 1970; Sadat; Mubarak 1981 to 2011; Morsi; Sisi since 2014
polities.rel: Sunni Islam the state religion; Copts about 10 per cent
polities.pop: About 107 million, the Arab world's largest
polities.econ: Canal fees, remittances, gas, tourism; repeated IMF programmes; a military-owned economic sector
polities.now: The Arab world's centre of gravity: Nasser nationalised the Canal and led Arab nationalism, Sadat made peace with Israel in 1979, Mubarak's thirty years ended in the 2011 uprising, and Sisi's coup of 2013 restored army rule.
polities.how: The 1952 coup, the 1956 Suez crisis, defeat in 1967 and the 1973 war set the state's course; US aid since Camp David underwrites the army.
polities.next: Debt, population growth and the Nile dispute with Ethiopia are the structural pressures.

polities.gov: Timurid princes in Herat and Samarkand; the Aq Qoyunlu (White Sheep) Turkmen confederation in the west
polities.head: Shah Rukh, Ulugh Beg; Uzun Hasan of the White Sheep
polities.rel: Sunni Islam with Sufi orders; Shia Safavid order rising at Ardabil
polities.econ: Silk Road trade; Herat's miniature painting and Ulugh Beg's observatory
polities.now: The successors of Timur rule Khorasan and Transoxiana as patrons of art and science while the White Sheep Turkmen hold western Persia; both are about to be swept away.
polities.how: Timur's empire fragmented at his death in 1405 among sons and grandsons.
polities.next: Ismail of the Safavid order takes Tabriz in 1501 and makes Persia Shia; the Uzbeks take Samarkand.

polities.gov: Hereditary shahdom claiming descent from the Imams; a Qizilbash tribal army replaced by slave regiments under Abbas I
polities.head: Ismail I, Tahmasp I, Abbas I (the Great, 1588 to 1629), the later shahs
polities.cap: Tabriz, then Qazvin, then Isfahan from 1598
polities.rel: Twelver Shia Islam imposed as the state religion from 1501, which separates Persia from its Sunni neighbours to this day
polities.econ: Silk exports through Armenian merchants; Isfahan among the great cities of the world under Abbas
polities.now: The dynasty that made Persia Shia and rebuilt it as a state: Abbas the Great drove out the Uzbeks and Ottomans, moved the capital to Isfahan, and traded with Europe through the Gulf. After him the court weakens and the frontiers open.
polities.how: Ismail's Qizilbash followers conquered Persia in a decade; Chaldiran in 1514 fixed the Ottoman frontier; Abbas's reforms made the state last.
polities.next: An Afghan army takes Isfahan in 1722; Nader Shah expels the Afghans and ends the dynasty in 1736.

polities.t: Persia under the Afsharids, Zands and Qajars
polities.gov: Tribal dynasties; the Qajar shahs from 1794 rule a weak centre with a constitution from 1906
polities.head: Nader Shah 1736 to 1747; Karim Khan Zand; Fath-Ali Shah, Nasir al-Din Shah (1848 to 1896), the last Qajars
polities.rel: Twelver Shia; the clergy a political force from the Tobacco Protest of 1891
polities.econ: Carpets, opium, tobacco concessions; oil found at Masjed Soleyman in 1908 and the Anglo-Persian Oil Company
polities.now: A country that sacked Delhi under Nader Shah, lost the Caucasus to Russia by 1828, and under the Qajars is divided into Russian and British spheres by the 1907 agreement, with a constitutional revolution of 1906 that the shah and the powers suppress.
polities.how: Nader's conquests ended in his murder; the Qajars held the throne by balancing Britain and Russia and selling concessions.
polities.next: Reza Khan, a Cossack brigade officer, seizes power in 1921 and crowns himself shah in 1925.

polities.gov: Modernising autocracy; Reza Shah to 1941, Mohammad Reza Shah to 1979; the SAVAK secret police
polities.head: Reza Shah Pahlavi; Mohammad Reza Shah Pahlavi; prime minister Mosaddegh 1951 to 1953
polities.rel: Shia Islam; the state secularising; the clergy under Khomeini in opposition from 1963
polities.econ: Oil, nationalised 1951, restored to a Western consortium after the 1953 coup; the 1973 price rise funds the shah's arms and the White Revolution
polities.now: A monarchy modernising by decree, allied to the United States since the CIA- and MI6-backed coup of 1953 removed Mosaddegh, and spending the oil boom on arms and land reform faster than society can absorb.
polities.how: Reza Shah built the army, railways and secular law; the Allies deposed him in 1941; his son's rule rested on the 1953 coup and oil.
polities.next: Mass protests from 1978 end the monarchy; Khomeini returns in February 1979 and founds the Islamic Republic.

polities.gov: Theocratic republic: an elected president and parliament under an unelected Supreme Leader, the Guardian Council and the Revolutionary Guards
polities.head: Ayatollah Khomeini 1979 to 1989; Ayatollah Khamenei since 1989; presidents from Bani-Sadr to Pezeshkian
polities.rel: Twelver Shia Islam as the state; Sunni, Christian, Jewish, Zoroastrian and Baha'i minorities, the last persecuted
polities.econ: Oil and gas under sanctions; a Guard-owned economic sector; chronic inflation
polities.now: The revolution's state fought Iraq for eight years, built a network of allied militias from Lebanon to Yemen, pursued a nuclear programme the 2015 deal paused and the 2018 US withdrawal revived, and faces recurrent mass protests, the largest in 2022.
polities.how: The 1979 revolution, the hostage crisis, and the war of 1980 to 1988 consolidated clerical rule and enmity with the United States.
polities.next: The succession to Khamenei, the nuclear question and the regional network's fate after 2024 are the variables.

polities.gov: Tribal emirates; the Saudi-Wahhabi state of Diriyah (1744 to 1818), a second state at Riyadh, then Ibn Saud's conquests from 1902
polities.head: The Al Saud with the Wahhabi clerical alliance; the Rashidis of Hail; Ibn Saud from 1902
polities.rel: Sunni Islam in the Wahhabi reform movement from 1744
polities.pop: About 2 to 3 million across the peninsula
polities.econ: Pastoral and oasis economy; pilgrimage revenue in the Hejaz; pearls on the Gulf coast
polities.now: The interior of Arabia is contested between the Saudi-Wahhabi alliance and its rivals; the first Saudi state took Mecca in 1803 and was destroyed by Egypt in 1818; Ibn Saud retook Riyadh in 1902 and is conquering the peninsula.
polities.how: Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab's pact with Muhammad ibn Saud in 1744 joined a reform movement to a dynasty.
polities.next: Ibn Saud takes the Hejaz in 1925 and proclaims the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia in 1932; oil is found in 1938.

polities.gov: Hashemite kingdom under Sharif Hussein, who led the Arab Revolt of 1916
polities.head: Hussein bin Ali, king 1916 to 1924
polities.rel: Sunni Islam; guardianship of the holy cities
polities.econ: Pilgrimage; British subsidy
polities.now: The Hashemite state of the Arab Revolt, promised an Arab kingdom by Britain and given only the Hejaz, while Hussein's sons rule Iraq and Transjordan under British mandate.
polities.how: Hussein rose against the Ottomans in 1916 with British gold and Lawrence's liaison.
polities.next: Ibn Saud conquers the Hejaz in 1925; the Hashemites keep Iraq to 1958 and Jordan to this day.

polities.gov: Absolute monarchy of the Al Saud with the Wahhabi clerical establishment, whose power has been cut since 2017
polities.head: Ibn Saud to 1953; Saud, Faisal, Khalid, Fahd, Abdullah, Salman; Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman the effective ruler since 2017
polities.rel: Sunni Islam in the Wahhabi tradition; Shia minority in the Eastern Province; Mecca and Medina
polities.pop: About 36 million, a third of them foreign workers
polities.econ: The world's largest oil exporter since the 1940s; Aramco; Vision 2030 diversification
polities.now: The oil state that funded Islam's global missions and the Afghan jihad, allied with the United States since 1945, fought a war in Yemen from 2015, and under Mohammed bin Salman is loosening religious rules while tightening political control.
polities.how: Ibn Saud's conquests and the 1933 oil concession to Standard Oil of California made the kingdom; the 1973 embargo made it a power.
polities.next: The transition away from oil and the crown prince's succession to the throne are the horizon.

polities.gov: Zaydi imamate in the highlands; Ottoman provinces on the coast 1538 to 1635 and again from 1872
polities.head: Zaydi imams of the Qasimi line; Ottoman governors
polities.rel: Zaydi Shia in the north, Shafi'i Sunni in the south and coast
polities.econ: Coffee exported through Mocha, the world's source until the eighteenth century
polities.now: A highland imamate that expelled the Ottomans in 1635 and lost the coast to them again in 1872, with Britain at Aden from 1839.
polities.how: The Zaydi imams held the mountains against every invader; Mocha coffee made the coast valuable.
polities.next: The Ottomans withdraw in 1918; Imam Yahya rules the north until 1948; Aden stays British until 1967.

polities.gov: Zaydi imamate to 1962, then the Yemen Arab Republic; British Aden to 1967, then the Marxist People's Democratic Republic in the south
polities.head: Imams Yahya and Ahmad; Ali Abdullah Saleh in the north from 1978; the Socialist Party in the south
polities.rel: Zaydi and Shafi'i Islam
polities.econ: Remittances from the Gulf; Aden's port; oil found in the 1980s
polities.now: Two states: a republic in the north that won a civil war against the imamate with Egyptian help, and the Arab world's only Marxist state in the south, formed when Britain left Aden in 1967.
polities.how: The 1962 revolution and the 1962 to 1970 civil war in the north; the insurgency that forced Britain from Aden.
polities.next: The two Yemens unite in May 1990 under Saleh.

polities.gov: Unified republic under Saleh to 2012; since 2014 a civil war between the Houthi movement in Sana'a and a recognised government backed by Saudi Arabia
polities.head: Ali Abdullah Saleh 1990 to 2012; Hadi; the Presidential Leadership Council; Houthi leader Abdul-Malik al-Houthi
polities.cap: Sana'a, held by the Houthis; Aden for the recognised government
polities.rel: Zaydi north, Sunni south
polities.pop: About 34 million; the war has caused one of the world's worst humanitarian crises
polities.econ: Collapsed; oil exports halted; aid dependence
polities.now: Unified in 1990, wracked by the 1994 civil war, the 2011 uprising and the Houthi seizure of Sana'a in 2014, which brought a Saudi-led intervention; since 2023 the Houthis attack Red Sea shipping in the Gaza war's name.
polities.how: Saleh's thirty-year balancing act collapsed in 2011; the Houthis, a Zaydi revivalist movement at war with the state since 2004, filled the vacuum with Iranian support.
polities.next: A Saudi-Houthi settlement has been in negotiation since 2022.

polities.gov: Ibadi imamate and the Al Said sultanate from 1749; absolute monarchy
polities.head: Sultans of the Al Said; Qaboos 1970 to 2020; Haitham since
polities.rel: Ibadi Islam, a third branch distinct from Sunni and Shia
polities.econ: Indian Ocean trade and the Zanzibar clove empire in the nineteenth century; oil from 1967
polities.now: A maritime sultanate that expelled the Portuguese in 1650, ruled Zanzibar and the Swahili coast until 1856, became a British client, and under Qaboos modernised from a closed medieval state into a neutral mediator in Gulf disputes.
polities.how: The Ya'rubi imams and then the Al Said built the Indian Ocean empire; British support and the 1970 palace coup made the modern state.
polities.next: Oil depletion earlier than its neighbours drives diversification.

polities.gov: Hereditary emirate of the Al Sabah with an elected National Assembly, suspended repeatedly
polities.head: Emir of the Al Sabah
polities.rel: Sunni majority, Shia third
polities.econ: Oil since 1938; one of the largest sovereign funds
polities.now: A British protectorate from 1899 to 1961, invaded by Iraq in August 1990 and freed by the US-led coalition in 1991; the Gulf's most parliamentary monarchy, in recurrent deadlock between emir and assembly.
polities.how: The Al Sabah's British treaty kept the Ottomans and Saudis out; oil made it rich from the 1950s.
polities.next: Political reform and fiscal dependence on oil remain unresolved.

polities.gov: Hereditary emirate of the Al Thani; absolute monarchy
polities.head: Emir Tamim bin Hamad since 2013
polities.rel: Sunni Islam in the Wahhabi tradition
polities.pop: About 2.9 million, nearly 90 per cent foreign
polities.econ: The world's largest liquefied natural gas exporter; the richest country per head
polities.now: A British protectorate from 1916 to 1971, Qatar has used gas wealth, Al Jazeera, the US air base at Al Udeid and mediation between enemies to punch far above its size, surviving a Saudi-led blockade from 2017 to 2021.
polities.how: The Al Thani gained British protection against Bahrain and the Ottomans; gas from the North Field changed everything after 1997.
polities.next: Its mediation role in Gaza, Afghanistan and elsewhere is its strategic asset.

polities.gov: Federation of seven hereditary emirates since 1971; Abu Dhabi dominant
polities.head: President from Abu Dhabi's Al Nahyan; Mohammed bin Zayed since 2022
polities.rel: Sunni Islam; Hindu, Christian and other minorities among expatriates
polities.pop: About 10 million, about 88 per cent foreign
polities.econ: Abu Dhabi's oil; Dubai's trade, aviation, property and finance
polities.now: The Trucial States under British protection from 1820 became a federation in 1971; Dubai built a global hub without oil and Abu Dhabi a sovereign fund with it, and the UAE now projects power from Libya to Yemen and the Horn.
polities.how: Britain's 'trucial' treaties suppressed piracy and kept rivals out; oil at Abu Dhabi from 1958 and Sheikh Zayed's federation followed.
polities.next: Its regional interventions and the model's dependence on migrant labour are the exposures.

polities.gov: Tribal sultanates of the Kathiri and later Qu'aiti; Mahra sultans at Qishn
polities.head: Local sultans
polities.rel: Shafi'i Sunni Islam; Tarim a centre of Sufi learning
polities.econ: Frankincense, date groves, emigration to India and the East Indies
polities.now: The valley of the mud-brick towers, whose merchants and scholars settled across the Indian Ocean from Gujarat to Java.
polities.how: Hadrami sayyid families spread Shafi'i Islam and trade networks across the ocean from the fifteenth century.
polities.next: The British Aden Protectorate absorbs the sultanates in the nineteenth century; the south Yemeni state abolishes them in 1967.

polities.t: French Mandate of Syria and Lebanon
polities.gov: League of Nations mandate under France; separate states for Lebanon, Syria, the Alawites and the Druze
polities.head: French high commissioners
polities.rel: Sunni majority; Alawite, Druze, Christian and Shia communities; Lebanon built with a Christian majority
polities.econ: Agriculture, Beirut's port and banks
polities.now: The Arab kingdom Faisal proclaimed in Damascus in 1920 lasted four months before French troops arrived; France governs the mandate by division, creating Greater Lebanon in 1920 and crushing the 1925 revolt.
polities.how: Sykes-Picot in 1916 and San Remo in 1920 gave France the Levant against the promises made to the Arabs.
polities.next: Syria and Lebanon become independent in 1943 to 1946; French troops leave in 1946.
polities.wk: Mandate for Syria and the Lebanon

polities.gov: Coups to 1970; Hafez al-Assad's Ba'athist security state 1970 to 2000, Bashar's to 2024; a transitional Islamist-led government since December 2024
polities.head: Hafez al-Assad; Bashar al-Assad; Ahmed al-Sharaa since 2024
polities.rel: Sunni majority; Alawite minority that supplied the Assad regime's core; Christians, Druze, Kurds
polities.pop: About 23 million; half displaced by the war since 2011
polities.econ: Destroyed by civil war; oil fields in the east; sanctions easing from 2025
polities.now: Independent in 1946, united with Egypt 1958 to 1961, ruled by the Assads for fifty-four years, and from 2011 the site of a civil war that drew in Iran, Russia, Turkey, the United States and the Islamic State; the regime fell in December 2024 to a rebel offensive.
polities.how: Military coups, the Ba'ath's 1963 seizure, and Hafez al-Assad's 1970 'corrective movement' built the regime; the 2011 uprising broke it over thirteen years.
polities.next: Whether the new government can hold the country's communities together is the question of the decade.

polities.gov: Confessional republic: a Maronite president, Sunni prime minister, Shia speaker by the 1943 pact and the 1989 Taif accord
polities.head: President; prime minister; Hezbollah as a state within the state
polities.rel: Eighteen recognised communities; Shia, Sunni and Christians each roughly a third
polities.pop: About 5.5 million plus 1.5 million Syrian and Palestinian refugees
polities.econ: Banking and services until the 2019 collapse, the worst financial crisis in modern records; the 2020 port explosion
polities.now: The Switzerland of the Middle East until the civil war of 1975 to 1990, occupied by Syria to 2005 and Israel to 2000, dominated by Hezbollah's arms, and bankrupt since 2019; the 2024 war with Israel gutted Hezbollah's leadership.
polities.how: The confessional system froze a 1932 census; Palestinian refugees and the Israeli-Syrian struggle made it a battleground.
polities.next: A new president in 2025 and Hezbollah's disarmament are the tests.

polities.gov: Hashemite monarchy 1921 to 1958; republics by coup; Saddam Hussein's Ba'athist dictatorship 1979 to 2003; parliamentary republic under the 2005 constitution
polities.head: Faisal I; Qasim; Saddam Hussein; prime ministers since 2005
polities.rel: Shia majority, Sunni Arab minority that ruled until 2003, Kurds in the north
polities.econ: Oil, nationalised 1972; wars and sanctions 1980 to 2003; reconstruction
polities.now: A British-made state of three Ottoman provinces, independent in 1932, that fought Iran for eight years, invaded Kuwait in 1990, was invaded by the United States in 2003, lost a third of its territory to the Islamic State in 2014, and is governed by Shia parties under Iranian and American influence.
polities.how: The 1958 revolution ended the monarchy; Saddam's 1979 takeover and his wars; the 2003 invasion and de-Ba'athification; the sectarian war of 2006 to 2008.
polities.next: Militia power, oil dependence and the Kurdish region's status remain unsettled.

polities.gov: Hashemite constitutional monarchy with the king holding real power
polities.head: Abdullah I, Hussein 1952 to 1999, Abdullah II
polities.rel: Sunni Islam; Christian minority
polities.pop: About 11 million, half of Palestinian origin, plus Syrian refugees
polities.econ: Aid-dependent; phosphates, remittances, US and Gulf support
polities.now: Carved from the Palestine mandate in 1921 for Abdullah, Jordan took the West Bank in 1948 and lost it in 1967, expelled the PLO in 1970, made peace with Israel in 1994, and survives on alliances and the army.
polities.how: British creation, the 1948 and 1967 wars, and Black September shaped a state defined by refugees.
polities.next: Water, debt and the West Bank's fate are the pressures.

polities.gov: Parliamentary democracy; coalition governments; occupation of the West Bank since 1967
polities.head: Prime ministers Ben-Gurion, Meir, Begin, Rabin, Netanyahu (longest-serving)
polities.cap: Jerusalem, claimed; most embassies in Tel Aviv
polities.rel: Jewish majority; Arab Muslim and Christian minority of about 20 per cent
polities.econ: Technology, defence industry, diamonds, gas; the highest GDP per head in the region
polities.now: Founded in 1948 and at war with its neighbours in 1948, 1956, 1967, 1973 and 1982, at peace with Egypt and Jordan, and since the Hamas attack of October 2023 in the longest and most destructive Gaza war; the occupation of the West Bank is unresolved after fifty-eight years.
polities.how: Zionist settlement from the 1880s, the Balfour Declaration, the Holocaust and the 1947 partition vote produced the state; the 1967 war produced the occupation.
polities.next: The Palestinian question and the domestic conflict over the judiciary and religion decide its character.

polities.gov: British mandate under the League of Nations from 1920
polities.head: British high commissioner
polities.rel: Muslim majority; Jewish population rising from 11 per cent in 1922 to a third by 1947 through immigration; Christians
polities.econ: Citrus, Jewish-funded industry, Haifa's refinery
polities.now: The territory Britain promised to the Zionists in 1917 and to the Arabs earlier, governed by a mandate that satisfied neither; the Arab revolt of 1936 to 1939 and Jewish insurgency after 1944 exhaust Britain.
polities.how: Ottoman Palestine fell to Britain in 1917; the mandate's dual obligation was contradictory from the start.
polities.next: The UN partition vote of November 1947, war, and Israel's declaration in May 1948; about 700,000 Palestinians become refugees.

polities.gov: Hafsid dynasty claiming the caliphate; city-states in Tlemcen under the Zayyanids
polities.head: Hafsid sultans
polities.rel: Maliki Sunni Islam
polities.econ: Grain, Saharan gold and slaves, corsairing
polities.now: The Hafsid state of Tunis and the Zayyanid kingdom of Tlemcen hold the central Maghreb between Morocco and Mamluk Egypt, with Spain and the Ottomans closing in.
polities.how: The Hafsids inherited the Almohad caliphate's eastern provinces in 1229.
polities.next: Ottoman corsairs and Spanish fleets contest the coast; the Ottomans take Tunis for good in 1574.

polities.gov: Ottoman province under local beys; the Husainid dynasty hereditary from 1705
polities.head: Husainid beys
polities.rel: Maliki Sunni Islam; Jewish community
polities.econ: Grain, olive oil, corsairing until 1816; the first Arab constitution in 1861; bankruptcy in 1869
polities.now: A near-independent beylik under nominal Ottoman rule, which abolished slavery in 1846, adopted a constitution in 1861, and went bankrupt building a modern state on European loans.
polities.how: The Husainids made the office hereditary; European consuls and creditors took control of the finances in 1869.
polities.next: France invades from Algeria in 1881 and makes Tunisia a protectorate.

polities.gov: Protectorate: the bey kept as figurehead, a French resident-general governing
polities.head: French residents-general; Habib Bourguiba's Neo-Destour from 1934
polities.rel: Sunni Islam; European settlers about 250,000 by 1950
polities.econ: Phosphates, olive oil, wine; settler farms
polities.now: A protectorate run by France with the bey as a signature, whose nationalist movement under Bourguiba negotiates rather than fights its way to independence.
polities.how: France took Tunisia in 1881 to forestall Italy; the Neo-Destour built a mass party.
polities.next: Independence in March 1956; the monarchy abolished in 1957.

polities.gov: One-party presidential republic under Bourguiba and Ben Ali to 2011; a decade of democracy; presidential rule by decree under Kais Saied since 2021
polities.head: Habib Bourguiba 1957 to 1987; Zine el-Abidine Ben Ali to 2011; Kais Saied since 2019
polities.rel: Sunni Islam; the most secular legal code in the Arab world
polities.econ: Tourism, textiles, phosphates, olive oil; chronic unemployment
polities.now: The country whose street vendor's self-immolation in December 2010 began the Arab Spring, the only one to build a democracy from it, and the one that lost it again when Saied suspended parliament in 2021.
polities.how: Bourguiba's secular state, Ben Ali's police state, and the 2011 revolution.
polities.next: Debt and emigration pressures under a personalised presidency.

polities.gov: Ottoman regency; the dey elected by the Janissary council from 1671
polities.head: Deys of Algiers
polities.rel: Maliki Sunni Islam; Jewish community
polities.econ: Corsairing and ransom of captives; grain exports; tribute from European states
polities.now: A corsair republic under nominal Ottoman sovereignty, living on captures and ransoms, which the United States fought in 1815 and the European powers bombarded in 1816.
polities.how: The Barbarossa brothers brought Algiers under the Ottomans in 1516; the Janissary corps made the dey its elected chief.
polities.next: A dispute over a debt and a fly-whisk gives France its pretext; the French land in June 1830.

polities.gov: Military conquest 1830 to 1847; from 1848 three French départements with a settler electorate and a disenfranchised Muslim majority
polities.head: French governors-general; the FLN from 1954
polities.rel: Sunni Islam majority; a million European settlers by 1954, Catholic; the Jews made French citizens in 1870
polities.pop: About 9 million Muslims and 1 million Europeans in 1954
polities.econ: Settler wine and wheat; oil found in the Sahara in 1956
polities.now: Part of France by law and a colony in fact: Abd al-Qadir's resistance was crushed by 1847, the 1945 Sétif massacre killed thousands, and the war of independence from 1954 to 1962 costs hundreds of thousands of lives and brings down the Fourth Republic.
polities.how: The 1830 landing, decades of conquest, and settler dominance made an inequality the war of 1954 ended.
polities.next: The Évian accords of March 1962; independence in July; the settlers leave within months.

polities.gov: One-party FLN state to 1989; army-dominated presidential republic since the civil war of the 1990s
polities.head: Ben Bella; Boumédiène; Chadli; Bouteflika 1999 to 2019; Tebboune
polities.rel: Sunni Islam the state religion
polities.econ: Oil and gas supply more than 90 per cent of exports; state-dominated
polities.now: Independent in 1962 after the war, Algeria cancelled an Islamist election win in 1992 and fought a civil war that killed about 150,000; mass protests in 2019 removed Bouteflika without removing the army's system.
polities.how: The FLN's victory, Boumédiène's socialism, the 1988 riots, the 1990s war.
polities.next: Gas revenues, youth unemployment, and rivalry with Morocco over Western Sahara.

polities.t: Morocco under the Wattasids and Saadians
polities.gov: Wattasid sultanate to 1554; the Saadian sharifian dynasty after
polities.head: Wattasid sultans; Ahmad al-Mansur (1578 to 1603)
polities.rel: Maliki Sunni Islam; the sultans claim descent from the Prophet
polities.econ: Sugar, gold from the Songhai conquest of 1591, Portuguese enclaves on the coast
polities.now: A sultanate that destroyed a Portuguese army at Alcácer Quibir in 1578, which killed the king of Portugal, and sent an army across the Sahara to seize Songhai's gold in 1591.
polities.how: The Saadians rose as holy warriors against the Portuguese forts and took Fez in 1554.
polities.next: Civil war after 1603; the Alaouite dynasty, which still reigns, takes power from 1666.

polities.gov: Sharifian sultanate; the Alaouite dynasty from 1666
polities.head: Moulay Ismail (1672 to 1727) and successors to Abdelhafid
polities.cap: Fez and Marrakesh; Meknes under Ismail
polities.rel: Maliki Sunni Islam
polities.econ: Caravan trade, grain, European commercial penetration from the 1850s; bankruptcy and the 1906 Algeciras conference
polities.now: The one Maghreb state the Ottomans never ruled, held together by the sultan's religious authority and Moulay Ismail's black slave army, and by 1900 the object of a French-German-Spanish contest.
polities.how: The Alaouites took power in the 1660s; the defeat by France at Isly in 1844 and by Spain in 1860 opened the country to European control.
polities.next: The Treaty of Fez in 1912 makes Morocco a French protectorate, with a Spanish zone in the north.

polities.gov: French protectorate under Resident-General Lyautey and successors; Spanish protectorate in the Rif; the sultan kept as figurehead
polities.head: Lyautey 1912 to 1925; Sultan Mohammed V from 1927
polities.rel: Sunni Islam; a large Jewish community
polities.econ: Phosphates, settler agriculture, Casablanca's port
polities.now: Lyautey's indirect rule preserved the sultanate's forms while France built the modern state; the Rif war of 1921 to 1926 under Abd el-Krim nearly expelled Spain; Mohammed V's exile in 1953 made him the nationalist symbol.
polities.how: The protectorate treaty of 1912 and the Rif war set the pattern.
polities.next: France restores the sultan and grants independence in March 1956.

polities.gov: Constitutional monarchy in form; the king holds decisive power
polities.head: Mohammed V; Hassan II 1961 to 1999; Mohammed VI
polities.rel: Sunni Islam; the king as Commander of the Faithful
polities.econ: Phosphates (the world's largest reserves), agriculture, tourism, cars, remittances
polities.now: A monarchy that survived two coup attempts in the 1970s, annexed Western Sahara in 1975 and holds it against the Polisario, weathered the Arab Spring with a new constitution in 2011, and normalised with Israel in 2020 for US recognition of its Sahara claim.
polities.how: Independence in 1956, Hassan II's years of lead, the Green March of 1975.
polities.next: Western Sahara's status and inequality are the long questions.

polities.gov: Ottoman province; the Karamanli dynasty autonomous 1711 to 1835; direct Ottoman rule after
polities.head: Karamanli pashas; Ottoman governors; the Sanusi order in Cyrenaica
polities.rel: Maliki Sunni Islam; the Sanusi Sufi order from 1843
polities.econ: Trans-Saharan caravan trade, corsairing to 1815; the US Marines at Derna in 1805
polities.now: Three Ottoman provinces, Tripoli, Cyrenaica and Fezzan, lightly governed, with the Sanusi order as the real authority in the interior.
polities.how: The Karamanlis ruled as hereditary pashas; the Ottomans reasserted control in 1835 to keep the French out.
polities.next: Italy invades in 1911 and spends twenty years conquering the interior.

polities.gov: Italian colony; the 'fourth shore' settled with Italians from the 1930s
polities.head: Italian governors; Omar Mukhtar's resistance to 1931; Idris of the Sanusi
polities.rel: Sunni Islam; Italian Catholic settlers
polities.econ: Settler farms; the war of 1940 to 1943 fought across its coast
polities.now: Italy's conquest, completed only in 1932 after concentration camps killed tens of thousands in Cyrenaica, ends with British and French occupation in 1943.
polities.how: The 1911 war with the Ottomans, the Sanusi resistance, Mussolini's settlement programme.
polities.next: The UN makes Libya independent under King Idris in 1951.

polities.gov: Sanusi monarchy to 1969; Gaddafi's 'state of the masses' to 2011; divided between rival governments in Tripoli and the east since 2014
polities.head: King Idris; Muammar Gaddafi 1969 to 2011; rival prime ministers; Khalifa Haftar in the east
polities.rel: Sunni Islam
polities.econ: Oil, found in 1959; Africa's largest reserves; output hostage to the political split
polities.now: Gaddafi's coup of 1969 made Libya an oil-funded sponsor of revolution and terrorism and then a Western partner after 2003; NATO's 2011 intervention helped overthrow him and left a state that has not been reassembled.
polities.how: Oil, the 1969 coup, Lockerbie, the 2011 revolt and the 2014 split.
polities.next: Elections have been promised and postponed since 2021.

polities.gov: Sultanate of the Funj with Arab and Nubian vassals
polities.head: Funj sultans
polities.rel: Sunni Islam; Islamisation of the Nilotic Sudan
polities.econ: Gold, slaves, gum arabic; caravans to Egypt and the Red Sea
polities.now: The kingdom that made the central Nile Islamic, replacing Christian Nubia, and ruled from Sennar for three centuries.
polities.how: Funj and Arab forces took Soba around 1504 and founded the sultanate.
polities.next: Muhammad Ali's Egyptian army conquers Sennar in 1821.

polities.gov: Egyptian conquest 1821; the Mahdist state 1885 to 1898; Anglo-Egyptian condominium from 1899, British in practice
polities.head: Egyptian governors including Gordon; the Mahdi and the Khalifa; British governors-general
polities.rel: Sunni Islam in the north; the Mahdi's messianic movement; animist and Christian south
polities.econ: Gezira cotton scheme from 1925; slave trade suppressed in law
polities.now: Conquered for slaves and gold by Egypt, lost to the Mahdi's revolt in 1885 when Gordon died at Khartoum, retaken by Kitchener at Omdurman in 1898 with 10,000 Sudanese dead, and governed by Britain with the south closed off from the north.
polities.how: Egyptian rule, the Mahdist state, and the condominium; the 'Southern Policy' of the 1930s separated the regions.
polities.next: Independence in January 1956; the southern mutiny of 1955 begins a civil war.

polities.gov: Alternating military regimes and short parliaments; Omar al-Bashir's Islamist military rule 1989 to 2019; a transition overturned by the 2021 coup; civil war between the army and the RSF since April 2023
polities.head: Nimeiri; Sadiq al-Mahdi; Omar al-Bashir; General Burhan and the RSF's Hemedti
polities.cap: Khartoum, devastated since 2023; government operating from Port Sudan
polities.rel: Sunni Islam; the Christian and animist south seceded in 2011
polities.pop: About 48 million; more than 10 million displaced since 2023
polities.econ: Oil mostly lost with South Sudan; gold, gum arabic; famine conditions since 2024
polities.now: Two civil wars with the south, the Darfur genocide from 2003, the 2019 revolution that removed Bashir, and since 2023 a war between two generals that has produced the world's largest displacement crisis.
polities.how: The north-south wars of 1955 to 1972 and 1983 to 2005; the 2005 peace and 2011 secession; the army-RSF partnership that turned on itself.
polities.next: No settlement is in sight; partition along the army-RSF front is possible.

polities.gov: Christian monarchy claiming descent from Solomon; the Era of the Princes (1769 to 1855) leaves emperors as puppets of regional lords
polities.head: Zara Yaqob (1434 to 1468), Lebna Dengel, Fasilides; figurehead emperors after 1769
polities.rel: Ethiopian Orthodox Christianity; Muslim lowlands; Oromo migrations from the 1530s
polities.econ: Highland agriculture, tribute, slaves and ivory to the Red Sea
polities.now: Africa's oldest Christian state, nearly destroyed by Adal's jihad in the 1530s and saved by Portuguese musketeers, then confined to the highlands by Oromo expansion, and after 1769 fragmented among warlords.
polities.how: The Solomonic restoration of 1270, the wars with Adal, the Gondar monarchy, and the princes' era.
polities.next: Tewodros II defeats the regional lords and crowns himself emperor in 1855.

polities.gov: Imperial monarchy rebuilt by Tewodros, Yohannes IV and Menelik II; a constitution in 1931 under Haile Selassie
polities.head: Tewodros II, Yohannes IV, Menelik II (1889 to 1913), Haile Selassie from 1930
polities.rel: Ethiopian Orthodox; Muslim and other conquered peoples in the south
polities.econ: Coffee, the Djibouti railway from 1917, firearms bought with ivory and gold
polities.now: The one African state to defeat a European army, at Adwa in 1896, which doubled its territory southward under Menelik and entered the League of Nations in 1923.
polities.how: Tewodros's reunification, Yohannes's wars with Egypt and the Mahdists, Menelik's conquests and Adwa.
polities.next: Mussolini invades in October 1935 and takes Addis Ababa in May 1936.

polities.gov: Italian colony merged with Eritrea and Somaliland
polities.head: Viceroy; Haile Selassie in exile at Bath
polities.rel: Orthodox and Muslim; the Church persecuted after the 1937 attempt on the viceroy
polities.econ: Roads and settler schemes; poison gas used in the conquest
polities.now: Mussolini's empire in the Horn, won with mustard gas and held by massacre, which the League of Nations failed to prevent.
polities.how: The invasion of 1935 and the fall of Addis Ababa in May 1936; sanctions failed.
polities.next: British and Ethiopian forces restore Haile Selassie in May 1941.

polities.gov: Imperial autocracy with a nominal parliament
polities.head: Emperor Haile Selassie I
polities.cap: Addis Ababa, seat of the Organisation of African Unity from 1963
polities.rel: Ethiopian Orthodox; Muslim third
polities.econ: Coffee; feudal land tenure; famine in Wollo 1972 to 1974
polities.now: The restored emperor made Addis Ababa the capital of African diplomacy, federated and then annexed Eritrea, and left a feudal countryside that famine and a student movement turned against him.
polities.how: The 1941 restoration, the 1952 Eritrean federation, the 1960 coup attempt.
polities.next: A military committee, the Derg, deposes the emperor in September 1974 and murders him in 1975.

polities.gov: Marxist-Leninist military junta; a one-party state from 1987
polities.head: Mengistu Haile Mariam
polities.rel: Orthodox and Muslim; state atheism
polities.econ: Collectivised agriculture; the 1984 to 1985 famine killed up to a million; Soviet and Cuban military aid
polities.now: The Derg's revolution nationalised land, killed tens of thousands in the Red Terror, fought Somalia in the Ogaden in 1977 with Soviet help, and lost the wars against Eritrean and Tigrayan insurgents.
polities.how: The 1974 revolution, Mengistu's consolidation by 1977, Soviet patronage.
polities.next: The EPRDF takes Addis Ababa in May 1991; Eritrea becomes independent in 1993.

polities.gov: Ethnic federation under the EPRDF's dominant-party rule to 2018; Abiy Ahmed's Prosperity Party since
polities.head: Meles Zenawi 1991 to 2012; Hailemariam; Abiy Ahmed since 2018
polities.rel: Orthodox and Muslim roughly 40 and 35 per cent; Protestant growth
polities.econ: One of Africa's fastest growth rates 2004 to 2019; the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam; the Tigray war's costs
polities.now: Africa's second most populous state, federal by ethnicity since 1995, at war with Eritrea 1998 to 2000, reconciled under Abiy in 2018, and then at war with Tigray from 2020 to 2022 at a cost of hundreds of thousands of lives; insurgencies continue in Amhara and Oromia.
polities.how: The EPRDF's victory, Meles's developmental state, Abiy's rise and the Tigray war.
polities.next: Sea access, the Nile dam dispute with Egypt, and internal insurgencies are the fronts.

polities.gov: Muslim sultanate of the Afar and Somali lowlands
polities.head: Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi, 'Gragn', 1527 to 1543
polities.rel: Sunni Islam
polities.econ: Trade through Zeila; Ottoman firearms
polities.now: The sultanate whose imam Ahmad Gragn conquered most of Christian Ethiopia between 1529 and 1543 with Ottoman muskets, until Portuguese musketeers helped kill him.
polities.how: Adal grew from the Ifat sultanate as the Muslim rival to the Christian highlands.
polities.next: Oromo expansion and the loss of Gragn break Adal; Harar survives as a city-state.

polities.t: Eritrea under Italy, Britain and Ethiopia
polities.gov: Italian colony from 1890; British administration 1941 to 1952; federated with Ethiopia 1952, annexed 1962
polities.head: Italian and British governors; Haile Selassie; the EPLF insurgency from 1961
polities.rel: Orthodox Christian and Sunni Muslim in near-equal shares
polities.econ: Asmara's Italian-built industry; war economy after 1961
polities.now: Italy's first colony, with an Art Deco capital, which Ethiopia annexed in 1962 and fought for thirty years.
polities.how: Italian colonisation from 1885, the federation the UN arranged, its abolition.
polities.next: The EPLF takes Asmara in 1991; independence by referendum in 1993.

polities.gov: One-party state under Isaias Afwerki; no elections, no constitution in force, indefinite conscription
polities.head: Isaias Afwerki since 1993
polities.rel: Orthodox and Muslim
polities.econ: Subsistence, mining, remittances; closed
polities.now: Independent since 1993 and governed since by its liberation movement's leader without elections, Eritrea fought Ethiopia in 1998 to 2000, made peace in 2018, and joined the Tigray war on Ethiopia's side.
polities.how: Thirty years of war built a militarised state that never demobilised.
polities.next: Succession to Isaias is the only question.

polities.gov: Sultanates of Majeerteen and Hobyo, the Geledi; British Somaliland protectorate from 1884; Italian Somaliland from 1889; the Dervish state 1899 to 1920
polities.head: Sultans; Sayyid Mohammed Abdullah Hassan, the 'Mad Mullah'; colonial governors
polities.rel: Sunni Islam
polities.econ: Livestock, bananas on Italian plantations, frankincense
polities.now: A coast of clan sultanates divided among Britain, Italy, France and Ethiopia, where the Dervish movement fought the British for twenty years until aircraft ended it in 1920.
polities.how: The scramble partitioned the Somali lands five ways.
polities.next: British and Italian Somaliland unite as independent Somalia in July 1960.

polities.gov: Parliamentary republic 1960 to 1969; Siad Barre's military socialism to 1991; state collapse; a federal government since 2012 controlling little beyond the cities
polities.head: Siad Barre 1969 to 1991; presidents since 2012; Al-Shabaab in the countryside
polities.rel: Sunni Islam
polities.econ: Livestock exports, remittances, piracy in the 2000s; aid dependence
polities.now: Siad Barre's defeat in the 1977 Ogaden war and the clan rebellions of the 1980s destroyed the state in 1991; the US intervention of 1992 to 1994 failed; Al-Shabaab has fought the federal government and African Union troops since 2007; Somaliland in the north has governed itself since 1991 without recognition.
polities.how: Independence, the 1969 coup, the Ogaden war, the 1991 collapse.
polities.next: Somaliland's recognition bid and the drawdown of AU forces are the next turns.

polities.gov: French colony to 1977; presidential republic under one family since
polities.head: Hassan Gouled; Ismaïl Omar Guelleh since 1999
polities.rel: Sunni Islam
polities.econ: Port and rail outlet for Ethiopia; rent from French, American, Chinese, Japanese and Italian bases
polities.now: A port at the mouth of the Red Sea that lives on Ethiopia's trade and foreign military bases, including China's first overseas base from 2017.
polities.how: France took the coast in the 1880s for the railway to Addis Ababa.
polities.next: Its strategic rent rises with every Red Sea crisis.

polities.gov: Uzbek khanates of Bukhara, Khiva and Kokand; the Kazakh hordes; nomadic confederations
polities.head: Shaybanid and later Uzbek khans; Kazakh khans
polities.rel: Sunni Islam; Bukhara a centre of learning
polities.econ: Silk Road caravans in decline after the sea routes; cotton and slaves; the Russian trade
polities.now: The Timurid lands fell to the Uzbeks in 1500 and fragmented into khanates that fought each other and raided Persia, while Russia advanced across the Kazakh steppe from the 1730s.
polities.how: Shaybani Khan's conquest of Samarkand in 1500; the Kazakh khanate's split into three hordes.
polities.next: Russia takes Tashkent in 1865, Samarkand in 1868 and Khiva in 1873; the khanates become protectorates and then Soviet republics.

polities.gov: Giray khanate, a Golden Horde successor under Ottoman suzerainty from 1475
polities.head: Giray khans
polities.rel: Sunni Islam
polities.econ: Slave raids into Russia and Poland sold at Kaffa to the Ottomans
polities.now: The Tatar state that burned Moscow in 1571 and supplied the Ottoman slave markets from Slavic raids for two centuries.
polities.how: The Girays broke from the Golden Horde in the 1440s and accepted Ottoman overlordship.
polities.next: Russia annexes the Crimea in 1783.

polities.gov: Durrani monarchy from 1747; British-controlled foreign policy 1880 to 1919; constitutional monarchy 1964; republic by Daoud's coup 1973
polities.head: Ahmad Shah Durrani; Dost Mohammad; Abdur Rahman (1880 to 1901); Amanullah; Zahir Shah 1933 to 1973; Daoud
polities.rel: Sunni Islam; Shia Hazara minority
polities.econ: Subsistence agriculture, karakul, transit trade; Soviet and American aid rivalry after 1955
polities.now: The buffer state between Russia and British India, which beat the British in 1842 and 1880, lost control of its foreign policy to them until 1919, and under Zahir Shah tried cautious modernisation before Daoud's coup and the communist coup of 1978.
polities.how: Ahmad Shah's empire, the Anglo-Afghan wars, Abdur Rahman's iron rule and the Durand Line of 1893.
polities.next: The communist coup of April 1978 and the Soviet invasion of December 1979 begin four decades of war.

polities.gov: Soviet-backed communist government to 1992; mujahideen civil war; Taliban emirate 1996 to 2001; US-backed republic 2001 to 2021; Taliban emirate since August 2021
polities.head: Najibullah; the Taliban's Mullah Omar; Karzai; Ghani; Hibatullah Akhundzada
polities.rel: Sunni Islam under Taliban law; girls barred from secondary school since 2021
polities.econ: Aid-dependent to 2021; opium until the Taliban ban of 2022; sanctions and frozen reserves
polities.now: Invaded by the Soviets in 1979 and by the United States in 2001, Afghanistan has had a war on its soil for forty-five years; the Taliban returned when the US withdrew in August 2021 and govern without recognition.
polities.how: The Soviet war killed about a million; the civil war destroyed Kabul; the Taliban's first rule hosted al-Qaeda; the twenty-year US war ended in collapse.
polities.next: Recognition, the economy and the exclusion of women are the standing questions.

polities.gov: Presidential authoritarian state; Nazarbayev 1991 to 2019, Tokayev since
polities.head: Nursultan Nazarbayev; Kassym-Jomart Tokayev
polities.rel: Sunni Islam majority; Orthodox Russian minority
polities.econ: Oil, uranium, grain, metals; the largest economy in Central Asia
polities.now: The ninth-largest country by area, Soviet until 1991, which gave up its nuclear weapons, moved its capital north to anchor the Russian-populated region, and after the January 2022 unrest tilted carefully away from Moscow.
polities.how: The Kazakh khanate, Russian conquest, the famine of 1930 to 1933 that killed a third of Kazakhs, and Nazarbayev's state.
polities.next: Balancing Russia, China and the West defines its foreign policy.

polities.gov: Presidential authoritarian state; Karimov 1991 to 2016; Mirziyoyev's cautious opening since
polities.head: Islam Karimov; Shavkat Mirziyoyev
polities.rel: Sunni Islam
polities.econ: Cotton, gold, gas; forced labour in cotton ended in the 2010s
polities.now: Heir to Bukhara and Samarkand, closed and repressive under Karimov, including the Andijan massacre of 2005, and opening economically since 2016.
polities.how: The Uzbek SSR became a state in 1991 under its last communist boss.
polities.next: Reform's depth and the succession.

polities.gov: Personal dictatorship; Niyazov to 2006, the Berdimuhamedow family since
polities.head: Saparmurat Niyazov; Gurbanguly and Serdar Berdimuhamedow
polities.rel: Sunni Islam
polities.econ: Gas exports, mostly to China; among the most closed economies in the world
polities.now: A gas-rich desert state ruled as a personality cult since 1991, permanently neutral by UN resolution, and nearly closed to the outside.
polities.how: The Turkmen SSR's party boss made himself Türkmenbaşy.
polities.next: Gas routes to China and possibly Europe are its only external question.

polities.gov: The region's most contested politics: three presidents overthrown by protest in 2005, 2010 and 2020; presidential system since 2021
polities.head: Sadyr Japarov since 2021
polities.rel: Sunni Islam
polities.econ: Gold, remittances from Russia, hydropower
polities.now: A mountain republic that has changed government by street revolt three times and hosted both American and Russian bases.
polities.how: Independence in 1991; the Tulip Revolution of 2005.
polities.next: Dependence on Russian remittances and Chinese loans.

polities.gov: Presidential dictatorship under Rahmon since 1992
polities.head: Emomali Rahmon
polities.rel: Sunni Islam; Ismaili Pamiris
polities.econ: The poorest post-Soviet state; remittances near half of GDP; aluminium, hydropower
polities.now: A civil war of 1992 to 1997 killed tens of thousands; Rahmon has ruled since, with a Russian base and a border with Taliban Afghanistan.
polities.how: The Persian-speaking Soviet republic's independence and war.
polities.next: Succession to Rahmon's son and the Afghan border.

polities.gov: Hereditary empire; the emperor rules through a civil service recruited by examination and, from the sixteenth century, through palace eunuchs
polities.head: Yongle (1402 to 1424), Zhengtong, Jiajing, Wanli (1572 to 1620), Chongzhen
polities.rel: Confucian state orthodoxy; Buddhism and Daoism; Jesuits at court from 1601
polities.pop: About 65 million in 1400, perhaps 150 million by 1600, the largest in the world
polities.econ: The largest economy on earth; silver from Japan and Spanish America monetises taxes after the 1570s; porcelain and silk exports
polities.now: The most populous and richest state in the world, which sent Zheng He's fleets to Africa in the 1400s and then turned inward, rebuilt the Great Wall after the Tumu disaster of 1449, and by the 1620s is bankrupt, famine-struck and facing the Manchus.
polities.how: The Ming expelled the Mongols in 1368; Yongle's capital and canal fixed the state's shape; the single-whip tax reform tied China to the world silver supply.
polities.next: Li Zicheng's rebels take Beijing in April 1644; the last emperor hangs himself; a Ming general opens the Wall to the Manchus.

polities.t: The Ming-Qing transition in the south
polities.gov: Rival Ming courts and the Three Feudatories, Chinese generals holding the south as fiefs under the Qing until their revolt of 1673 to 1681
polities.head: Southern Ming princes; Wu Sangui; Koxinga on Taiwan
polities.rel: Confucian orthodoxy
polities.pop: Tens of millions in the war-ravaged south
polities.econ: Devastation; coastal evacuation to starve Koxinga's Taiwan
polities.now: Forty years of resistance to the Manchus in the south: Ming loyalist courts to 1662, Koxinga's maritime state on Taiwan to 1683, and the revolt of the three generals the Qing had rewarded.
polities.how: The Manchu conquest of the north in 1644 left the south to Ming princes and warlords.
polities.next: The Kangxi emperor crushes the feudatories by 1681 and takes Taiwan in 1683.

polities.gov: Manchu conquest dynasty ruling through the Ming bureaucracy, the Eight Banners and a Grand Council from 1733
polities.head: Shunzhi, Kangxi (1661 to 1722), Yongzheng, Qianlong (1735 to 1796)
polities.rel: Confucian orthodoxy; Tibetan Buddhism patronised for Mongol and Tibetan subjects; Christianity banned 1724
polities.econ: The world's largest economy; tea, silk and porcelain exports for silver; the Canton system restricts Western trade from 1757
polities.now: A Manchu minority ruling the largest and richest state on earth, which doubled China's territory by conquering Taiwan, Mongolia, Tibet and Xinjiang, and under three long-lived emperors delivered a century of peace and population growth.
polities.how: The Manchus took Beijing in 1644 and the south by 1683; Kangxi fixed the Russian border at Nerchinsk in 1689; Qianlong's campaigns completed the empire.
polities.next: Population outruns land; the White Lotus rebellion of 1796 and the opium trade begin the decline.

polities.gov: Qing dynasty under pressure; the Self-Strengthening reforms after 1861; Empress Dowager Cixi the real power 1861 to 1908; a constitution promised 1908
polities.head: Jiaqing, Daoguang, Xianfeng, Tongzhi, Guangxu, Cixi, Puyi
polities.rel: Confucian orthodoxy; the Taiping's heterodox Christianity; missionaries under treaty protection
polities.econ: Opium imports drain silver; treaty ports from 1842; foreign loans and indemnities after 1895; the first railways and arsenals
polities.now: The empire humiliated by Britain in the Opium Wars, nearly destroyed by the Taiping rebellion of 1850 to 1864 that killed some 20 million, beaten by Japan in 1895, occupied after the Boxer rising of 1900, and attempting reform too late.
polities.how: Opium, the treaty system, the mid-century rebellions and the failure of reform against conservative resistance.
polities.next: The Wuchang rising of October 1911; the child emperor abdicates in February 1912.

polities.t: Republic of China, the warlord era
polities.gov: Republic proclaimed 1912; Yuan Shikai's dictatorship to 1916; provincial generals govern their own regions; the Nationalists in Guangzhou
polities.head: Sun Yat-sen; Yuan Shikai; warlords Zhang Zuolin, Wu Peifu, Feng Yuxiang; Chiang Kai-shek from 1926
polities.cap: Beijing nominally; Guangzhou for the Nationalists
polities.rel: Confucian order under attack from the May Fourth movement of 1919
polities.econ: Treaty-port industry in Shanghai; rural immiseration; Japanese demands of 1915
polities.now: A republic without a government: Yuan Shikai's death in 1916 left China to rival generals, while the May Fourth movement, the Nationalist party and the Communist party founded in 1921 compete for the future.
polities.how: The 1911 revolution ended the monarchy without building a state; Yuan's attempt to become emperor failed.
polities.next: Chiang's Northern Expedition of 1926 to 1928 unifies the country nominally and breaks with the Communists in the Shanghai massacre of 1927.

polities.t: Republic of China under the Nationalists
polities.gov: One-party Nationalist (Kuomintang) tutelage; Chiang Kai-shek as leader; the Communists in rival base areas
polities.head: Chiang Kai-shek; Mao Zedong leading the Communist Party from 1935
polities.rel: New Life movement's Confucian revival; Christianity among the elite
polities.econ: Nanjing decade's modest growth; the war with Japan from 1937 destroys the economy; hyperinflation by 1948
polities.now: The Nationalist state built the beginnings of a modern government in the Nanjing decade, lost Manchuria to Japan in 1931 and the coast in 1937, fought the Japanese for eight years, and lost the civil war that followed to the Communists.
polities.how: The Northern Expedition, the Long March of 1934 to 1935, the Xi'an incident of 1936 forcing a united front, and the war of 1937 to 1945.
polities.next: The People's Republic is proclaimed in October 1949; the Nationalists withdraw to Taiwan.

polities.t: People's Republic of China under Mao
polities.gov: One-party communist state; the Chairman's personal rule over party and state
polities.head: Mao Zedong; Zhou Enlai as premier
polities.rel: State atheism; religion suppressed, temples and churches closed in the Cultural Revolution
polities.econ: Soviet-model industrialisation; the Great Leap Forward of 1958 to 1962 causes a famine of 30 to 45 million deaths; the Cultural Revolution halts growth
polities.now: Mao's China unified the country, fought the United States to a standstill in Korea, broke with the Soviet Union, tested a nuclear weapon in 1964, and twice turned on its own society: the Great Leap's famine and the Cultural Revolution of 1966 to 1976.
polities.how: Victory in the civil war, land reform, the Leap, the split with Moscow, and Mao's purge of the party through the Red Guards.
polities.next: Mao dies in September 1976; Deng Xiaoping takes control by 1978 and opens the economy.
polities.wk: History of the People's Republic of China (1949–1976)

polities.t: People's Republic of China, reform and rise
polities.gov: One-party state; collective leadership from Deng to Hu; personalised rule under Xi Jinping since 2012, term limits abolished 2018
polities.head: Deng Xiaoping; Jiang Zemin; Hu Jintao; Xi Jinping
polities.rel: Officially atheist; Buddhism, Daoism, folk religion, Christianity and Islam practised under control; Uyghur internment from 2017
polities.econ: From 2 per cent of world output in 1980 to about 18 per cent; the world's largest manufacturer and exporter; WTO entry 2001; property and debt strains since 2021
polities.now: The reforms from 1978 produced the largest and fastest economic rise in history and a party that crushed the 1989 Tiananmen protests and never loosened; under Xi the state has reasserted control over the economy, built the world's largest navy, and set Taiwan's unification as a goal.
polities.how: Deng's opening, the 1989 crackdown, WTO accession, and Xi's centralisation.
polities.next: Demographic decline, the property overhang, Taiwan and the rivalry with the United States set the horizon.

polities.gov: Austronesian peoples; Dutch colony 1624 to 1662; Koxinga's Ming loyalist kingdom to 1683; Qing prefecture, a province from 1887
polities.head: Dutch governors; Koxinga; Qing officials
polities.rel: Indigenous traditions; Chinese folk religion with settlement
polities.econ: Deer hides and sugar under the Dutch; rice and camphor under the Qing
polities.now: An island on the edge of the Chinese world, held by the Dutch, then by the last Ming loyalists, and settled from Fujian under a Qing administration that governed it lightly until the French threat of 1884.
polities.how: The Dutch East India Company, Koxinga's conquest in 1662, the Qing annexation of 1683.
polities.next: Japan takes Taiwan from the Qing in 1895 after the first Sino-Japanese war.

polities.gov: Japanese colony under a governor-general
polities.head: Japanese governors-general
polities.rel: Shinto promoted; Chinese folk religion continued
polities.econ: Sugar and rice for Japan; railways, schools, public health; industrialisation in the 1930s
polities.now: Japan's model colony, developed for sugar and rice, with assimilation pushed hardest in the war years.
polities.how: Ceded at Shimonoseki in 1895; resistance suppressed by 1902.
polities.next: Returned to the Republic of China in 1945; the 1947 massacre of February 28 poisons relations with the mainlanders who arrive in 1949.

polities.gov: Nationalist one-party rule under martial law 1949 to 1987; democracy since the 1990s with direct presidential elections from 1996
polities.head: Chiang Kai-shek; Chiang Ching-kuo; Lee Teng-hui; Chen Shui-bian; Ma Ying-jeou; Tsai Ing-wen; Lai Ching-te
polities.rel: Buddhist, Daoist and folk religion; Christian minority
polities.econ: Land reform, export manufacturing, and the semiconductor industry: TSMC makes most of the world's advanced chips
polities.now: The Nationalists' refuge after 1949 became one of Asia's richest economies and, since the 1990s, a full democracy that Beijing claims and has not renounced force to take; recognised by a dozen states, defended informally by the United States.
polities.how: American protection from 1950, land reform, the export boom, Chiang Ching-kuo's liberalisation and Lee's democratisation.
polities.next: Whether the status quo in the strait holds is the question that could decide the century.

polities.gov: Chinese provincial governors ruling autonomously; Soviet influence under Sheng Shicai 1933 to 1944
polities.head: Yang Zengxin; Jin Shuren; Sheng Shicai
polities.rel: Sunni Muslim Uyghur and Kazakh majority; Han Chinese administration
polities.econ: Pastoralism, oases, Soviet trade
polities.now: The Qing's last conquest, nominally a Chinese province, governed by its own strongmen with Soviet backing, and the site of two short-lived East Turkestan republics in 1933 and 1944.
polities.how: Qing conquest in the 1750s, a province from 1884, warlord autonomy after 1911.
polities.next: The People's Liberation Army enters in 1949; an autonomous region from 1955; mass internment of Uyghurs from 2017.
polities.wk: Xinjiang under Republic of China rule

polities.gov: Buddhist theocracy under the Dalai Lamas from 1642, with Qing protectorate 1720 to 1912 and de facto independence after
polities.head: Dalai Lamas; the Great Fifth (1642 to 1682); the Thirteenth (1895 to 1933)
polities.rel: Tibetan Buddhism; the Gelug school dominant
polities.econ: Pastoral and monastic economy; wool, salt, tea trade with China
polities.now: A theocratic state on the roof of Asia, governed from the Potala by the Dalai Lama's regency, under Qing overlordship exercised through residents at Lhasa, and from 1913 effectively independent while Britain, Russia and China contested it.
polities.how: The Mongol Gushri Khan installed the Fifth Dalai Lama in 1642; the Qing intervened in 1720 and 1792; the Younghusband expedition of 1904 opened it to Britain.
polities.next: The People's Liberation Army enters in 1950; the 1959 rising fails and the Dalai Lama flees to India.

polities.gov: Theocratic monarchy under the Bogd Khan 1911 to 1924; Soviet-aligned People's Republic 1924 to 1990; parliamentary democracy since
polities.head: The Bogd Khan; Choibalsan; Tsedenbal; presidents and prime ministers since 1990
polities.rel: Tibetan Buddhism, suppressed 1937 to 1939 with 17,000 monks killed, revived since 1990
polities.econ: Herding; coal and copper exports to China dominate since 2010
polities.now: Outer Mongolia left the Qing in 1911, became the second communist state in 1924, lost its monasteries to Stalinist purges, and in 1990 became a democracy wedged between Russia and China.
polities.how: The Qing collapse, Soviet protection, the 1990 revolution.
polities.next: Mineral dependence on China is the structural fact.

polities.gov: Zhang Zuolin's warlord domain to 1928; Japanese puppet state of Manchukuo 1932 to 1945 under Puyi
polities.head: Zhang Zuolin; Zhang Xueliang; Puyi as emperor of Manchukuo; the Kwantung Army
polities.rel: Chinese folk religion; Shinto imposed
polities.econ: Soybeans, coal, steel at Anshan; Japan's heavy-industrial base; the South Manchuria Railway
polities.now: The Manchu homeland, flooded with Han settlers, held by the Zhang warlords and seized by Japan's Kwantung Army in September 1931, which installed the last Qing emperor as a puppet.
polities.how: The Russo-Japanese war of 1905 gave Japan the railway zone; the Mukden incident of 1931 gave it the whole.
polities.next: The Soviet army overruns Manchukuo in August 1945; the Communists use it as their base to win the civil war.

polities.gov: British crown colony 1842 to 1997; special administrative region of China since, with autonomy curtailed by the 2020 national security law
polities.head: British governors; chief executives since 1997
polities.rel: Buddhist, Daoist, Christian; freedom of religion
polities.econ: Entrepôt, then manufacturing, then one of the world's three largest financial centres
polities.now: Taken by Britain in the Opium War and returned to China in 1997 under 'one country, two systems'; the 2019 protests and the 2020 security law ended most of its political freedoms.
polities.how: The 1842 treaty, the 1898 lease of the New Territories, the 1984 Joint Declaration.
polities.next: Its role as China's financial window depends on trust Beijing has spent.

polities.gov: The Ashikaga shogunate a nullity; daimyo lords rule their own domains; unification under Nobunaga and Hideyoshi from the 1560s
polities.head: Oda Nobunaga; Toyotomi Hideyoshi (ruler 1585 to 1598); the emperor in Kyoto without power
polities.rel: Buddhism, Shinto; Jesuit missions from 1549 win 300,000 converts; Hideyoshi's expulsion edict of 1587
polities.econ: Portuguese traders bring muskets in 1543; silver from Iwami makes Japan a major exporter
