polities.now: A century of civil war among feudal lords ending in unification: Nobunaga destroyed the Buddhist armies, Hideyoshi conquered the rest, disarmed the peasants, and invaded Korea twice.
polities.how: The Onin war of 1467 broke central authority; firearms and castle-building concentrated power in the strongest lords.
polities.next: Tokugawa Ieyasu wins at Sekigahara in 1600 and founds a shogunate that lasts to 1868.

polities.gov: Shogunate at Edo over some 260 domains; the emperor in Kyoto as sacred figurehead; a hereditary caste order
polities.head: Tokugawa Ieyasu and fourteen successor shoguns
polities.cap: Edo (Tokyo) for the shogun; Kyoto for the emperor
polities.rel: Buddhism and Shinto; Christianity banned from 1614 and exterminated after the Shimabara revolt of 1637
polities.econ: Closed to all but Dutch and Chinese trade at Nagasaki from 1639; a commercial economy with Edo the largest city in the world around 1700
polities.now: Two and a half centuries of internal peace under a closed-country policy, with high literacy, a national market and a samurai class with nothing to fight; Perry's ships in 1853 force the ports open and expose the shogunate's weakness.
polities.how: Sekigahara, the sakoku edicts of the 1630s, the alternate attendance system that bankrupted the lords.
polities.next: Satsuma and Choshu overthrow the shogunate; the Meiji emperor is restored to power in January 1868.

polities.gov: Constitutional monarchy from 1889 with the emperor sovereign and the army answerable to him alone; party cabinets in the 1920s; military domination from 1932
polities.head: Emperor Meiji (to 1912), Taisho, Hirohito; Ito Hirobumi; Tojo Hideki prime minister 1941 to 1944
polities.rel: State Shinto with the emperor as divine descendant; Buddhism
polities.econ: Industrialised in a generation: railways, textiles, shipyards, the zaibatsu conglomerates; empire for raw materials
polities.now: The Meiji state abolished feudalism, built a conscript army and modern industry, defeated China in 1895 and Russia in 1905, annexed Korea in 1910, seized Manchuria in 1931, invaded China in 1937, and attacked Pearl Harbor in December 1941.
polities.how: The restoration of 1868, the constitution of 1889, the victories of 1895 and 1905, the Depression and the army's takeover of policy.
polities.next: Atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki and Soviet entry bring surrender in August 1945.

polities.gov: Constitutional monarchy under the 1947 constitution written by the US occupation; parliamentary democracy; the Liberal Democratic Party in power almost continuously since 1955
polities.head: Emperor as symbol; prime ministers Yoshida, Sato, Nakasone, Koizumi, Abe (longest-serving)
polities.rel: Shinto and Buddhism as customs; constitutional secularism
polities.econ: The second-largest economy from 1968 to 2010; cars, electronics, robotics; the 1990 bubble's collapse and three decades of slow growth
polities.now: Occupied, disarmed and democratised by the United States, Japan grew into the world's second economy by 1968, stagnated after 1990, and is rearming cautiously as China rises; its population is the oldest in the world.
polities.how: The occupation reforms, the 1951 treaty and US alliance, the economic miracle, the bubble.
polities.next: Demography, debt, and the defence build-up against China and North Korea.

polities.gov: Confucian monarchy of the Yi dynasty; a scholar-official bureaucracy; the Korean Empire from 1897
polities.head: Sejong (1418 to 1450), Seonjo, Yeongjo, Gojong (1864 to 1907)
polities.rel: Neo-Confucian state orthodoxy; Buddhism suppressed; Catholicism persecuted in the nineteenth century
polities.econ: Rice agriculture; tribute relations with China; ginseng; isolation from the West until 1876
polities.now: A Confucian kingdom for five centuries, which invented its alphabet under Sejong, survived the Japanese invasions of 1592 to 1598 and the Manchu invasions of the 1630s, closed itself as the 'hermit kingdom', and after 1876 became the prize China, Japan and Russia fought over.
polities.how: The Yi dynasty's founding in 1392, Confucianisation, the Imjin war, the opening by Japan in 1876, and the wars of 1894 and 1904 fought on its soil.
polities.next: Japan makes Korea a protectorate in 1905 and annexes it in August 1910.

polities.gov: Japanese colony under a governor-general, usually a general
polities.head: Japanese governors-general
polities.rel: Shinto shrine worship imposed; Christianity grows as a nationalist faith
polities.econ: Rice for Japan; northern heavy industry and hydropower; forced labour and 'comfort women' in the war
polities.now: Thirty-five years of colonial rule that built railways and industry, suppressed the March First independence movement of 1919, and in the war years tried to erase Korean language and names.
polities.how: Annexation in 1910; the 1919 uprising; assimilation policy from the 1930s.
polities.next: Soviet and American forces divide Korea at the 38th parallel in August 1945.

polities.gov: American military government to 1948; Syngman Rhee's autocracy; military rule under Park Chung-hee and Chun Doo-hwan 1961 to 1987; democracy since 1987
polities.head: Syngman Rhee; Park Chung-hee 1961 to 1979; Kim Dae-jung; presidents since, several imprisoned after office
polities.rel: Christian about 30 per cent, Buddhist about 20 per cent, half no religion
polities.pop: About 51 million; the world's lowest birth rate
polities.econ: From aid-dependent to the tenth-largest economy: Samsung, Hyundai, shipbuilding, semiconductors; the 1997 crisis and recovery
polities.now: Founded in 1948, invaded in 1950 and saved by the United States and the UN, industrialised by force under Park, democratised in 1987, and now a rich democracy facing a nuclear North and the lowest fertility rate ever recorded.
polities.how: The Korean war of 1950 to 1953, the 1961 coup, export-led growth, the June 1987 democracy movement.
polities.next: Demography and the North are the fixed problems; the US alliance the fixed answer.

polities.gov: Totalitarian hereditary dictatorship under the Kim family and the Workers' Party
polities.head: Kim Il Sung 1948 to 1994; Kim Jong Il to 2011; Kim Jong Un
polities.rel: State ideology of juche; religion suppressed
polities.econ: Command economy; famine of the mid-1990s killed hundreds of thousands; illicit trade, Chinese support, nuclear and missile programmes
polities.now: The Soviet-installed state that invaded the South in 1950, built a cult around three generations of Kims, starved in the 1990s, and has tested nuclear weapons since 2006; it supplies Russia with shells and troops for the Ukraine war.
polities.how: Soviet occupation, the war, the purges that made Kim Il Sung supreme, and the dynastic successions of 1994 and 2011.
polities.next: Its nuclear arsenal is now a fact the region plans around.

polities.gov: Turkic and Afghan sultanates ruling northern India from Delhi; the Sayyid and Lodi dynasties after Timur's sack of 1398
polities.head: Sayyid sultans; Lodi sultans Bahlul, Sikandar, Ibrahim
polities.rel: Sunni Islam ruling a Hindu majority; Sufi orders; bhakti movements
polities.econ: Agriculture, textiles, the Indian Ocean trade through Gujarat
polities.now: A sultanate reduced by Timur's sack of 1398 to a regional power, with Bengal, Gujarat, Malwa and the Deccan sultanates independent and Vijayanagara dominant in the south.
polities.how: Turkic conquests from 1192 built the sultanate; Tughluq overreach and Timur broke it.
polities.next: Babur defeats Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat in 1526 and founds the Mughal Empire.

polities.gov: Hindu monarchy over the southern Deccan with a military-feudal nayaka system
polities.head: Deva Raya II; Krishnadevaraya (1509 to 1529)
polities.cap: Vijayanagara (Hampi), among the largest cities in the world around 1500
polities.rel: Hinduism; patronage of temples; Muslim soldiers employed
polities.econ: Cotton, spices, diamonds from Golconda; trade with the Portuguese at Goa for horses
polities.now: The last great Hindu empire of the south, at its peak under Krishnadevaraya, holding the Deccan sultanates to the north with cavalry bought from the Portuguese.
polities.how: Founded in 1336 as a Hindu bulwark against the Delhi sultanate's southern expansion.
polities.next: The combined sultanates destroy the army at Talikota in 1565 and sack the capital; successor nayaka states survive to the seventeenth century.

polities.gov: Five Muslim sultanates, Bijapur, Ahmadnagar, Golconda, Bidar and Berar, successors of the Bahmani kingdom
polities.head: Adil Shahi, Nizam Shahi and Qutb Shahi dynasties
polities.rel: Shia and Sunni Islam ruling Hindu populations; Persian culture
polities.econ: Golconda's diamonds, including the Koh-i-Noor; Bijapur's cotton; trade through Goa and Masulipatnam
polities.now: The Bahmani successor states that destroyed Vijayanagara in 1565 and then fought each other and the Mughals for a century.
polities.how: The Bahmani sultanate broke up between 1490 and 1527.
polities.next: Aurangzeb annexes Bijapur in 1686 and Golconda in 1687.

polities.gov: Hereditary Muslim empire over most of India; the mansabdar ranking system; a centralised land-revenue administration under Akbar
polities.head: Babur, Humayun, Akbar (1556 to 1605), Jahangir, Shah Jahan, Aurangzeb (1658 to 1707)
polities.cap: Agra, Fatehpur Sikri, Lahore, Delhi (Shahjahanabad from 1648)
polities.rel: Sunni Islam; Akbar's policy of tolerance and the jizya's abolition; Aurangzeb's reimposition of orthodoxy
polities.pop: About 100 million in 1600, 150 million by 1700, about a quarter of humanity
polities.econ: About a quarter of world output; cotton textiles exported to Europe, Africa and Asia; the richest state in the world in revenue
polities.now: The richest empire on earth, built by Akbar on religious accommodation and a revenue system that reached every village, and extended by Aurangzeb to its largest size at the cost of a Deccan war that exhausted it.
polities.how: Babur's victory at Panipat in 1526, Akbar's conquests and settlement, the Taj Mahal's builder's wars, Aurangzeb's fifty-year reign.
polities.next: After Aurangzeb's death in 1707 the empire fragments; Nader Shah sacks Delhi in 1739.

polities.gov: Mughal emperors as figureheads; Marathas, Nizam, Awadh, Bengal, Sikhs and Mysore as the real powers; the East India Company a territorial state from 1765
polities.head: Later Mughals; Maratha peshwas; the Nizam of Hyderabad; Haidar Ali and Tipu Sultan of Mysore
polities.rel: Islam, Hinduism, Sikhism; the Company neutral by policy
polities.econ: Bengal's textiles under Company exaction; the Company's diwani of Bengal from 1765; the famine of 1770
polities.now: The empire has dissolved into successor states fighting for its remains, with the East India Company turning from trader to ruler after Plassey in 1757 and the grant of Bengal's revenues in 1765.
polities.how: Aurangzeb's overextension, Nader Shah's sack, the Maratha expansion, and the Company's victories at Plassey and Buxar.
polities.next: The Company takes Delhi in 1803 and the Mughal becomes its pensioner; the Marathas are broken by 1818.

polities.gov: Hindu confederacy under the Peshwa at Pune, with the Scindia, Holkar, Gaekwad and Bhonsle houses nearly independent
polities.head: Peshwas Baji Rao I (1720 to 1740) and successors; Mahadji Scindia
polities.rel: Hinduism
polities.pop: Tens of millions under Maratha tribute
polities.econ: Chauth tribute levied across India; cavalry armies
polities.now: Shivaji's kingdom grown into the largest power in India by 1760, collecting tribute from Delhi to the Carnatic, checked at Panipat by the Afghans in 1761, and then fighting three wars with the Company.
polities.how: Shivaji's rising against the Mughals from 1674; the Peshwas' expansion north.
polities.next: The third Anglo-Maratha war of 1817 to 1818 ends the confederacy.

polities.gov: Monarchy of Ranjit Singh over the Punjab from 1799; chaos after his death
polities.head: Maharaja Ranjit Singh (1801 to 1839)
polities.rel: Sikhism; Muslim and Hindu majority subjects
polities.econ: Punjab agriculture; a European-trained army of 80,000
polities.now: The Sikh misls united under Ranjit Singh into the last independent power in India, with a modern army that the Company fought twice after his death.
polities.how: The Sikh confederacies rose in the Mughal collapse; Ranjit Singh took Lahore in 1799.
polities.next: The Company annexes the Punjab in 1849 after the second Anglo-Sikh war.

polities.gov: Independent sultanate to 1576; Mughal province; nawabs effectively independent from 1717
polities.head: Husain Shahi sultans; Mughal governors; Nawabs Murshid Quli Khan, Alivardi Khan, Siraj ud-Daulah
polities.rel: Islam and Hinduism; Bengali Vaishnavism
polities.econ: The richest province of India: muslin and silk, rice, saltpetre; European factories at Hooghly and Calcutta
polities.now: The richest province in Mughal India, governed by its own nawabs after 1717, with the English, French and Dutch companies trading from fortified posts.
polities.how: Bengal's sultans, the Mughal conquest of 1576, the nawabi's rise.
polities.next: Clive defeats Siraj ud-Daulah at Plassey in June 1757; the Company controls Bengal within a decade.

polities.gov: A chartered company governing through a governor-general under parliamentary oversight from 1784
polities.head: Governors-general Hastings, Cornwallis, Wellesley, Bentinck, Dalhousie
polities.rel: Neutrality in religion, with missionaries admitted from 1813; sati abolished 1829
polities.econ: Land revenue; opium grown for China; Indian textiles destroyed by Lancashire imports; railways from 1853
polities.now: A trading company turned into the government of India by conquest, taxation and the doctrine of lapse, ruling directly or through 500 princely states, and building the railways, telegraph and English-language education that outlast it.
polities.how: Plassey, the diwani of 1765, Wellesley's wars, the annexations of Punjab, Sind and Awadh.
polities.next: The rebellion of 1857 to 1858 ends Company rule; the Crown takes over in 1858.

polities.gov: Crown colony under a viceroy, with Indian participation widened by the reforms of 1909, 1919 and 1935; the princely states under paramountcy
polities.head: Viceroys Curzon, Irwin, Mountbatten; Gandhi and Nehru of Congress; Jinnah of the Muslim League
polities.rel: Hindu majority, Muslim quarter; religion politicised by separate electorates from 1909
polities.econ: Railways, jute, tea, cotton; famines of the 1870s and 1890s and Bengal 1943; India a captive market and a source of soldiers
polities.now: The jewel of the empire, governed by a few thousand British officials and an Indian army, whose nationalist movement under Gandhi moved from petition to mass civil disobedience in 1920, 1930 and 1942 while the Muslim League demanded a separate Pakistan.
polities.how: The 1858 settlement, Congress's founding in 1885, the 1919 Amritsar massacre, the Round Table conferences, the war.
polities.next: Partition and independence in August 1947 displace 15 million and kill up to a million.

polities.gov: Federal parliamentary democracy under the 1950 constitution; Congress dominance to 1989; the BJP under Modi since 2014; the Emergency of 1975 to 1977 the one suspension
polities.head: Prime ministers Nehru (1947 to 1964), Indira Gandhi, Rajiv Gandhi, Rao, Vajpayee, Manmohan Singh, Narendra Modi
polities.rel: Hindu 80 per cent, Muslim 14 per cent, Christian, Sikh, Buddhist, Jain; secular constitution under strain from Hindu nationalism
polities.pop: About 1.43 billion, the world's largest since 2023
polities.econ: Planned economy to 1991, then liberalisation; the fifth-largest economy; software, pharmaceuticals, services; a third of the world's poor in 1990, far fewer now
polities.now: The world's largest democracy, held together through partition, four wars with Pakistan, a nuclear test in 1974 and 1998, the 1991 reforms, and the rise of a Hindu nationalist government that has changed the state's secular character.
polities.how: Nehru's institutions, the Green Revolution, the 1971 war that created Bangladesh, the 1991 crisis and reforms, and the BJP's majorities.
polities.next: Jobs for a young population, the China frontier, and the Hindu-Muslim question are the long tests.

polities.gov: Parliamentary republic in form; four periods of military rule totalling about 33 years; the army the permanent power
polities.head: Jinnah; Ayub Khan; Zulfikar Ali Bhutto; Zia ul-Haq; Benazir Bhutto; Musharraf; Imran Khan; the army chief
polities.rel: Islamic republic; Sunni majority, Shia minority; blasphemy laws
polities.econ: Textiles, remittances, agriculture; recurrent IMF programmes, the twenty-fourth in 2024; Chinese CPEC investment
polities.now: Created as a Muslim homeland in 1947, Pakistan lost its eastern half as Bangladesh in 1971, acquired nuclear weapons in 1998, backed the Afghan Taliban and suffered its own, and alternates between elected governments the army removes and generals who hand back power.
polities.how: Partition, the 1958 coup, the 1971 war, Zia's Islamisation and the Afghan jihad, the Musharraf years.
polities.next: Debt, the Taliban-ruled Afghan border, and civil-military relations.

polities.gov: Parliamentary republic; military rule 1975 to 1990; Sheikh Hasina's increasingly authoritarian rule 2009 to 2024; an interim government since the 2024 uprising
polities.head: Sheikh Mujibur Rahman; Ziaur Rahman; Ershad; Khaleda Zia; Sheikh Hasina; Muhammad Yunus as interim chief adviser
polities.rel: Sunni Islam the state religion; Hindu minority
polities.econ: Garment exports, the second-largest in the world; remittances; growth above 6 per cent for two decades
polities.now: East Pakistan broke away in the 1971 war with Indian help at a cost of hundreds of thousands of lives; from a 'basket case' it became a garment-export success, until the student uprising of 2024 drove Hasina out.
polities.how: The language movement, the 1970 election, the war, the 1975 assassination of Mujib.
polities.next: Elections and the cost of climate change on a delta are the horizon.

polities.gov: Malla kingdoms to 1768; Gorkha Shah monarchy; Rana hereditary prime ministers 1846 to 1951; absolute monarchy under Mahendra; federal republic since 2008
polities.head: Prithvi Narayan Shah; the Rana prime ministers; King Birendra; presidents and prime ministers since 2008
polities.rel: Hindu majority with Buddhist minority; the only Hindu kingdom until 2008
polities.econ: Remittances a quarter of GDP; tourism; hydropower potential
polities.now: Unified by Gorkha in 1768, checked by the Company in 1816, ruled by the Ranas for a century, and after a Maoist insurgency of 1996 to 2006 and the 2001 palace massacre, a republic since 2008.
polities.how: Prithvi Narayan's conquest, the Anglo-Nepalese war, the Rana regime, the democratic movements of 1990 and 2006.
polities.next: Political instability and dependence on India and China.

polities.gov: Buddhist theocracy under the Zhabdrung from 1616; hereditary monarchy of the Wangchuck dynasty from 1907; constitutional monarchy since 2008
polities.head: Druk Gyalpo (king) of the Wangchuck dynasty
polities.rel: Vajrayana Buddhism the state religion; Hindu Nepali minority, many expelled in the 1990s
polities.econ: Hydropower sold to India; 'gross national happiness'; tourism by quota
polities.now: A Himalayan kingdom that stayed closed until the 1960s, guided by India in foreign affairs by the 1949 treaty, and which introduced democracy from the throne in 2008.
polities.how: Unification by the Zhabdrung, the 1907 monarchy, Indian alignment.
polities.next: Its border with China and youth emigration.

polities.t: Ceylon under Europeans and the Kandyan kingdom
polities.gov: Kotte and Jaffna kingdoms; the Portuguese coast 1505 to 1658; the Dutch coast to 1796; the Kandyan kingdom in the highlands until 1815; British crown colony from 1802
polities.head: Kandyan kings; Dutch and British governors
polities.rel: Theravada Buddhism; Hindu Tamils in the north; Christians from the Portuguese missions
polities.econ: Cinnamon under the Dutch; coffee, then tea and rubber plantations under Britain with Tamil labour from India
polities.now: An island whose coasts the Portuguese, Dutch and British held in turn while the Kandyan kingdom survived in the mountains until 1815; Britain made it a plantation colony with a universal franchise from 1931.
polities.how: Portuguese arrival 1505, Dutch conquest, British annexation of Kandy.
polities.next: Independence as a dominion in February 1948.

polities.gov: Parliamentary democracy; executive presidency since 1978
polities.head: Senanayake; Bandaranaike; Jayewardene; the Rajapaksa brothers; Dissanayake since 2024
polities.rel: Buddhist majority; Hindu, Muslim, Christian minorities
polities.econ: Tea, garments, tourism, remittances; sovereign default in 2022
polities.now: Independent in 1948, Sri Lanka elected the world's first woman prime minister in 1960, fought a Tamil separatist war from 1983 to 2009 that ended in the Tigers' destruction with heavy civilian deaths, and went bankrupt in 2022, which brought down the Rajapaksas.
polities.how: Sinhala-only politics from 1956, the 1983 pogrom, the war, the 2022 crisis.
polities.next: Debt restructuring and reconciliation with the Tamil north.

polities.gov: Siamese monarchy with a sacred king and a hierarchy of ranked officials
polities.head: Kings of Ayutthaya; Naresuan (1590 to 1605); Narai (1656 to 1688)
polities.cap: Ayutthaya, a cosmopolitan river city of perhaps 200,000
polities.rel: Theravada Buddhism with Hindu court ritual
polities.econ: Rice, deer hides, sappanwood; trade with China, Japan, Persia and Europe; the French embassy of 1685
polities.now: The Siamese kingdom that dominated the Chao Phraya basin, fought Burma for two centuries, and under Narai received French and Persian embassies before expelling the French in 1688.
polities.how: Founded in 1351; sacked by Burma in 1569 and liberated by Naresuan.
polities.next: Burma destroys Ayutthaya in 1767; Taksin and then the Chakri dynasty rebuild Siam at Bangkok.

polities.gov: Absolute monarchy; modernised by Chulalongkorn from 1868
polities.head: Rama I (1782 to 1809); Mongkut (Rama IV); Chulalongkorn (Rama V, 1868 to 1910); Vajiravudh; Prajadhipok
polities.rel: Theravada Buddhism; Islam in the Malay south
polities.econ: Rice exports after the Bowring treaty of 1855; railways; teak
polities.now: The one Southeast Asian state never colonised, which gave up Laos, western Cambodia and the northern Malay states to France and Britain to keep its core, and modernised its administration, army and law under Chulalongkorn.
polities.how: Rama I's refounding, the Bowring treaty opening trade, Chulalongkorn's reforms and the 1893 crisis with France.
polities.next: A coup in June 1932 ends absolute monarchy.

polities.gov: Constitutional monarchy in name; about a dozen successful coups since 1932, most recently 2014; elected governments between
polities.head: Kings Bhumibol (1946 to 2016) and Vajiralongkorn; Phibun; Sarit; Thaksin Shinawatra; Prayut
polities.rel: Theravada Buddhism; the monarchy sacralised; Muslim insurgency in the south
polities.econ: Rice, cars, electronics, tourism; the 1997 Asian crisis began here
polities.now: A state cycling between elections and coups, allied to the United States in the Cold War, whose king Bhumibol was the stabilising figure for seventy years, and whose politics since 2006 pit the Shinawatra parties against the army and palace.
polities.how: The 1932 revolution, Phibun's nationalism, Sarit's development dictatorship, the 1973 and 1992 uprisings, the Thaksin era.
polities.next: The monarchy's role under Vajiralongkorn and an ageing population.

polities.gov: Rival kingdoms of Ava (Burman), Pegu (Mon), Arakan and the Shan states; united by the Toungoo dynasty in the 1550s and the Konbaung from 1752
polities.head: Bayinnaung (1550 to 1581); Alaungpaya (1752 to 1760); Bodawpaya
polities.rel: Theravada Buddhism
polities.econ: Rice, teak, rubies; Mon ports; Arakan's Bengal trade
polities.now: A valley contested by Burmans, Mons and Shans, twice united by conquest: Bayinnaung's Toungoo empire reached Siam and Laos, and the Konbaung kings destroyed Ayutthaya in 1767 and took Arakan in 1785.
polities.how: Ava and Pegu's forty years' war, Toungoo unification, Konbaung reconquest.
polities.next: The Konbaung kingdom's expansion into Assam collides with the Company in 1824.

polities.gov: Absolute Buddhist monarchy; lost Arakan and Tenasserim in 1826 and Lower Burma in 1852 to Britain
polities.head: Bodawpaya; Bagyidaw; Mindon (1853 to 1878); Thibaw
polities.rel: Theravada Buddhism
polities.econ: Rice in the British delta; teak; Mindon's reforms and steamers
polities.now: A kingdom reduced by two wars with Britain to the upper valley, which Mindon reformed and Thibaw lost.
polities.how: The first and second Anglo-Burmese wars of 1824 and 1852 took the coast and delta.
polities.next: Britain deposes Thibaw in November 1885 and annexes Upper Burma to India.

polities.gov: Province of British India to 1937, then a separate colony with a parliament; Japanese occupation 1942 to 1945
polities.head: British governors; Aung San's independence movement
polities.rel: Theravada Buddhism; Christian hill minorities; Indian Hindu and Muslim migrants
polities.econ: The world's largest rice exporter; oil at Yenangyaung; Indian moneylenders own the delta
polities.now: A rice colony governed as an appendage of India, whose Burman nationalism grew around monks and students and whose Thirty Comrades under Aung San fought first with Japan, then against it.
polities.how: Annexation in 1886, pacification, the 1930s separation from India, the war.
polities.next: Independence in January 1948, outside the Commonwealth; Aung San assassinated six months before.

polities.gov: Parliamentary democracy to 1962; Ne Win's military socialism to 1988; junta rule; a partial civilian government 2011 to 2021; military rule and civil war since the February 2021 coup
polities.head: U Nu; Ne Win; Than Shwe; Thein Sein; Aung San Suu Kyi as state counsellor 2016 to 2021; Min Aung Hlaing
polities.rel: Theravada Buddhism; Muslim Rohingya expelled in 2017; Christian Karen, Kachin, Chin
polities.econ: Rice, gas, jade, timber; sanctions; collapse since 2021
polities.now: A state at civil war with its ethnic minorities since 1948, ruled by the army since 1962 with a decade's opening from 2011, which expelled 700,000 Rohingya in 2017 and in 2021 overthrew Aung San Suu Kyi's elected government, igniting a nationwide resistance that now holds much of the country.
polities.how: Independence, the 1962 coup, the 1988 uprising, the 2010 opening, the 2021 coup.
polities.next: The army's survival is in question for the first time since 1962.

polities.gov: Lê dynasty from 1428 with the Trịnh lords in the north and Nguyễn lords in the south as real rulers from the 1600s; Tây Sơn revolt; the Nguyễn empire from 1802
polities.head: Lê Lợi; the Trịnh and Nguyễn lords; Gia Long (1802 to 1820); Minh Mạng; Tự Đức
polities.rel: Confucian state, Mahayana Buddhism; Catholic missions from the 1600s, persecuted in the 1800s
polities.econ: Rice; the southward expansion into Champa and the Mekong delta
polities.now: A Confucian monarchy that expelled the Ming in 1428, marched south over Champa and into the Mekong delta, split between rival lordly houses, and was reunified under the Nguyễn with French help in 1802, a debt the French would collect.
polities.how: Lê Lợi's war of independence, the Trịnh-Nguyễn division, the Tây Sơn rebellion, Gia Long's reunification.
polities.next: France takes Saigon in 1859 and the Mekong provinces in 1862; the protectorate over the rest follows in 1883.

polities.gov: Colony of Cochinchina and protectorates of Annam, Tonkin, Cambodia and Laos under a governor-general; Vichy administration under Japanese occupation 1940 to 1945
polities.head: French governors-general; the Nguyễn emperors as figureheads; Ho Chi Minh's Viet Minh from 1941
polities.rel: Buddhism, Confucianism, Catholicism, Cao Đài; Theravada in Cambodia and Laos
polities.econ: Rice and rubber exports; Michelin plantations; the Yunnan railway; famine of 1944 to 1945 killing up to two million in Tonkin
polities.now: France's richest Asian possession, run for rice and rubber, where the nationalist and communist movements grew in prisons and exile until the Japanese coup of March 1945 broke French rule.
polities.how: Conquest from 1859 to 1885, the union of 1887, the suppression of the 1930 risings.
polities.next: Ho Chi Minh declares independence in September 1945; the French war runs to Dien Bien Phu in 1954.

polities.gov: The Democratic Republic in the north under the Communist party; the State of Vietnam, then Republic of Vietnam in the south under Diệm and the generals; partition at the 17th parallel from 1954
polities.head: Ho Chi Minh; Lê Duẩn; Ngô Đình Diệm; Nguyễn Văn Thiệu
polities.rel: Buddhist majority; Catholic elite in the south; the 1963 Buddhist crisis
polities.econ: War economies sustained by China, the Soviet Union and the United States
polities.now: Thirty years of war: France's defeat in 1954, partition, the insurgency in the south, American intervention peaking at 540,000 troops in 1969, the Tet offensive, the Paris accords of 1973, and the north's conquest of Saigon in April 1975 at a cost of some three million Vietnamese and 58,000 American dead.
polities.how: The August revolution, Dien Bien Phu, Geneva, Diệm's overthrow, Americanisation, Vietnamisation.
polities.next: Reunification in 1976; invasion of Cambodia in 1978; China's punitive war in 1979.

polities.gov: One-party communist state
polities.head: General secretaries Lê Duẩn, Nguyễn Văn Linh, Nguyễn Phú Trọng (2011 to 2024), Tô Lâm
polities.rel: Buddhist, Catholic, folk religion; controlled
polities.econ: Đổi Mới reforms from 1986; among the fastest-growing economies; electronics assembly, garments, coffee; US trade partner since 2001
polities.now: Reunified in 1975, isolated and poor until the 1986 reforms, and since then an export economy courted by the United States and Japan as a counterweight to China, with which it fought in 1979 and disputes the South China Sea.
polities.how: Post-war collectivisation's failure, Cambodia, the Chinese war, Đổi Mới, normalisation with the US in 1995.
polities.next: Growth, the South China Sea and leadership succession.

polities.gov: Khmer monarchy, a vassal alternately of Siam and Vietnam
polities.head: Khmer kings at Lovek, Oudong
polities.rel: Theravada Buddhism
polities.econ: Rice, fish of the Tonlé Sap; tribute to neighbours
polities.now: The Khmer kingdom shrunk from the Angkor empire to a buffer squeezed between Siam and Vietnam, which took the Mekong delta in the seventeenth century.
polities.how: Angkor abandoned around 1431 after Siamese sacks; the capital moved south.
polities.next: King Norodom accepts a French protectorate in 1863 to escape his neighbours.

polities.gov: Sihanouk's monarchy to 1970; Lon Nol's republic; the Khmer Rouge 1975 to 1979; Vietnamese-installed government; constitutional monarchy under Hun Sen's one-party dominance since 1993
polities.head: Norodom Sihanouk; Pol Pot; Hun Sen 1985 to 2023; Hun Manet
polities.rel: Theravada Buddhism; abolished by the Khmer Rouge, restored after
polities.econ: Garments, tourism to Angkor, Chinese investment; scam compounds since the 2010s
polities.now: Independent in 1953, drawn into the Vietnam war and bombed by the United States, then subjected to the Khmer Rouge's four years, which killed about a quarter of the population; Hun Sen has ruled since 1985 and passed power to his son.
polities.how: Sihanouk's neutrality, the 1970 coup, the Khmer Rouge victory and genocide, the Vietnamese invasion of 1978, the UN settlement of 1991.
polities.next: Chinese dependence and dynastic succession.

polities.t: Lan Xang and the Lao kingdoms
polities.gov: Kingdom of Lan Xang to 1707, then Luang Prabang, Vientiane and Champasak as Siamese vassals
polities.head: Kings of Lan Xang; Setthathirath; Souligna Vongsa (1637 to 1694)
polities.rel: Theravada Buddhism
polities.econ: Rice, forest products, river trade
polities.now: The 'land of a million elephants', split into three kingdoms after 1707 and reduced to Siamese vassalage; Siam sacked Vientiane in 1828.
polities.how: Lan Xang's founding in 1353, its split, the 1828 rebellion against Siam.
polities.next: France takes the left bank of the Mekong from Siam in 1893.

polities.gov: Constitutional monarchy 1953 to 1975 amid civil war; one-party communist state since December 1975
polities.head: King Sisavang Vatthana; Prince Souvanna Phouma; Kaysone Phomvihane; the Lao People's Revolutionary Party
polities.rel: Theravada Buddhism; animist highland peoples
polities.econ: Hydropower sold to Thailand; Chinese railway and debt; the most bombed country per head in history
polities.now: A kingdom torn by civil war between royalists and the Pathet Lao, bombed by the United States for nine years, and communist since 1975, now heavily indebted to China.
polities.how: Independence in 1953, the Geneva accords, the secret war, the Pathet Lao's takeover.
polities.next: Debt distress and Chinese dependence.

polities.gov: Malacca sultanate to 1511; Portuguese then Dutch Malacca; Johor, Aceh, Perak and other sultanates; the Minangkabau of Sumatra
polities.head: Sultans of Malacca and Johor; Portuguese and Dutch governors
polities.rel: Sunni Islam, spread through Malacca from the fifteenth century
polities.pop: Perhaps 1 to 2 million across the peninsula and Sumatra
polities.econ: The strait's entrepôt trade in spices, tin, pepper; Chinese and Indian merchants
polities.now: Malacca's fall to the Portuguese in 1511 scattered its court into the sultanates of Johor and others, while the strait's trade continued under European forts and Chinese junks.
polities.how: Parameswara founded Malacca around 1400; Albuquerque took it in 1511; the Dutch in 1641.
polities.next: Britain takes Penang in 1786, Singapore in 1819, Malacca in 1824, and intervenes in the sultanates from 1874.

polities.gov: Federated and Unfederated Malay States under British residents, the Straits Settlements as a crown colony; Japanese occupation 1942 to 1945; the Malayan Emergency from 1948
polities.head: British high commissioners; the Malay sultans retained
polities.rel: Islam among Malays; Chinese Buddhism and Daoism; Indian Hinduism
polities.econ: The world's largest tin and rubber producer; Chinese and Indian labour imported
polities.now: A plural society built by British capital and Chinese and Indian labour, occupied by Japan, and then the site of a twelve-year communist insurgency that Britain defeated with a strategy later studied everywhere.
polities.how: The Pangkor treaty of 1874, the federation of 1896, the fall of Singapore in 1942, the Emergency.
polities.next: Independence as the Federation of Malaya in August 1957; Malaysia formed in 1963 with Singapore, Sabah and Sarawak.

polities.gov: Federal constitutional monarchy with a rotating king; parliamentary democracy under one coalition from 1957 to 2018
polities.head: Tunku Abdul Rahman; Mahathir Mohamad (1981 to 2003 and 2018 to 2020); Najib Razak, convicted in the 1MDB scandal; Anwar Ibrahim
polities.rel: Islam the official religion; Buddhist, Hindu, Christian minorities
polities.econ: Palm oil, electronics, oil and gas; the New Economic Policy of 1971 favouring Malays
polities.now: Formed in 1963 and separated from Singapore in 1965, Malaysia built an electronics economy under Mahathir while entrenching Malay preference after the 1969 riots; the 1MDB scandal ended sixty years of one coalition's rule in 2018.
polities.how: Independence, the 1969 riots, the NEP, Mahathir's Vision 2020.
polities.next: Ethnic politics and the middle-income trap.

polities.gov: Absolute monarchy; sultanate under British protection 1888 to 1984; sharia penal code from 2014
polities.head: Sultan Hassanal Bolkiah since 1967
polities.rel: Sunni Islam the state religion
polities.econ: Oil and gas since 1929; among the richest per head
polities.now: A sultanate that once ruled much of Borneo, shrank to a British protectorate, and stayed out of Malaysia to keep its oil; the sultan has ruled since 1967 and introduced a sharia code in 2014.
polities.how: The Brooke rajahs of Sarawak and the North Borneo Company took its territory in the nineteenth century.
polities.next: Oil reserves' depletion in the coming decades.

polities.gov: The Dutch East India Company (VOC) from 1602 to 1799, then a state colony; the Cultivation System of forced crops 1830 to 1870; 'Ethical Policy' from 1901
polities.head: VOC governors-general at Batavia; Dutch governors-general; Sukarno's nationalists from 1927
polities.rel: Islam the majority faith since the sixteenth century; Hindu Bali; Christian missions in the east
polities.pop: About 60 million by 1930, most on Java
polities.econ: Spices from the Moluccas, then coffee, sugar and tobacco; oil from Sumatra and Borneo in the twentieth century; the Aceh war of 1873 to 1904
polities.now: The Company's spice monopoly became a state colony that made the Netherlands rich on Javanese forced labour, conquered the outer islands only by 1910, and faced a nationalist movement it jailed.
polities.how: The VOC's monopolies, the Java war of 1825 to 1830, the Cultivation System, the conquest of Aceh and Bali.
polities.next: Japan occupies the islands in 1942; Sukarno declares independence in August 1945.

polities.gov: Sukarno's republic and 'Guided Democracy' to 1966; Suharto's New Order military regime to 1998; democracy since, with direct presidential elections from 2004
polities.head: Sukarno; Suharto 1967 to 1998; Habibie; Megawati; Yudhoyono; Joko Widodo; Prabowo Subianto
polities.cap: Jakarta; a new capital Nusantara under construction
polities.rel: The world's largest Muslim population; Hindu Bali; Christian and other minorities; Pancasila pluralism
polities.econ: Oil, palm oil, nickel, coal; the largest economy in Southeast Asia; the 1997 crisis ended Suharto
polities.now: Independent after a four-year war with the Dutch, Indonesia killed about half a million alleged communists in 1965 to 1966, invaded East Timor in 1975, and since 1998 has been the world's third-largest democracy, with a former general elected president in 2024.
polities.how: The revolution, the 1965 killings, Suharto's development state, the 1998 fall and reformasi.
polities.next: Nickel-based industrial policy, the new capital, and democratic backsliding are watched.

polities.gov: Spanish colony governed from Mexico until 1821, then from Madrid; the friars the real power in the provinces
polities.head: Spanish governors-general; the religious orders
polities.rel: Catholic conversion of the lowlands; Muslim sultanates of Sulu and Maguindanao in the south never conquered
polities.econ: The Manila galleon carrying Mexican silver to China 1565 to 1815; sugar and hemp exports in the nineteenth century
polities.now: Spain's Asian colony, Catholic and friar-ruled, linked to the Americas by the galleon, with a Filipino elite educated in Europe producing Rizal and the revolution of 1896.
polities.how: Legazpi's conquest from 1565; the galleon trade; the Muslim south's resistance; the 1872 Cavite mutiny and the propaganda movement.
polities.next: The United States takes Manila in 1898, buys the islands from Spain, and fights the Filipino republic until 1902.

polities.gov: US colony after the Philippine-American war; the Commonwealth with Filipino self-government from 1935; Japanese occupation 1942 to 1945
polities.head: American governors-general; Manuel Quezon as Commonwealth president
polities.rel: Catholic majority; Protestant missions; Muslim south
polities.econ: Sugar, coconut and hemp for the American market; public schools in English
polities.now: America's one large colony, taken in a war that killed some 200,000 Filipinos, governed with schools and roads and a promise of independence, and destroyed in the 1945 battle for Manila.
polities.how: The 1898 treaty, the war of 1899 to 1902, the Jones Act, the Tydings-McDuffie Act of 1934.
polities.next: Independence in July 1946 with US bases retained.

polities.gov: Presidential republic on the American model; Marcos's martial law 1972 to 1986; democracy restored by the People Power revolution
polities.head: Ferdinand Marcos 1965 to 1986; Corazon Aquino; Duterte; Ferdinand Marcos Jr. since 2022
polities.rel: Catholic about 80 per cent; Muslim Bangsamoro region in the south
polities.econ: Remittances from 10 million overseas workers; call centres; electronics; persistent poverty
polities.now: A democracy that elected and then expelled a dictator, closed the US bases in 1992 and reopened the alliance against China's claims in the South China Sea, and in 2022 elected the dictator's son.
polities.how: Independence, the Marcos years, People Power in 1986, the Moro peace process, Duterte's drug war.
polities.next: The South China Sea stand-off and dynastic politics.

polities.gov: Hundreds of stateless societies; German and British claims from 1884; Australian administration 1914 to 1975; parliamentary democracy since 1975
polities.head: Prime ministers since 1975; the Australian administrators before
polities.rel: Traditional religions and Christianity since the missions
polities.econ: Subsistence agriculture, gold, copper, liquefied natural gas
polities.now: The world's most linguistically diverse island, whose highlands were unknown to outsiders until the 1930s, partitioned between the Dutch, Germans and British, run by Australia, and independent since 1975 with a weak state and a Bougainville secession referendum in 2019.
polities.how: Colonial claims of 1884, the Australian mandate, the Bougainville war of 1988 to 1998.
polities.next: Bougainville's independence and resource governance.

polities.gov: Mansa's empire over the upper Niger, in decline; provinces breaking away
polities.head: Mansas of the Keita dynasty
polities.rel: Islam at court; traditional religion in the countryside
polities.pop: Perhaps 5 million at its height a century earlier
polities.econ: Gold from Bambuk and Bure, salt from the Sahara, Timbuktu's trade
polities.now: The empire of Mansa Musa's pilgrimage of 1324 is losing its eastern provinces to Songhai and its northern trade to Tuareg raiders; by 1500 it is a rump on the upper Niger.
polities.how: Sundiata founded it around 1235; succession disputes and Songhai's rise reduced it.
polities.next: Songhai takes Timbuktu in 1468 and Jenne in 1473; the Bambara of Segu absorb the remains after 1600.

polities.gov: Askia dynasty's empire over the middle Niger with a standing army and provincial governors
polities.head: Sunni Ali (1464 to 1492); Askia Muhammad (1493 to 1528)
polities.rel: Islam; Timbuktu's Sankore mosque a centre of scholarship
polities.econ: The trans-Saharan gold and salt trade; Timbuktu and Jenne as market cities
polities.now: The largest state in West African history, from the Atlantic approaches to the Hausa lands, with Timbuktu at its height of learning under Askia Muhammad.
polities.how: Sunni Ali's conquests from Gao; Askia Muhammad's administration and pilgrimage.
polities.next: A Moroccan army with firearms destroys the Songhai army at Tondibi in 1591; the empire fragments.

polities.gov: Moroccan pashas at Timbuktu, then the Bambara kingdoms of Segu and Kaarta from the 1710s
polities.head: Arma pashas; Biton Coulibaly of Segu; Ngolo Diarra
polities.rel: Traditional Bambara religion with Islam in the towns
polities.econ: Slaves, gold, grain along the river; the Atlantic trade's pull southward
polities.now: The Moroccan garrison went native and lost control; Bambara warrior kingdoms rule the middle Niger on slave-raiding and river trade.
polities.how: Tondibi in 1591 and the pashalik's decay; Bambara state-building at Segu.
polities.next: Umar Tall's Tukulor jihad conquers Segu in 1861; France takes it in 1890.

polities.t: Jihad states of the western Sudan
polities.gov: Islamic states founded by jihad: the Tukulor empire of Umar Tall, Samori Touré's Wassoulou empire, the imamates of Futa Jalon and Futa Toro
polities.head: Umar Tall (to 1864); Ahmadu Tall; Samori Touré (to 1898)
polities.rel: Sunni Islam in the Tijaniyya and Qadiriyya orders
polities.econ: Slaves and gold; Samori's blacksmiths copied European rifles
polities.now: The last independent states of the western Sudan, built by Muslim reformers with armies of the faithful, fighting the French advance from Senegal through the 1880s and 1890s.
polities.how: Umar Tall's jihad from 1852; Samori's rise from a trader to emperor in the 1870s.
polities.next: France takes Segu in 1890 and captures Samori in 1898; the territory becomes French West Africa.

polities.gov: Sefuwa dynasty's sultanate, among the longest-lived in Africa; al-Kanemi's shehus from 1810
polities.head: Mai Idris Alooma (1564 to 1596); the al-Kanemi shehus
polities.rel: Sunni Islam since the eleventh century
polities.econ: Trans-Saharan trade in slaves and horses through Tripoli; Lake Chad agriculture
polities.now: The Lake Chad sultanate that used Ottoman muskets under Idris Alooma to dominate the central Sudan, and survived a thousand years of dynastic rule.
polities.how: Kanem's founding before 1000, the move to Bornu around 1380, Alooma's reforms.
polities.next: Rabih az-Zubayr's army destroys Kukawa in 1893; France, Britain and Germany partition the territory.

polities.gov: Seven walled city-states, Kano, Katsina, Zaria, Gobir and others, each under a sarki
polities.head: Sarkis of the Hausa cities
polities.rel: Islam among rulers and traders from the fifteenth century; traditional religion among farmers
polities.econ: Kano's dyed cloth and leather sold across the Sahara; the Kano market among the largest in Africa
polities.now: Trading cities competing for the Saharan and Sudanic trade, Islamic in their courts, tributary at times to Songhai and Bornu.
polities.how: The Hausa cities formed from the eleventh century; Islam came with Wangara traders.
polities.next: Usman dan Fodio's Fulani jihad of 1804 conquers the Hausa cities and founds the Sokoto Caliphate.

polities.gov: Islamic caliphate over emirates governed by Fulani emirs owing allegiance to Sokoto
polities.head: Usman dan Fodio; Muhammad Bello; the caliphs at Sokoto
polities.rel: Sunni Islam; the jihad against syncretism
polities.pop: About 10 million, among the largest slave populations in the world
polities.econ: Plantation agriculture worked by slaves; cloth, leather, the caravan trade
polities.now: The largest state in Africa in the nineteenth century, created by a Fulani jihad that unified the Hausa lands under emirs and Islamic law.
polities.how: Dan Fodio's revolt against Gobir in 1804 spread to every Hausa city within a decade.
polities.next: Lugard's British force takes Sokoto in 1903; the emirs are kept under indirect rule.

polities.gov: Yoruba monarchy with the alafin checked by the Oyo Mesi council and the Ogboni society
polities.head: Alafins of Oyo
polities.rel: Yoruba religion; the alafin's sacred kingship
polities.econ: Cavalry power on the savanna; slaves exported through Porto-Novo and Badagry
polities.now: The Yoruba cavalry empire that dominated the Bight of Benin's hinterland and made Dahomey its tributary in the eighteenth century.
polities.how: Oyo's horses from the north and its position on the trade routes built the empire.
polities.next: Internal revolt and the Fulani jihad break Oyo by 1835; Yoruba civil wars follow until the British occupation.

polities.gov: Oba's monarchy with palace associations and town chiefs
polities.head: Obas of Benin; Ewuare (around 1440 to 1473); Ovonramwen
polities.cap: Benin City, walled, with the bronze-casting guilds
polities.rel: Edo religion; the Oba as divine king
polities.econ: Pepper, ivory, cloth, and slaves traded with the Portuguese from 1485; the brass for the Benin bronzes came from Europe
polities.now: The Edo kingdom whose bronzes record four centuries of kings, which traded with Portugal from 1485 and kept its independence until the British punitive expedition.
polities.how: Ewuare's reforms and the guild system; the Portuguese trade.
polities.next: A British force sacks Benin City in 1897 and loots the bronzes; the Oba is exiled.

polities.gov: Akan states; the Asante confederacy under the Asantehene from about 1700, bound by the Golden Stool
polities.head: Osei Tutu; Opoku Ware; Asantehenes to Prempeh I
polities.rel: Akan religion; the Golden Stool as the nation's soul
polities.econ: Gold mines, kola nuts, the Atlantic slave trade through the Fante coast; European forts at Elmina and Cape Coast
polities.now: The Akan goldfields supported a series of states culminating in Asante, which dominated the Gold Coast's hinterland and fought Britain five times in the nineteenth century.
polities.how: Osei Tutu's union under the Golden Stool around 1700; expansion to the coast.
polities.next: Britain annexes Asante in 1902 after the war of the Golden Stool.

polities.gov: Absolute monarchy with a professional army including the female 'Amazon' regiments
polities.head: Kings Agaja, Gezo (1818 to 1858), Glele, Behanzin
polities.rel: Vodun; the Annual Customs with human sacrifice
polities.econ: The slave trade through Ouidah, then palm oil after British suppression
polities.now: A militarised kingdom that supplied the Atlantic slave trade through Ouidah and broke free of Oyo under Gezo.
polities.how: Expansion to the coast in the 1720s; tribute to Oyo until 1823.
polities.next: France conquers Dahomey in two wars, 1890 and 1892 to 1894.

polities.gov: Kingdoms of Ouagadougou and Yatenga under the Mogho Naba
polities.head: Mogho Naba of Ouagadougou
polities.rel: Mossi traditional religion; resistance to Islam until the nineteenth century
polities.econ: Cavalry raiding, cotton, trade between the forest and the Sahel
polities.now: Cavalry kingdoms of the Volta basin that raided Timbuktu and resisted Mali, Songhai and Islam alike.
polities.how: Founded around the eleventh to fifteenth centuries by Dagomba-related horsemen.
polities.next: France takes Ouagadougou in 1896; the Mogho Naba survives as a traditional ruler.

polities.gov: The Jolof empire's breakup into Cayor, Baol, Walo and Sine-Saloum; French posts at Saint-Louis and Gorée
polities.head: Damels of Cayor; Lat Dior (to 1886)
polities.rel: Islam spreading through marabouts; the Mouride order from 1883
polities.econ: Gum arabic, slaves, then groundnuts for France from the 1840s
polities.now: The Wolof states of the Senegal valley, the first African region in sustained contact with France, which the groundnut trade and Faidherbe's railway bring under French control.
polities.how: The Jolof empire broke up around 1549; French forts from 1659; Faidherbe's conquests from 1854.
polities.next: Lat Dior dies fighting the railway in 1886; Senegal becomes the core of French West Africa.

polities.gov: Federation of eight colonies under a governor-general at Dakar; direct rule; forced labour until 1946
polities.head: Governors-general; Blaise Diagne as the first African deputy from 1914
polities.rel: Islam across the Sahel; Christian missions on the coast
polities.econ: Groundnuts, cocoa, cotton, the Dakar-Niger railway; head taxes and forced labour
polities.now: Four million square kilometres from Dakar to Niamey governed as one federation, which supplied 200,000 soldiers in the First World War and whose elites won citizenship in 1946 and self-government by the loi-cadre of 1956.
polities.how: Conquest from 1880 to 1900, the federation of 1895, the Brazzaville conference of 1944.
polities.next: Guinea votes no to de Gaulle in 1958; the rest become independent in 1960.

polities.gov: Federation of Gabon, Middle Congo, Ubangi-Shari and Chad under a governor-general at Brazzaville; concessionary companies
polities.head: Governors-general; Félix Éboué, the first black governor, who rallied to de Gaulle in 1940
polities.rel: Catholic missions; Islam in Chad
polities.econ: Rubber and ivory under concession companies whose abuses were exposed in 1905; the Congo-Océan railway built with forced labour killed some 17,000
polities.now: The poorer of France's African federations, run through concession companies, whose rally to Free France in 1940 gave de Gaulle his first territory.
polities.how: Brazza's treaties of the 1880s; the concession regime; the 1940 rally.
polities.next: Four republics independent in 1960.

polities.gov: British crown colony with the Asante and the Northern Territories added by 1902; an African majority legislature from 1951
polities.head: British governors; Kwame Nkrumah as leader of government business from 1951
polities.rel: Christianity on the coast, Islam in the north, Akan religion
polities.econ: The world's largest cocoa producer by 1911; gold; the 1948 riots over prices
polities.now: Britain's model African colony, rich on cocoa, where Nkrumah's Convention People's Party turned the 1948 riots into a mass movement that won self-government by 1951.
polities.how: The coastal forts, the Asante wars, the cocoa boom, the 1948 riots.
polities.next: Independence as Ghana in March 1957, the first in sub-Saharan Africa.

polities.gov: Nkrumah's one-party state to 1966; four coups; Rawlings's rule 1981 to 2000; stable multiparty democracy since 1992 with power alternating
polities.head: Kwame Nkrumah; Jerry Rawlings; Kufuor; Mahama; Akufo-Addo; Mahama again from 2025
polities.rel: Christian majority, Muslim north
polities.econ: Cocoa, gold, oil since 2010; a debt default in 2022 and IMF programme
polities.now: The first independent black African state, a pan-African beacon under Nkrumah, which went through coups and Rawlings's revolution before settling into the continent's most dependable electoral democracy, with recurrent debt crises.
polities.how: Independence, Nkrumah's fall, the Rawlings years, the 1992 constitution.
polities.next: Debt and gold-mining pollution are the current problems.

polities.gov: British colony and protectorate amalgamated in 1914; indirect rule through emirs and chiefs; regional self-government from the 1950s
polities.head: Frederick Lugard; British governors; Azikiwe, Awolowo and Ahmadu Bello as regional leaders
polities.rel: Islam in the north, Christianity in the south, Yoruba and Igbo traditions
polities.econ: Palm oil, cocoa, groundnuts, tin; oil found at Oloibiri in 1956
polities.now: Three regions with different religions, economies and histories joined by Lugard's amalgamation and governed through their own rulers, a structure that fixed the fault lines the republic inherited.
polities.how: The Niger Company, the conquest of Sokoto, amalgamation, the 1951 and 1954 constitutions.
polities.next: Independence in October 1960 as a federation of three regions.

polities.gov: Federal republic; military rule for 29 of its first 39 years; civilian presidential democracy since 1999
polities.head: Gowon; Obasanjo; Babangida; Abacha; Buhari; Tinubu since 2023
polities.rel: Muslim north, Christian south, roughly equal; sharia in twelve northern states
polities.econ: Oil since the 1970s, about 90 per cent of exports; Lagos among Africa's largest economies; chronic insecurity and inflation
polities.now: Africa's most populous state, which fought the Biafran civil war of 1967 to 1970 at a cost of about a million lives, cycled through coups to 1999, and now faces Boko Haram in the northeast, banditry in the northwest and separatism in the southeast.
polities.how: The 1966 coups, Biafra, oil, the Abacha dictatorship, the 1999 transition.
polities.next: Whether the state can provide security and jobs for 225 million people.

polities.gov: Republic founded by freed American slaves in 1847; True Whig one-party rule to 1980; Doe's coup; civil wars 1989 to 2003; democracy since
polities.head: Tubman; Tolbert; Samuel Doe; Charles Taylor; Ellen Johnson Sirleaf; George Weah; Boakai
polities.rel: Christian majority
polities.econ: Rubber under Firestone, iron ore, the ship registry; the civil wars destroyed the economy
polities.now: Africa's oldest republic, ruled by an Americo-Liberian elite over the indigenous majority until Doe's coup in 1980, then destroyed by two civil wars that killed about 250,000 before a UN mission and Africa's first elected woman president restored order.
polities.how: The American Colonization Society, the 1980 coup, Taylor's war.
polities.next: Reconstruction after Ebola and the UN's departure.

polities.gov: British colony for freed slaves from 1808; protectorate inland; independent since 1961; civil war 1991 to 2002; democracy since
polities.head: British governors; Siaka Stevens; the RUF's Foday Sankoh; Ahmad Tejan Kabbah; Julius Maada Bio
polities.rel: Muslim majority, Christian minority, religious tolerance
polities.econ: Diamonds, which funded the war; iron ore; among the poorest countries
polities.now: Founded as a home for freed slaves and the base for Britain's anti-slavery squadron, Sierra Leone descended into a diamond-fuelled civil war in the 1990s notorious for amputations, ended by British intervention in 2000.
polities.how: Freetown's founding, the 1898 Hut Tax war, Stevens's one-party state, the RUF war.
polities.next: Poverty and Ebola's legacy.

polities.gov: French colony from 1893; Houphouët-Boigny's one-party state 1960 to 1993; civil wars 2002 to 2011; presidential republic under Ouattara since 2011
polities.head: Félix Houphouët-Boigny; Laurent Gbagbo; Alassane Ouattara
polities.rel: Muslim north, Christian south, traditional religions
polities.econ: The world's largest cocoa producer; coffee, rubber, oil; the 'Ivorian miracle' of the 1960s and 1970s
polities.now: France's richest African colony became Houphouët-Boigny's stable one-party state; after his death a north-south divide over 'Ivoirité' produced two civil wars, ended when French and UN forces removed Gbagbo in 2011.
polities.how: Houphouët's thirty-three years, the 1999 coup, the 2002 rebellion, the 2010 election crisis.
polities.next: Ouattara's succession and cocoa prices.

polities.gov: French colony with four communes of citizens; independent since 1960; Senghor's one-party state liberalised from 1976; the only West African state without a coup
polities.head: Léopold Sédar Senghor; Abdou Diouf; Abdoulaye Wade; Macky Sall; Bassirou Diomaye Faye since 2024
polities.rel: Sunni Islam in Sufi brotherhoods, the Mourides above all
polities.econ: Groundnuts, fish, phosphates; oil and gas from 2024
polities.now: The oldest French African colony and the region's most stable democracy, where the Sufi brotherhoods mediate between state and society and power has changed hands peacefully in 2000, 2012 and 2024.
polities.how: The four communes' citizenship, Senghor's rule, the alternations.
polities.next: Oil revenues and a young, impatient electorate.

polities.gov: French colony; Sékou Touré's one-party state 1958 to 1984; military rule; a flawed democracy 2010 to 2021; junta since the 2021 coup
polities.head: Ahmed Sékou Touré; Lansana Conté; Alpha Condé; Mamady Doumbouya
polities.rel: Sunni Islam
polities.econ: The world's largest bauxite reserves; iron ore at Simandou; poverty despite minerals
polities.now: The colony that voted no to de Gaulle in 1958 and was punished with an abrupt French withdrawal, Guinea suffered Touré's paranoid dictatorship and has had only one civilian transfer of power, undone by the 2021 coup.
polities.how: The 1958 referendum, Touré's camp Boiro, Conté's rule, the 2009 stadium massacre.
polities.next: The Simandou iron project and the junta's promised elections.

polities.gov: One-party socialism under Keita; Traoré's military rule to 1991; democracy 1992 to 2012; coups in 2012, 2020 and 2021; military junta since
polities.head: Modibo Keita; Moussa Traoré; Alpha Oumar Konaré; Amadou Toumani Touré; Assimi Goïta
polities.rel: Sunni Islam
polities.econ: Gold, cotton, livestock; among the poorest countries; aid cut after the coups
polities.now: Independent in 1960 and a democracy from 1992, Mali lost its north to Tuareg and jihadist rebels in 2012, was saved by French intervention in 2013, and since 2021 has been ruled by a junta that expelled France and the UN and hired Russian mercenaries.
polities.how: The Tuareg rebellions, the 2012 collapse, Operation Serval, the 2020 coup.
polities.next: Jihadist groups control much of the countryside.

polities.gov: French colony; one-party and military rule; coups in 1974, 1996, 1999, 2010 and 2023; a junta since July 2023
polities.head: Hamani Diori; Mamadou Tandja; Mahamadou Issoufou; Mohamed Bazoum, overthrown 2023; Abdourahamane Tchiani
polities.rel: Sunni Islam
polities.pop: About 27 million, the world's highest birth rate
polities.econ: Uranium for France, oil since 2011; the poorest country by the UN's index
polities.now: A Sahelian state with the world's fastest-growing population, which lost its elected president to a coup in 2023 and joined Mali and Burkina Faso in expelling French and American forces.
polities.how: Uranium, the Tuareg rebellions, the 2010 and 2023 coups.
polities.next: Jihadist insurgency and the break with the West.

polities.gov: French colony; civil war from 1965; Habré's dictatorship 1982 to 1990; Idriss Déby's rule 1990 to 2021; his son by military succession since
polities.head: François Tombalbaye; Hissène Habré; Idriss Déby; Mahamat Déby
polities.rel: Muslim north, Christian and animist south
polities.econ: Oil since 2003; cotton, livestock; French military base until 2024
polities.now: A north-south divide, a civil war that drew in Libya and France, Habré's regime convicted of crimes against humanity in 2016, and a Déby dynasty that France protected until Chad asked it to leave.
polities.how: The 1965 revolt, the Libyan war of the 1980s, Déby's 1990 takeover.
polities.next: Sudanese refugees and the Sahel's jihadists press on its borders.

polities.gov: German colony to 1916; French and British mandates; independent 1960; Ahidjo's one-party state; Paul Biya president since 1982
polities.head: Ahmadou Ahidjo; Paul Biya
polities.rel: Christian south, Muslim north
polities.econ: Oil, cocoa, timber; the port of Douala
polities.now: A German colony divided between France and Britain, reunited in 1961, and governed since 1982 by Paul Biya, the world's longest-serving non-royal leader, with an anglophone separatist war since 2017 and Boko Haram in the north.
polities.how: The German period, the UPC insurgency France crushed in the 1950s, Biya's forty years.
polities.next: The anglophone crisis and Biya's succession.

polities.gov: German colony to 1914; French mandate; independent 1960; the Eyadéma family since the 1967 coup
polities.head: Sylvanus Olympio, assassinated 1963; Gnassingbé Eyadéma 1967 to 2005; Faure Gnassingbé since
polities.rel: Christian, Muslim and traditional
polities.econ: Phosphates, cotton, the port of Lomé
polities.now: A German 'model colony' partitioned by France and Britain, whose first president was killed in Africa's first post-independence coup and which has been ruled by one family since 1967.
polities.how: The Gnassingbé dynasty's two generations.
polities.next: Constitutional changes in 2024 removed term limits by moving to a parliamentary system under the same ruler.

polities.gov: Dahomey's coups to 1972; Kérékou's Marxist state to 1990; the national conference model of democracy since; Talon's tightening since 2016
polities.head: Mathieu Kérékou; Nicéphore Soglo; Boni Yayi; Patrice Talon
polities.cap: Porto-Novo; Cotonou the seat of government
polities.rel: Vodun, Christianity, Islam
polities.econ: Cotton, the port of Cotonou's trade with Nigeria
polities.now: Formerly Dahomey, renamed Benin in 1975, which pioneered Africa's 'national conference' transition to democracy in 1990 and has narrowed it under Talon.
polities.how: Kérékou's Marxism, the 1990 conference, the alternations.
polities.next: Jihadist spillover from the Sahel in the north.

polities.gov: British colony; independent 1965; Jawara's democracy; Jammeh's dictatorship 1994 to 2017; democracy since
polities.head: Dawda Jawara; Yahya Jammeh; Adama Barrow
polities.rel: Sunni Islam
polities.econ: Groundnuts, tourism, remittances
polities.now: A river colony inside Senegal, Africa's smallest mainland state, which lost its democracy to Jammeh's coup in 1994 and recovered it when West African troops forced him out in 2017.
polities.how: British trading post, independence, the 1994 coup, the 2016 election.
polities.next: Transitional justice for Jammeh's crimes.

polities.gov: Portuguese colony to 1974 after Cabral's liberation war; one-party state; coups and instability since 1998
polities.head: Amílcar Cabral, assassinated 1973; Luís Cabral; João Bernardo Vieira; Umaro Sissoco Embaló
polities.rel: Islam, Christianity, traditional
polities.econ: Cashews; a transit point for Latin American cocaine
polities.now: Won from Portugal by Amílcar Cabral's PAIGC in a war that helped bring down the Lisbon regime, and since then among Africa's most unstable states, with no president completing a term between 1998 and 2019.
polities.how: The liberation war, the 1980 coup, the 1998 civil war.
polities.next: Drug-trafficking's hold on the army.

polities.gov: Coups in 1966, 1980, 1982, 1983, 1987, 2014, 2015 and 2022; Sankara's revolution 1983 to 1987; Compaoré's rule to 2014; junta since 2022
polities.head: Thomas Sankara; Blaise Compaoré; Ibrahim Traoré
polities.rel: Islam, Christianity, traditional
polities.econ: Gold, cotton; among the poorest; half the territory outside state control
polities.now: Upper Volta renamed by Sankara, whose four years of revolution ended in his murder by Compaoré, who ruled for twenty-seven years; since 2015 jihadist insurgency has taken half the country and two coups have brought a young captain to power.
polities.how: Sankara, Compaoré, the 2014 uprising, the insurgency, the 2022 coups.
polities.next: The war with the jihadists is being lost.

polities.gov: French colony; one-party rule; military governments since 1978 with elections since 2007
polities.head: Moktar Ould Daddah; a succession of generals; Mohamed Ould Ghazouani
polities.rel: Sunni Islam; an Islamic republic
polities.econ: Iron ore, fish, gold, gas from 2025; slavery abolished in 1981 and criminalised in 2007, persisting in practice
polities.now: A Saharan state bridging the Arab Maghreb and black Africa, with a caste system that kept slavery alive longest of any country, governed by officers since 1978.
polities.how: Independence 1960, the Western Sahara war, the 1989 clashes with Senegal.
polities.next: Gas exports and Sahel spillover.

polities.gov: Spanish colony to 1975; occupied and annexed by Morocco; the Polisario Front's Sahrawi Republic in exile and a strip of the east
polities.head: Moroccan administration; the Polisario leadership at Tindouf
polities.rel: Sunni Islam
polities.pop: About 600,000, many of them Moroccan settlers; 170,000 refugees in Algeria
polities.econ: Phosphates at Bou Craa, fishing
polities.now: Spain's last colony, taken by Morocco's Green March in 1975, fought over until a 1991 ceasefire, with a promised referendum never held; the United States recognised Morocco's claim in 2020.
polities.how: Spanish rule, the 1975 ICJ opinion, the Green March, the war to 1991.
polities.next: Morocco's autonomy plan gains support; the Polisario resumed fighting in 2020.

polities.gov: Elective monarchy of the Bakongo under the manikongo; provinces under appointed governors
polities.head: Nzinga a Nkuwu, baptised João I in 1491; Afonso I (1509 to 1543); Garcia II
polities.rel: Catholic by royal conversion from 1491, mixed with Kongo religion
polities.econ: Copper, raffia cloth, nzimbu shells; the slave trade with the Portuguese from the 1500s
polities.now: The one African kingdom that adopted Christianity as a state religion at its own choice, corresponded with the pope, and was drawn into the Portuguese slave trade that Afonso I protested and could not stop.
polities.how: Founded around 1390; the Portuguese arrival in 1483 and the conversion of 1491.
polities.next: Portuguese forces kill the king at Ambuila in 1665; the kingdom fragments into civil war.

polities.gov: Portuguese colony from Luanda, founded 1576; the Ndongo and Matamba kingdoms resisting under Queen Nzinga; effective occupation of the interior only by the 1920s
polities.head: Portuguese governors; Queen Nzinga (1624 to 1663)
polities.rel: Catholic missions; Kongo and Mbundu religion
polities.econ: The largest source of slaves for Brazil for three centuries; coffee and diamonds in the twentieth
polities.now: Portugal's oldest African colony, founded for the slave trade to Brazil, which held only the coast for most of its history and was settled by Portuguese in the 1950s.
polities.how: Luanda's founding, the wars with Nzinga, the slave trade, the Berlin conference, Salazar's settlement.
polities.next: The liberation war begins in 1961; independence in November 1975 brings civil war.

polities.gov: Liberation war 1961 to 1974; MPLA one-party Marxist state; civil war with UNITA 1975 to 2002; presidential republic under the MPLA since
polities.head: Agostinho Neto; José Eduardo dos Santos 1979 to 2017; João Lourenço
polities.rel: Christian majority
polities.econ: Oil and diamonds; Chinese loans; extreme inequality
polities.now: A Cold War battlefield where Cuban troops, South African forces and American aid sustained a civil war that killed about half a million before UNITA's Savimbi died in 2002; oil has enriched the MPLA elite since.
polities.how: The three movements, the 1975 intervention, Cuito Cuanavale in 1988, the 1992 election's collapse.
polities.next: Oil dependence and Lourenço's succession.

polities.gov: Sacred kingships of the Luba on the upper Congo and the Lunda mwant yav's empire with tributary kingdoms including Kazembe
polities.head: Luba mulopwe; Lunda mwant yav; Kazembe
polities.rel: Luba and Lunda ancestral religion; the king's sacred power
polities.econ: Copper, salt, ivory; long-distance trade to both coasts by the eighteenth century
polities.now: The savanna kingdoms of the southern Congo basin, whose model of sacred kingship spread across central Africa and whose trade reached the Portuguese on both coasts.
polities.how: Luba state-building from the sixteenth century; Lunda expansion in the seventeenth.
polities.next: Swahili-Arab slave traders and then the Congo Free State and Belgium break the kingdoms by 1900.

polities.gov: Swahili-Arab trading empire of Tippu Tip in the eastern Congo, nominally under Zanzibar, then a Congo Free State governorship
polities.head: Tippu Tip (Hamad bin Muhammad)
polities.rel: Islam among the traders
polities.econ: Ivory and slaves to Zanzibar
polities.now: The Zanzibari ivory and slave trader's empire in the eastern Congo, which Leopold's state first employed and then destroyed in the Congo-Arab war of 1892 to 1894.
polities.how: Tippu Tip's caravans from the 1860s; his appointment as Free State governor in 1887.
polities.next: The Free State defeats the Zanzibari traders by 1894.

polities.t: Congo Free State and Belgian Congo
polities.gov: Leopold II's personal possession 1885 to 1908; Belgian colony after the atrocities were exposed; rule by the state, the Church and the companies
polities.head: Leopold II; Belgian governors-general
polities.rel: Catholic missions; Kimbanguism from 1921
polities.pop: About 13 million by 1955; millions died under Leopold
polities.econ: Rubber and ivory by forced labour; then copper from Katanga, diamonds, uranium for the Manhattan Project
polities.now: Leopold's rubber regime killed and mutilated on a scale that provoked the first international human rights campaign; Belgium took over in 1908 and ran a paternalist colony with no African university graduates until the 1950s.
polities.how: The Berlin conference, the rubber terror, the 1908 annexation, the Union Minière.
polities.next: Riots in 1959 and independence in June 1960 under Lumumba; the army mutinies within days.

polities.gov: Collapse at independence; Mobutu's kleptocracy 1965 to 1997; two Congo wars; Kabila father and son; Tshisekedi since 2019
polities.head: Patrice Lumumba, murdered 1961; Mobutu Sese Seko; Laurent and Joseph Kabila; Félix Tshisekedi
polities.rel: Catholic and Protestant majority, Kimbanguist
polities.econ: Cobalt (most of the world's), copper, diamonds, coltan; among the poorest per head; the UN's largest peacekeeping mission
polities.now: The Congo crisis of 1960 ended in Lumumba's murder and Mobutu's thirty-two-year dictatorship; the wars of 1996 to 2003 drew in nine African armies and killed millions; the east remains at war, with Rwandan-backed M23 taking Goma in 2025.
polities.how: Katanga's secession, Mobutu, the Rwandan genocide's spillover, the African world war.
polities.next: The east's war and the cobalt economy.

polities.gov: French colony; the Bongo family's rule 1967 to 2023; a military junta after the 2023 coup, with its leader elected in 2025
polities.head: Omar Bongo 1967 to 2009; Ali Bongo; Brice Oligui Nguema
polities.rel: Christian majority
polities.econ: Oil, manganese, timber; a high income per head unevenly shared
polities.now: An oil state ruled by one family for fifty-six years under French protection until officers removed Ali Bongo hours after a disputed election in 2023.
polities.how: Omar Bongo's forty-two years as France's closest African client.
polities.next: The junta leader's conversion into an elected president.

polities.gov: French colony of Ubangi-Shari; Bokassa's dictatorship and self-coronation as emperor 1976; coups; civil war since 2013; Russian mercenaries guarding the president since 2018
polities.head: Barthélemy Boganda; Jean-Bédel Bokassa; Ange-Félix Patassé; François Bozizé; Faustin-Archange Touadéra
polities.rel: Christian majority, Muslim minority; sectarian war since 2013
polities.econ: Diamonds, timber, gold; among the poorest countries
polities.now: A landlocked state whose emperor Bokassa France crowned and then removed, torn since 2013 by a war between Muslim Séléka and Christian anti-balaka militias, and now guarded by Wagner.
polities.how: Bokassa, the 2013 collapse, Russian entry in 2018.
polities.next: The state controls little beyond Bangui.

polities.gov: Spanish colony to 1968; Macías Nguema's terror to 1979; Teodoro Obiang's dictatorship since
polities.head: Francisco Macías Nguema; Teodoro Obiang Nguema, in power since 1979
polities.rel: Catholic
polities.econ: Oil since the mid-1990s; among the highest GDP per head in Africa and among the most unequal
polities.now: Spain's only sub-Saharan colony, destroyed by Macías's regime, which killed or exiled a third of the population, and ruled by his nephew Obiang since 1979, Africa's longest-serving president, on oil money.
polities.how: Independence 1968, the 1979 coup, oil.
polities.next: Dynastic succession to Obiang's son.

polities.gov: Omani possession from 1698; the sultanate seated at Zanzibar from 1840; British protectorate from 1890
polities.head: Sultan Seyyid Said (1806 to 1856); the Busaidi sultans
polities.rel: Ibadi and Sunni Islam; Hindu Indian merchants
polities.pop: About 200,000 on the islands; a mainland empire of caravan routes
polities.econ: Cloves on slave plantations; the ivory and slave trade from the interior; the world's largest slave market until 1873
polities.now: The Omani sultans moved to Zanzibar in 1840 and built a commercial empire of cloves, ivory and slaves reaching the Great Lakes, until Britain forced the closure of the slave market and took the islands as a protectorate.
polities.how: Oman's expulsion of the Portuguese, Seyyid Said's move, the 1873 treaty, the 38-minute war of 1896.
polities.next: Independence in December 1963; the revolution of January 1964 overthrows the sultan and unites Zanzibar with Tanganyika.

polities.gov: German colony 1885 to 1918; British mandate as Tanganyika under indirect rule
polities.head: German governors; the Maji Maji rebellion of 1905 to 1907; British governors; Julius Nyerere's TANU from 1954
polities.rel: Islam on the coast, Christianity inland through missions, traditional religions
polities.econ: Sisal, coffee, cotton; the Central Railway; the groundnut scheme's failure in the 1940s
polities.now: Germany's largest colony, where the Maji Maji revolt and its suppression killed up to 300,000, became Britain's mandate, and produced in Nyerere's TANU the most disciplined nationalist movement in East Africa.
polities.how: Peters's treaties, the Maji Maji war, Lettow-Vorbeck's campaign of 1914 to 1918, the mandate.
polities.next: Independence in December 1961; union with Zanzibar in 1964 as Tanzania.

polities.gov: Nyerere's one-party socialist state under ujamaa; multiparty since 1992 with the same ruling party, CCM, winning every election
polities.head: Julius Nyerere 1961 to 1985; Mwinyi; Mkapa; Kikwete; John Magufuli; Samia Suluhu Hassan since 2021
polities.cap: Dodoma; Dar es Salaam the commercial capital
polities.rel: Christian and Muslim in roughly equal shares; Zanzibar Muslim
polities.econ: Gold, tourism, agriculture; ujamaa's collectivisation failed by 1980; steady growth since 2000
polities.now: Nyerere's Tanzania was the Cold War's non-aligned model of African socialism, host to the liberation movements of southern Africa, and the state that invaded Uganda to remove Idi Amin in 1979; the ruling party has never lost power.
polities.how: Independence, the Arusha Declaration of 1967, the union with Zanzibar, the 1992 opening.
polities.next: Whether the dominant party permits a competitive election.

polities.gov: East Africa Protectorate from 1895; crown colony from 1920 with a settler legislature; Mau Mau emergency 1952 to 1960
polities.head: British governors; Jomo Kenyatta, jailed 1953 to 1961
polities.rel: Christian missions, Islam on the coast, Kikuyu and other traditions
polities.econ: The Uganda railway; the White Highlands reserved for settlers; coffee and tea
polities.now: A settler colony where the best land went to Europeans, the Kikuyu were confined to reserves, and the Mau Mau insurgency was crushed with detention camps and some 11,000 rebel deaths, after which Britain conceded African rule.
polities.how: The railway, settler land policy, the Mau Mau war, the Lancaster House conferences.
polities.next: Independence in December 1963 under Kenyatta.

polities.gov: Kenyatta's and Moi's one-party state to 1991; multiparty since 1992; the 2010 constitution devolves power to 47 counties
polities.head: Jomo Kenyatta; Daniel arap Moi 1978 to 2002; Mwai Kibaki; Uhuru Kenyatta; William Ruto since 2022
polities.rel: Christian majority, Muslim coast and northeast
polities.econ: East Africa's largest economy: tea, horticulture, tourism, mobile money (M-Pesa), the Nairobi hub; debt to China
polities.now: Capitalist and Western-aligned from independence, Kenya survived Moi's repression, the 2007 election violence that killed about 1,200, and al-Shabaab attacks, and is the region's commercial and diplomatic hub, with youth protests against taxes in 2024.
polities.how: Kenyatta's settlement with the settlers, Moi, the 2002 alternation, the 2007 crisis, the 2010 constitution.
polities.next: Debt, ethnic politics and a young population's expectations.

polities.gov: Kingdom of Buganda under the kabaka; British protectorate from 1894 with Buganda's privileged agreement of 1900
polities.head: Kabakas Mutesa I and Mwanga; British commissioners and governors
