polities.rel: Catholic and Anglican missions competing from 1877; Islam; the Uganda martyrs of 1886
polities.econ: Cotton grown by Africans, coffee; Indian traders
polities.now: The Great Lakes kingdom that received Speke in 1862, converted amid wars of religion, and became the core of a protectorate run through its own chiefs under the 1900 agreement.
polities.how: Buganda's rise over Bunyoro, the missionaries, the Lugard intervention, the agreement.
polities.next: Independence in October 1962 with the kabaka as president and Milton Obote as prime minister.

polities.gov: Obote's abolition of the kingdoms; Idi Amin's dictatorship 1971 to 1979; Obote again; Museveni's 'no-party' then dominant-party rule since 1986
polities.head: Milton Obote; Idi Amin; Yoweri Museveni, in power since 1986
polities.rel: Christian majority, Muslim minority
polities.pop: About 48 million, among the youngest populations
polities.econ: Coffee, oil from 2025, remittances; refugee host for 1.7 million
polities.now: Amin's eight years killed up to 300,000 and expelled the Asians; Museveni's bush war ended the Obote era and he has ruled for nearly forty years, with the Lord's Resistance Army's war in the north and the constitution amended to remove age limits.
polities.how: The 1966 crisis, Amin, the Tanzanian invasion of 1979, Museveni's NRA victory.
polities.next: Succession and oil.

polities.gov: Tutsi monarchy under the mwami with a Hutu majority; German then Belgian rule through the court from 1899
polities.head: Mwami Rwabugiri (around 1853 to 1895); Mutara III
polities.rel: Traditional religion; Catholic conversion in the twentieth century
polities.econ: Cattle and banana agriculture on terraced hills; coffee under Belgium
polities.now: A centralised kingdom whose Belgian rulers hardened the Hutu-Tutsi distinction with identity cards in 1933 and then switched support to the Hutu majority in the 1950s.
polities.how: Rwabugiri's state, German and Belgian indirect rule, the 1959 Hutu revolution.
polities.next: The monarchy is abolished in 1961; independence in 1962 under Hutu rule with Tutsi refugees in exile.

polities.gov: Hutu republics under Kayibanda and Habyarimana; the 1994 genocide; the RPF's authoritarian state under Kagame since
polities.head: Grégoire Kayibanda; Juvénal Habyarimana; Paul Kagame, in power since 1994
polities.rel: Christian majority
polities.econ: Coffee, tea, tourism, services; rapid growth and low corruption; aid dependence; minerals from eastern Congo
polities.now: The genocide of April to July 1994 killed about 800,000 Tutsi and moderate Hutu in a hundred days; the RPF that stopped it has governed since with order, growth and no tolerated opposition, and fights proxy wars in Congo.
polities.how: The 1959 revolution, the RPF invasion of 1990, the genocide, the Congo wars.
polities.next: Kagame's succession and the Congo intervention.

polities.gov: Tutsi monarchy under the mwami; Belgian rule; independent 1962; Tutsi military regimes; civil war 1993 to 2005; CNDD-FDD rule since
polities.head: Mwami Mwambutsa IV; Michel Micombero; Pierre Buyoya; Pierre Nkurunziza; Évariste Ndayishimiye
polities.rel: Catholic majority
polities.econ: Coffee, tea; among the poorest countries in the world
polities.now: Rwanda's twin kingdom, where the Tutsi army's 1972 massacre of Hutu killed up to 200,000, and a civil war after the 1993 murder of the first Hutu president killed 300,000; the ruling party has closed the political space since 2015.
polities.how: The monarchy, the 1972 killings, the 1993 war, the Arusha accord.
polities.next: Isolation and poverty.

polities.gov: Portuguese forts from 1505; the prazo estates of the Zambezi; a colony effectively occupied only by the 1920s; FRELIMO's war from 1964
polities.head: Portuguese governors; Eduardo Mondlane, assassinated 1969; Samora Machel
polities.cap: Mozambique Island, then Lourenço Marques (Maputo) from 1898
polities.rel: Catholic; Islam on the north coast; traditional religions
polities.econ: Gold trade with Mutapa, then slaves; migrant labour to South Africa's mines; sugar and cotton
polities.now: A chain of Portuguese ports on the Indian Ocean for four centuries, a labour reserve for the Rand mines, and the site of a ten-year liberation war.
polities.how: The Portuguese arrival in 1498, the Zambezi prazos, the Berlin conference, Salazar's settlement.
polities.next: Independence in June 1975; civil war with RENAMO from 1977 to 1992.

polities.gov: FRELIMO one-party Marxist state to 1990; multiparty since with FRELIMO winning every election; contested results in 2024
polities.head: Samora Machel; Joaquim Chissano; Armando Guebuza; Filipe Nyusi; Daniel Chapo
polities.rel: Christian and Muslim
polities.econ: Gas in Cabo Delgado, aluminium, coal; the 'hidden debt' scandal of 2016; an Islamist insurgency in the north since 2017
polities.now: Independence brought a civil war with the Rhodesian- and South African-backed RENAMO that killed about a million; peace in 1992 brought FRELIMO dominance, a debt scandal, and a jihadist war around the gas fields.
polities.how: Machel's socialism, the war, the Rome accord, gas.
polities.next: Cabo Delgado's insurgency and the 2024 election protests.

polities.gov: Sakalava, Betsimisaraka and other kingdoms; the Merina kingdom of the highlands unified most of the island after 1810
polities.head: Andrianampoinimerina; Radama I (1810 to 1828); Queen Ranavalona I; Rainilaiarivony as prime minister 1864 to 1895
polities.rel: Ancestral religion; Protestant conversion of the court in 1869; missionaries expelled under Ranavalona I
polities.econ: Rice, cattle, slaves exported to the Mascarenes; British-trained army and printing press under Radama
polities.now: The Merina kings of the highlands used British arms and missionaries to conquer most of the island, then under Ranavalona I expelled the Europeans and persecuted Christians, before the court converted and the French arrived.
polities.how: Andrianampoinimerina's unification, Radama's British alliance, the 1869 conversion, French claims from 1883.
polities.next: France conquers the island in 1895 and abolishes the monarchy in 1897.

polities.gov: French colony to 1960, with the 1947 revolt killing tens of thousands; independent republic; Ratsiraka's socialism; coups and crises in 1991, 2002, 2009
polities.head: Philibert Tsiranana; Didier Ratsiraka; Marc Ravalomanana; Andry Rajoelina
polities.rel: Christian and traditional
polities.econ: Vanilla, nickel, textiles; among the poorest countries; deforestation
polities.now: A French colony where the 1947 rising was crushed at a cost of up to 90,000 lives, independent since 1960, and since then among the few countries to have grown poorer per head.
polities.how: Conquest, the 1947 revolt, Ratsiraka's years, the 2009 coup.
polities.next: Political instability and climate shocks in the south.

polities.gov: British protectorate of Nyasaland; the Central African Federation 1953 to 1963; Banda's one-party state 1964 to 1994; multiparty democracy since
polities.head: Hastings Kamuzu Banda; Bakili Muluzi; Bingu wa Mutharika; Joyce Banda; Lazarus Chakwera; Peter Mutharika
polities.rel: Christian majority, Muslim minority
polities.econ: Tobacco, tea, maize; among the poorest; aid-dependent
polities.now: Livingstone's lake country became a British protectorate, Banda's thirty-year personal rule, and since 1994 a democracy whose courts overturned a rigged election in 2020.
polities.how: The missionaries, the federation Africans rejected, Banda, the 1993 referendum.
polities.next: Food security and debt.

polities.gov: Shona kingdoms succeeding Great Zimbabwe; the Mutapa state on the Zambezi and the Rozvi empire of the Changamire from the 1680s
polities.head: Mwenemutapa; Changamire Dombo
polities.rel: Shona religion; the Mwari cult
polities.econ: Gold mined for the Swahili and Portuguese trade; cattle
polities.now: The Shona successors of Great Zimbabwe, trading gold to the coast, which the Portuguese tried to control and the Rozvi expelled in 1693.
polities.how: Great Zimbabwe's decline around 1450; the Portuguese penetration; Dombo's victories.
polities.next: The Nguni invasions of the 1830s destroy the Rozvi; the Ndebele take the land.

polities.gov: Dutch East India Company station from 1652; British colony from 1806; responsible government from 1872
polities.head: Jan van Riebeeck; Dutch governors; British governors; Cecil Rhodes as prime minister 1890 to 1896
polities.rel: Dutch Reformed; Anglican; Islam among Cape Malays; mission Christianity
polities.econ: A supply station, then wine, wool, and from 1867 diamonds at Kimberley
polities.now: A Dutch refreshment station that became a settler society with imported slaves, taken by Britain in 1806, from which the Boers trekked inland in the 1830s and from which Rhodes drove the British advance north.
polities.how: The VOC settlement, slavery, British abolition in 1834, the Great Trek, diamonds.
polities.next: Union with Natal, the Transvaal and the Orange Free State in 1910.

polities.gov: Shaka's military kingdom from 1816 with age regiments; British colony of Natal from 1843
polities.head: Shaka (1816 to 1828); Dingane; Mpande; Cetshwayo
polities.rel: Zulu religion; Christian missions in Natal
polities.pop: About 250,000 Zulu subjects; Natal's Indian indentured labourers from 1860
polities.econ: Cattle; Natal's sugar plantations
polities.now: Shaka's regiments built a kingdom whose wars set off the Mfecane migrations across southern Africa; Britain destroyed it in 1879 after losing a regiment at Isandlwana.
polities.how: The Mfecane, Blood River in 1838, the Anglo-Zulu war.
polities.next: Zululand is annexed to Natal in 1897; Gandhi organises Natal's Indians.

polities.gov: Afrikaner republics with elected presidents and volksraads; a franchise restricted to whites
polities.head: Paul Kruger, president of the Transvaal 1883 to 1900; M. T. Steyn of the Free State
polities.rel: Dutch Reformed Calvinism
polities.pop: About 300,000 whites and a larger black population in the Transvaal
polities.econ: Pastoral farming until the Witwatersrand gold discovery of 1886 made the Transvaal the richest state in Africa
polities.now: The trekkers' republics recognised by Britain in the 1850s, which gold turned into the prize of the South African war of 1899 to 1902, fought by 450,000 British troops against 60,000 Boers, with civilians in concentration camps.
polities.how: The Great Trek, the Sand River convention, the 1881 war, the gold rush, the Jameson raid.
polities.next: Annexed in 1902; self-government by 1907; union in 1910.

polities.gov: Dominion with a white electorate; segregation by the Natives Land Act of 1913; Afrikaner nationalism rising
polities.head: Botha, Smuts, Hertzog as prime ministers
polities.rel: Dutch Reformed, Anglican, African independent churches
polities.pop: About 12 million in 1946, a fifth white
polities.econ: Gold and diamonds; mine labour from across southern Africa; industrialisation in the Second World War
polities.now: A dominion built on gold and black labour, which fought for Britain in both world wars under Smuts while Afrikaner nationalism organised the white electorate against him.
polities.how: Union in 1910, the 1913 Land Act, the Rand revolt of 1922, the 1936 removal of Cape Africans from the roll.
polities.next: The National Party wins the 1948 election and legislates apartheid.

polities.gov: White minority rule under the National Party; apartheid laws from 1948; a republic outside the Commonwealth from 1961
polities.head: Malan, Verwoerd, Vorster, P. W. Botha, F. W. de Klerk; Mandela imprisoned 1962 to 1990
polities.rel: Dutch Reformed Church's theological defence of apartheid; the churches of resistance
polities.econ: Gold, coal, arms; sanctions and disinvestment in the 1980s; the economy's dependence on black labour it disenfranchised
polities.now: Legal separation of the races, the bantustans, Sharpeville in 1960, Soweto in 1976, a state of emergency through the 1980s, and a nuclear weapon, until de Klerk released Mandela in 1990 and negotiated the end.
polities.how: The 1948 election, the Group Areas and pass laws, the ANC's banning and armed struggle, the township revolt, sanctions, the 1990 opening.
polities.next: The first democratic election in April 1994; Mandela president.

polities.gov: Constitutional democracy under the 1996 constitution; the ANC in government since 1994, in coalition since losing its majority in 2024
polities.head: Nelson Mandela; Thabo Mbeki; Jacob Zuma; Cyril Ramaphosa
polities.rel: Christian majority; religious freedom
polities.econ: Africa's most industrialised economy; mining, finance, cars; unemployment above 30 per cent; electricity crisis; the Zuma-era 'state capture'
polities.now: The negotiated miracle of 1994 produced a constitution and a Truth Commission, then two decades of the ANC's decline into corruption under Zuma; in 2024 it lost its majority and governs with the opposition.
polities.how: The 1994 election, the TRC, Mbeki's AIDS denial, Zuma's state capture, Ramaphosa's reform.
polities.next: Growth, crime and the coalition's survival.

polities.gov: Rhodes's British South Africa Company to 1923; self-governing settler colony; the unilateral declaration of independence of 1965 under Ian Smith
polities.head: Cecil Rhodes; Ian Smith, prime minister 1964 to 1979
polities.rel: Christian missions; Shona and Ndebele religion
polities.pop: About 7 million by 1979, 250,000 of them white
polities.econ: Tobacco, gold, chrome; sanctions after 1965; the Bush war from 1972
polities.now: Rhodes's company colony, which crushed the Shona and Ndebele risings of 1896, became a settler state that declared independence rather than accept majority rule, and fought a guerrilla war it could not win.
polities.how: The pioneer column of 1890, the 1923 constitution, the federation, UDI, the war.
polities.next: The Lancaster House agreement of 1979; Zimbabwe independent under Mugabe in April 1980.

polities.gov: Mugabe's rule 1980 to 2017, one-party in practice, with the Gukurahundi massacres of the 1980s; Mnangagwa since the 2017 coup; ZANU-PF throughout
polities.head: Robert Mugabe; Emmerson Mnangagwa
polities.rel: Christian majority
polities.econ: Hyperinflation to 2009; land seizures from 2000 collapsed commercial farming; gold, platinum, tobacco; mass emigration
polities.now: Independence's early promise under Mugabe became Africa's most spectacular economic collapse after the farm invasions of 2000, with inflation reaching the hundreds of millions per cent; the army replaced Mugabe with his deputy in 2017.
polities.how: Lancaster House, Gukurahundi, the 2000 land seizures, the 2008 election violence, the coup.
polities.next: Currency chaos and ZANU-PF succession.

polities.gov: The Lozi kingdom of Barotseland; British protectorate as Northern Rhodesia from 1911; Kaunda's one-party state 1972 to 1991; multiparty democracy since with three alternations
polities.head: Lewanika of the Lozi; Kenneth Kaunda 1964 to 1991; Frederick Chiluba; Michael Sata; Edgar Lungu; Hakainde Hichilema
polities.rel: Christian nation by the 1996 constitution
polities.econ: Copper, about 70 per cent of exports; a debt default in 2020 and restructuring with China and bondholders
polities.now: Barotseland's king accepted British protection in 1890; the Copperbelt made Northern Rhodesia valuable; Kaunda's Zambia hosted the liberation movements and nationalised copper into decline; since 1991 power has changed hands at the ballot three times.
polities.how: Lewanika, the federation, Kaunda's humanism, the 1991 election.
polities.next: Copper prices and debt.

polities.gov: Bechuanaland Protectorate; independent 1966; the Botswana Democratic Party in power until 2024, when the opposition won
polities.head: Seretse Khama; Quett Masire; Festus Mogae; Ian Khama; Mokgweetsi Masisi; Duma Boko
polities.rel: Christian majority
polities.econ: Diamonds since 1967, managed through a De Beers partnership; the fastest growth in the world 1966 to 1999; HIV prevalence among the highest
polities.now: A protectorate Britain neglected became Africa's development success: diamonds, honest government under Seretse Khama's successors, and in 2024 the first change of ruling party since independence.
polities.how: The chiefs' 1895 appeal to London, Khama's leadership, the diamond deal.
polities.next: Diamond demand's decline.

polities.gov: German colony to 1915; South African mandate and then illegal occupation under apartheid; SWAPO's war from 1966; independent since 1990 under SWAPO
polities.head: German governors; Sam Nujoma 1990 to 2005; Hifikepunye Pohamba; Hage Geingob; Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah, the first woman president, since 2025
polities.rel: Christian majority
polities.econ: Diamonds, uranium, fishing; the world's second-lowest population density; green hydrogen plans
polities.now: Germany's genocide of the Herero and Nama in 1904 to 1908 killed up to 80,000; South Africa ruled the territory for seventy-five years against UN resolutions; SWAPO's war and the Cuban-South African settlement of 1988 brought independence in 1990.
polities.how: The Herero war, the mandate, the ICJ cases, Cuito Cuanavale, the 1989 election.
polities.next: Germany's reparations offer and land reform.

polities.gov: Moshoeshoe's kingdom, a British protectorate from 1868; constitutional monarchy since 1966 with coups and military rule
polities.head: Moshoeshoe I; kings Moshoeshoe II and Letsie III; prime ministers
polities.rel: Christian majority
polities.econ: Water sold to South Africa, garments, remittances from the mines; among the highest HIV rates
polities.now: Moshoeshoe built a mountain refuge from the Mfecane and asked for British protection against the Boers; the kingdom survived surrounded by South Africa, which it depends on entirely.
polities.how: The Basotho wars, the protectorate, independence in 1966, the coups.
polities.next: Dependence on South Africa and political instability.

polities.gov: Swazi kingdom; British protectorate from 1903; independent 1968; absolute monarchy since Sobhuza II suspended the constitution in 1973
polities.head: Sobhuza II (1921 to 1982); Mswati III since 1986
polities.rel: Christian and Swazi traditional
polities.econ: Sugar, forestry; South African dependence; the world's highest HIV prevalence
polities.now: Africa's last absolute monarchy, renamed Eswatini in 2018, where pro-democracy protests in 2021 were put down by force.
polities.how: Mswati II's kingdom, the concessions scandal, the 1973 decree.
polities.next: Pressure for constitutional reform.

polities.gov: Hudson's Bay Company's chartered territory over the drainage of Hudson Bay
polities.head: Company governors; the Cree, Assiniboine and other nations in fact
polities.rel: Indigenous religions; Catholic and Anglican missions
polities.pop: Perhaps 50,000 indigenous people and a few hundred traders
polities.econ: The fur trade in beaver
polities.now: A royal charter of 1670 gave the Company a third of North America on paper; in practice it ran trading posts among the Cree and Métis who supplied the furs.
polities.how: The 1670 charter; competition with the North West Company until the 1821 merger.
polities.next: Sold to Canada in 1870; the Red River rebellion follows.

polities.gov: Triple Alliance of Tenochtitlan, Texcoco and Tlacopan under the huey tlatoani of Tenochtitlan; tributary city-states kept their rulers
polities.head: Moctezuma I; Ahuitzotl; Moctezuma II (1502 to 1520)
polities.cap: Tenochtitlan, about 200,000 people, among the largest cities in the world
polities.rel: Mexica religion centred on Huitzilopochtli and Tlaloc, with human sacrifice at the Templo Mayor
polities.pop: About 5 to 6 million in the empire; central Mexico perhaps 15 to 25 million
polities.econ: Tribute in maize, cotton, cacao and feathers from some 400 towns; the Tlatelolco market; chinampa agriculture
polities.now: The Mexica alliance dominates central Mexico by war and tribute, with Tlaxcala and the Tarascans unconquered; Cortés lands in 1519 and finds allies among the tributaries.
polities.how: The Mexica founded Tenochtitlan around 1325 and overthrew their overlords in 1428.
polities.next: Smallpox and Spanish-Tlaxcalan siege destroy Tenochtitlan in August 1521.

polities.gov: Sapa Inca's absolute rule over four quarters (Tawantinsuyu) through a decimal administration, labour tax (mit'a) and the quipu
polities.head: Pachacuti; Topa Inca; Huayna Capac (died 1527); Atahualpa
polities.rel: Sun worship with the Inca as the sun's son; mummified ancestors
polities.econ: State storehouses, terraced agriculture, 40,000 kilometres of roads, llama caravans; no money or markets
polities.now: The largest state in the Americas, from Ecuador to Chile, held by roads, storehouses and labour tribute, and in civil war between two brothers when Pizarro arrives with 168 men in 1532.
polities.how: Pachacuti's expansion from 1438; Huayna Capac's death from smallpox before the Spanish arrived.
polities.next: Atahualpa is captured at Cajamarca in November 1532 and executed in 1533; Cusco falls; resistance at Vilcabamba lasts to 1572.

polities.gov: City-states and small kingdoms in Yucatán, the highlands and Oaxaca; the League of Mayapan dissolved around 1441
polities.head: Lords of Mayapan, the Quiché and Kaqchikel kingdoms, the Mixtec lords of Tilantongo
polities.rel: Maya and Mixtec religion; the codices
polities.econ: Maize, cacao, salt, cotton, obsidian; coastal canoe trade
polities.now: The Maya world's post-classic cities, divided and trading, and the Mixtec lordships of Oaxaca, conquered by Spain piecemeal between 1524 and 1697.
polities.how: The classic collapse of the ninth century; Mayapan's hegemony and fall.
polities.next: Alvarado conquers the highland Maya in 1524; the last Maya kingdom, the Itza at Tayasal, falls in 1697.

polities.gov: Tu'i Tonga sacred kingship over a maritime empire; civil war 1799 to 1852; Tupou I's constitutional monarchy from 1875
polities.head: Tu'i Tonga; George Tupou I (1845 to 1893)
polities.rel: Polynesian religion; Methodist conversion in the 1830s
polities.econ: Yam and taro, canoe fleets, tribute from Samoa and Fiji at the empire's height
polities.now: The Polynesian empire that ruled an ocean of islands from Tongatapu, later the one Pacific kingdom to write a constitution and avoid colonisation.
polities.how: The Tu'i Tonga dynasty from around 950; the empire's peak around 1200 to 1500; Tupou's unification.
polities.next: A British protectorate from 1900 that keeps its monarchy; fully independent in 1970.

polities.gov: Māori iwi and hapū under chiefs; no central authority; the Musket Wars of the 1810s to 1830s
polities.head: Rangatira of the iwi; Hongi Hika
polities.rel: Māori religion; Christian missions from 1814
polities.pop: About 100,000 Māori in 1800, falling with introduced disease and war
polities.econ: Kumara and fern-root cultivation, fishing; whaling and sealing stations; muskets traded for flax and potatoes
polities.now: The last large landmass settled by humans, around 1300, where muskets bought from traders set off twenty years of inter-tribal war that killed perhaps 20,000.
polities.how: Polynesian settlement around 1300; Cook's visits from 1769; the missions.
polities.next: The Treaty of Waitangi in 1840 makes New Zealand British.

polities.gov: Spanish viceroyalty from 1535 with audiencias at Mexico and Guadalajara; the Philippines governed from Mexico; Bourbon intendancies from 1786
polities.head: Viceroys from Antonio de Mendoza onward
polities.rel: Catholic conversion; the Virgin of Guadalupe from 1531; the Inquisition; the Jesuits expelled 1767
polities.pop: Indigenous population fell from perhaps 20 million to 1 million by 1620, recovering to 6 million by 1800 with Spanish and mestizo growth
polities.econ: Silver from Zacatecas and Guanajuato, the richest mines in the world; the Manila galleon; haciendas
polities.now: Spain's richest viceroyalty, producing most of the world's silver, governed by a viceroy and the Church, with a Creole elite excluded from high office and a population recovering from the demographic collapse of the conquest.
polities.how: The conquest of 1521, the epidemics, the silver boom from 1546, the Bourbon reforms.
polities.next: Hidalgo's rising of 1810 begins the independence war; Iturbide wins it in 1821.

polities.gov: Spanish viceroyalty covering most of South America until New Granada (1739) and Río de la Plata (1776) were split off
polities.head: Viceroys from Lima; Francisco de Toledo (1569 to 1581) organised the mita
polities.rel: Catholic; campaigns against indigenous religion; the Inquisition at Lima
polities.pop: Indigenous population fell from about 9 million to 600,000 by 1620
polities.econ: Potosí's silver mountain, the largest source in the world in the 1600s, worked by forced indigenous labour; mercury from Huancavelica
polities.now: The Spanish state in the Andes, built on Potosí's silver and the mita labour draft, governed from Lima for a Creole elite, and shaken by Túpac Amaru II's rebellion of 1780 to 1783.
polities.how: The conquest, Toledo's reforms, the silver cycle, the Bourbon partitions.
polities.next: San Martín takes Lima in 1821; Bolívar's victory at Ayacucho in 1824 ends Spanish rule.

polities.gov: Spanish viceroyalty covering modern Colombia, Venezuela, Ecuador and Panama
polities.head: Viceroys at Bogotá
polities.rel: Catholic
polities.econ: Gold from Antioquia, cacao from Caracas, the Cartagena slave port; the Comunero revolt of 1781 against taxes
polities.now: A late viceroyalty created to defend the Caribbean coast and reform revenue, whose Creoles produce Bolívar and the first juntas of 1810.
polities.how: Created in 1717, suppressed, and restored in 1739.
polities.next: Bolívar wins at Boyacá in 1819 and founds Gran Colombia.

polities.rx: ^viceroyalty of the río de la plata$|^united provinces of the río|^paraguay$
polities.gov: Spanish viceroyalty from 1776; the May Revolution of 1810; the United Provinces at war with Spain and with each other
polities.head: Viceroys at Buenos Aires; the junta of 1810; San Martín; Rivadavia
polities.rel: Catholic
polities.econ: Hides and salted beef; Potosí silver exported through Buenos Aires; British trade after 1810
polities.now: A viceroyalty built to stop Portuguese and British encroachment, which repelled British invasions in 1806 and 1807, declared independence in 1816, and fought civil wars between Buenos Aires and the provinces over its constitution.
polities.how: The 1776 creation, the British invasions, the May Revolution, independence at Tucumán.
polities.next: Rosas rules Buenos Aires from 1829; a national constitution comes in 1853.
polities.wk: Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata

polities.gov: Spanish colony governed by a captain-general; the last Spanish possession in the Americas with Puerto Rico
polities.head: Spanish captains-general; José Martí's independence movement
polities.rel: Catholic; African religions among the enslaved
polities.pop: About 1.6 million by 1890, a third black
polities.econ: Sugar on slave plantations, the world's largest producer; slavery abolished only in 1886
polities.now: The 'ever-faithful isle' that stayed Spanish after the mainland left, grew rich on sugar and slaves, and fought two independence wars from 1868 and 1895.
polities.how: Havana's role as the fleet's port, the sugar boom after Haiti's revolution, the Ten Years' War.
polities.next: The United States intervenes in 1898; Spain cedes Cuba; US occupation to 1902.

polities.gov: US occupation to 1902; a republic under the Platt Amendment to 1934; Batista's dictatorships
polities.head: Gerardo Machado; Fulgencio Batista 1933 to 1944 and 1952 to 1958
polities.rel: Catholic; Santería
polities.econ: Sugar for the US market; American ownership of utilities and land; Havana's casinos
polities.now: An independent republic under American tutelage, whose economy, sugar quota and politics ran through Washington, and whose dictator Batista faced Castro's guerrillas from 1956.
polities.how: The 1898 war, the Platt Amendment, the 1933 revolution, Batista's 1952 coup.
polities.next: Castro enters Havana on 1 January 1959.

polities.gov: One-party communist state under Fidel Castro to 2008, Raúl Castro to 2018, Díaz-Canel since
polities.head: Fidel Castro; Raúl Castro; Miguel Díaz-Canel
polities.rel: Catholic and Santería; religion restricted, then tolerated after 1992
polities.econ: Sugar under Soviet subsidy to 1991; the 'Special Period' collapse; tourism, remittances, doctors abroad; the US embargo since 1962; a currency crisis since 2021
polities.now: The revolution expelled American interests, survived the Bay of Pigs and the missile crisis of 1962, exported revolution and doctors, lost its Soviet patron in 1991, and is in its deepest economic crisis since.
polities.how: The revolution, the embargo, the Soviet alliance, the Special Period, the 2014 thaw and its reversal.
polities.next: Emigration at record levels and a government without resources.

polities.gov: French colony of plantation slavery; the slave revolution from 1791 under Toussaint Louverture
polities.head: French governors; Toussaint Louverture as governor-general 1801 to 1802
polities.rel: Catholic; Vodou among the enslaved
polities.pop: About 500,000 enslaved, 30,000 whites, 30,000 free people of colour in 1789
polities.econ: The richest colony in the world: half of Europe's sugar and coffee
polities.now: France's sugar colony, worked to death by half a million enslaved Africans, which rose in August 1791 in the only successful slave revolution in history and defeated British, Spanish and French armies.
polities.how: The French Revolution's rights of man, the 1791 rising, Toussaint's leadership, abolition in 1794, Napoleon's attempt to restore slavery.
polities.next: Dessalines declares the independent republic of Haiti on 1 January 1804.

polities.gov: Republic, empires and kingdoms in turn; US occupation 1915 to 1934; the Duvalier dictatorships 1957 to 1986; coups; Aristide; a state without an elected government since 2021
polities.head: Dessalines; Henri Christophe; François and Jean-Claude Duvalier; Jean-Bertrand Aristide; Jovenel Moïse, assassinated 2021
polities.cap: Port-au-Prince, largely controlled by gangs since 2023
polities.rel: Catholic and Vodou; Protestant growth
polities.econ: The poorest in the western hemisphere; the 1825 indemnity to France paid until 1947; the 2010 earthquake killed some 200,000
polities.now: The first black republic, punished by isolation and a French indemnity for its freedom, occupied by US Marines, ruled by the Duvaliers' terror, and since 2021 without an elected government while gangs control the capital.
polities.how: The indemnity of 1825, the occupation, Duvalierism, the earthquake, Moïse's murder.
polities.next: A Kenyan-led security mission and a transitional council attempt to restore elections.

polities.gov: Spanish colony of Santo Domingo; Haitian rule 1822 to 1844; republic; US occupation 1916 to 1924; Trujillo's dictatorship 1930 to 1961; democracy since the 1978 transition
polities.head: Rafael Trujillo; Joaquín Balaguer; Leonel Fernández; Luis Abinader
polities.cap: Santo Domingo, the oldest European city in the Americas
polities.rel: Catholic
polities.econ: Tourism, free-trade zones, remittances; the fastest growth in the region in the 2010s
polities.now: Columbus's first colony, which shared the island with Haiti in hostility, suffered Trujillo's thirty-one years, including the 1937 massacre of Haitians, and has become the Caribbean's largest economy.
polities.how: Spanish rule, the 1844 separation from Haiti, Trujillo, the 1965 US intervention, the 1978 alternation.
polities.next: Haitian migration and the border define its politics.

polities.gov: Spanish colony to 1898; US territory, a commonwealth since 1952; US citizens without a vote in presidential elections
polities.head: Governors elected since 1948
polities.rel: Catholic majority
polities.econ: Pharmaceuticals under tax incentives, tourism; bankruptcy in 2017; Hurricane Maria the same year
polities.now: Taken from Spain in 1898 and never made a state or a nation, Puerto Rico votes on its status repeatedly without result, and lost a tenth of its population after the 2017 fiscal and hurricane crises.
polities.how: The 1898 cession, the Jones Act of 1917, the commonwealth of 1952.
polities.next: Statehood, independence or status quo remains unsettled.

polities.gov: British sugar colony from 1655; crown colony after the 1865 Morant Bay rebellion; independent since 1962; parliamentary democracy
polities.head: British governors; Norman Manley; Alexander Bustamante; Michael Manley; Andrew Holness
polities.rel: Protestant; Rastafari
polities.econ: Sugar and slavery to 1834; bauxite, tourism, remittances; high debt and gang violence
polities.now: Britain's richest sugar colony, with the Maroons unconquered in the hills and the largest slave revolt in 1831, became an independent democracy in 1962 with one of the world's highest murder rates and a global cultural reach.
polities.how: The conquest of 1655, the slave economy, emancipation in 1834, Morant Bay, the 1938 riots, independence.
polities.next: Debt reduction and crime.

polities.gov: Portuguese captaincies, then a governor-general at Salvador; the Dutch in Pernambuco 1630 to 1654; a viceroyalty at Rio from 1763; the Portuguese court at Rio 1808 to 1821
polities.head: Governors-general; Johan Maurits for the Dutch; the Marquis of Pombal's reforms; King John VI at Rio
polities.cap: Salvador, then Rio de Janeiro from 1763
polities.rel: Catholic; the Jesuit missions; Candomblé among the enslaved
polities.pop: About 3 million in 1800, half enslaved or free blacks
polities.econ: Brazilwood, then sugar in the northeast, then gold and diamonds from Minas Gerais after 1695; about 4 million Africans imported, more than anywhere else
polities.now: Portugal's largest possession, built on sugar and gold with the largest slave population in the Americas, which became the seat of the Portuguese monarchy itself when Napoleon drove the court from Lisbon in 1807.
polities.how: Cabral's landing in 1500, the sugar cycle, the Dutch war, the gold rush, the court's arrival.
polities.next: The regent Pedro declares independence in September 1822 and is crowned emperor.

polities.gov: Constitutional monarchy under the Braganza emperors with a parliament and a 'moderating power' for the crown
polities.head: Pedro I; Pedro II (1831 to 1889)
polities.rel: Catholic established church
polities.econ: Coffee from São Paulo replaces sugar; the slave trade ended in 1850; the Paraguayan war of 1864 to 1870
polities.now: The only monarchy in independent Latin America, stable under Pedro II's long reign, the last state in the Americas to keep slavery, and victor in the bloodiest war in South American history.
polities.how: Independence in 1822, the regency's revolts, the coffee boom, the war against Paraguay.
polities.next: Slavery is abolished in May 1888; the army overthrows the emperor in November 1889.

polities.gov: Federal republic dominated by the São Paulo and Minas Gerais oligarchies, 'coffee with milk' politics; a narrow electorate
polities.head: Presidents Deodoro da Fonseca, Campos Sales and others
polities.rel: Church and state separated in 1890
polities.econ: Coffee about 70 per cent of exports; rubber in the Amazon; mass European immigration; the 1929 crash
polities.now: A republic run by state oligarchies trading the presidency, with the Canudos massacre of 1897 and the Contestado war showing the countryside's distance from Rio.
polities.how: The 1889 coup, the 1891 constitution, the governors' politics.
polities.next: Getúlio Vargas takes power in the revolution of 1930.

polities.gov: Vargas's provisional government, the Estado Novo dictatorship 1937 to 1945, democracy 1946 to 1964
polities.head: Getúlio Vargas 1930 to 1945 and 1951 to 1954; Juscelino Kubitschek; Jânio Quadros; João Goulart
polities.cap: Rio de Janeiro, then Brasília from 1960
polities.rel: Catholic majority
polities.econ: Import-substitution industrialisation; Petrobras 1953; Brasília and the car industry under Kubitschek; inflation
polities.now: Vargas built the modern Brazilian state, labour law and heavy industry as a dictator and then a populist, shot himself in 1954, and his heirs built Brasília and fifty years of progress in five before the 1964 coup.
polities.how: The 1930 revolution, the Estado Novo, Vargas's suicide, Kubitschek's developmentalism.
polities.next: The military overthrows Goulart in March 1964 and rules for twenty-one years.

polities.gov: Military dictatorship with controlled elections; torture under the AI-5 decree of 1968
polities.head: Generals Castelo Branco, Costa e Silva, Médici, Geisel, Figueiredo
polities.rel: Catholic; liberation theology in opposition
polities.econ: The 'economic miracle' of 1968 to 1973 at 10 per cent a year; the debt crisis of 1982; the Trans-Amazonian highway
polities.now: A regime that grew the economy fast and borrowed faster, tortured and killed hundreds, and handed power back gradually when the debt crisis arrived.
polities.how: The 1964 coup, the hard line of 1968, the abertura from 1974.
polities.next: Civilian rule returns in 1985; the 1988 constitution.

polities.gov: Presidential federal democracy under the 1988 constitution; impeachments in 1992 and 2016; the 2023 attack on the capital
polities.head: Fernando Henrique Cardoso; Lula da Silva 2003 to 2010 and since 2023; Dilma Rousseff; Jair Bolsonaro
polities.rel: Catholic majority, evangelical Protestant third and rising
polities.econ: Latin America's largest economy; soybeans, iron ore, oil, aircraft; the Real Plan of 1994 ended hyperinflation; Lava Jato corruption scandal
polities.now: A democracy that tamed inflation, lifted tens of millions from poverty under Lula, fell into recession and the Lava Jato scandal, elected Bolsonaro, and saw his supporters storm the capital in January 2023 after Lula's return.
polities.how: The 1988 constitution, the Real Plan, Lula's programmes, the 2016 impeachment, Bolsonaro.
polities.next: Amazon deforestation and polarisation.

polities.gov: Iturbide's empire 1822 to 1823; federal and centralist republics; Santa Anna eleven times president; the Reform laws; Maximilian's French-imposed empire 1864 to 1867
polities.head: Agustín de Iturbide; Antonio López de Santa Anna; Benito Juárez (1858 to 1872); Maximilian
polities.rel: Catholic; the Reform of the 1850s nationalised Church lands
polities.econ: Mining decline, bankruptcy, foreign debt; the loss of Texas in 1836 and half the national territory to the United States in 1848
polities.now: Half a century of coups, bankruptcy and invasion: Texas lost, the US war of 1846 to 1848 that took California and the Southwest, the liberal Reform, and the French intervention that ended with Maximilian before a firing squad.
polities.how: The independence settlement, Santa Anna, the Mexican-American war, the Reform war, the French.
polities.next: Porfirio Díaz seizes power in 1876 and holds it for thirty-five years.

polities.gov: Porfirio Díaz's dictatorship with the forms of a republic; 'order and progress'
polities.head: Porfirio Díaz
polities.rel: Catholic; the Church tolerated in practice
polities.econ: Railways, foreign investment in mines and oil, haciendas absorbing village land; growth with deep inequality
polities.now: Thirty-five years of stability and investment that modernised Mexico for foreigners and landowners while the peasantry lost its land, which is why it ended in revolution.
polities.how: Díaz's 1876 coup, his científico advisers, the 1910 election fraud.
polities.next: Madero's call to arms in November 1910; Díaz resigns in May 1911.

polities.gov: Civil war among Madero, Huerta, Carranza, Villa and Zapata; the 1917 constitution; the Cristero war of 1926 to 1929
polities.head: Francisco Madero; Venustiano Carranza; Álvaro Obregón; Plutarco Elías Calles
polities.rel: Catholic; the 1917 constitution's anticlerical articles provoke the Cristero rebellion
polities.pop: About 15 million; perhaps 1 to 2 million died
polities.econ: Oil boom at Tampico; land reform begins; US intervention at Veracruz 1914 and against Villa 1916
polities.now: A decade of civil war that killed a tenth of the population, wrote the most radical constitution of its time, and ended with the generals of Sonora in power.
polities.how: Madero's revolt, Huerta's coup, the Constitutionalist victory, Zapata's and Villa's defeats, Obregón's assassination in 1928.
polities.next: Calles founds the party of the revolution in 1929, which rules for seventy-one years.

polities.gov: One-party dominance of the Institutional Revolutionary Party; presidents chosen by their predecessors; elections won by fraud when needed
polities.head: Lázaro Cárdenas (1934 to 1940); Miguel Alemán; Díaz Ordaz; Salinas; Zedillo
polities.rel: Catholic; the state anticlerical in form, accommodating in practice
polities.econ: Oil nationalised 1938; the 'Mexican miracle' of 1940 to 1970; the 1982 debt default; NAFTA from 1994; the 1994 peso crisis
polities.now: The 'perfect dictatorship': a civilian one-party state that gave land under Cárdenas, nationalised oil, massacred students at Tlatelolco in 1968, defaulted in 1982, and opened to the United States with NAFTA.
polities.how: The party's founding, Cárdenas's reforms, the miracle, 1968, the debt crisis, Salinas's reforms.
polities.next: The PRI loses the presidency to Vicente Fox in 2000.

polities.gov: Multiparty presidential democracy; the PRI's return 2012 to 2018; López Obrador's Morena since 2018; Claudia Sheinbaum since 2024
polities.head: Vicente Fox; Felipe Calderón; Enrique Peña Nieto; Andrés Manuel López Obrador; Claudia Sheinbaum
polities.rel: Catholic majority, evangelical growth
polities.econ: The largest US trading partner; cars, electronics, remittances; the drug war since 2006 has killed more than 400,000
polities.now: A democracy since 2000 whose central fact is the drug war Calderón declared in 2006, with cartels controlling territory and a murder rate among the world's highest; Morena has concentrated power and reformed the judiciary.
polities.how: The 2000 alternation, the drug war, the 2014 Ayotzinapa disappearances, López Obrador's majorities.
polities.next: Cartel power and US pressure on trade and migration.

polities.gov: Rosas's dictatorship to 1852; the 1853 constitution; oligarchic republic; universal male suffrage 1912 and the Radicals in power from 1916
polities.head: Juan Manuel de Rosas; Bartolomé Mitre; Domingo Sarmiento; Julio Roca; Hipólito Yrigoyen
polities.rel: Catholic
polities.pop: About 1.8 million in 1869, 11 million by 1930, half of them immigrants or their children
polities.econ: Beef and wheat for Britain; British-built railways; among the ten richest countries per head by 1913
polities.now: From Rosas's tyranny to one of the richest countries in the world in two generations, on pampas beef and wheat, British capital and Italian and Spanish immigrants, with the indigenous south conquered in the 1879 'Conquest of the Desert'.
polities.how: The 1853 constitution, the Paraguayan war, the frontier campaigns, mass immigration, the 1912 franchise.
polities.next: The army overthrows Yrigoyen in 1930, the first of six coups.

polities.gov: Military coups in 1930, 1943, 1955, 1962, 1966 and 1976; Perón's presidency 1946 to 1955 and 1973 to 1974; the junta's 'dirty war' 1976 to 1983
polities.head: Juan Perón; Eva Perón; Generals Onganía, Videla, Galtieri
polities.rel: Catholic; the Church close to the military
polities.econ: Import substitution, labour power under Perón, chronic inflation, foreign debt; relative decline from the world's top ten to middle income
polities.now: Half a century of alternation between Peronism and the army, ending in a junta that disappeared up to 30,000 people and lost the Falklands war to Britain in 1982.
polities.how: The 1930 coup, Perón's rise, his overthrow and return, the Montoneros, the 1976 coup, the Falklands.
polities.next: Alfonsín's election in 1983 restores democracy and tries the junta.

polities.gov: Presidential democracy; Peronist and non-Peronist alternation; Javier Milei's libertarian presidency since 2023
polities.head: Raúl Alfonsín; Carlos Menem; Néstor and Cristina Kirchner; Mauricio Macri; Javier Milei
polities.rel: Catholic majority; Pope Francis an Argentine
polities.econ: Soybeans, lithium, shale gas at Vaca Muerta; defaults in 2001 and 2020; inflation above 200 per cent in 2023
polities.now: A democracy that tried the generals, pegged the peso and collapsed in 2001, swung to the Kirchners' populism, and in 2023 elected an economist promising to abolish the central bank.
polities.how: Alfonsín, Menem's convertibility, the 2001 crisis, Kirchnerism, Milei.
polities.next: Whether Milei's austerity stabilises the economy without breaking the social contract.

polities.gov: Portalian conservative republic from 1833; parliamentary republic 1891 to 1925; presidential democracy with stable elections from 1932; Allende's socialist government 1970 to 1973
polities.head: Diego Portales; Balmaceda; Arturo Alessandri; Eduardo Frei; Salvador Allende
polities.rel: Catholic; Church and state separated 1925
polities.econ: Nitrates after the War of the Pacific (1879 to 1884), then copper, nationalised by Allende in 1971
polities.now: The most stable republic in South America for a century, enriched by nitrates and copper taken from Bolivia and Peru, which in 1970 elected the world's first Marxist president by ballot.
polities.how: Portales's order, the 1891 civil war, the Alessandri reforms, the Popular Unity government.
polities.next: Pinochet's coup of 11 September 1973; Allende dies in the palace.

polities.gov: Pinochet's military dictatorship 1973 to 1990; democracy since the 1988 plebiscite; a rejected new constitution in 2022
polities.head: Augusto Pinochet; Patricio Aylwin; Ricardo Lagos; Michelle Bachelet; Sebastián Piñera; Gabriel Boric
polities.rel: Catholic majority, evangelical growth, rising non-religion
polities.econ: The Chicago Boys' free-market model; copper, lithium, salmon, wine; the highest income per head in South America with high inequality
polities.now: Pinochet's regime killed about 3,000 and built the region's most market-driven economy; democracy has kept the model while the 2019 protests and a failed constitutional rewrite showed its limits.
polities.how: The coup, the 1980 constitution, the 1988 plebiscite, the Concertación governments, the 2019 estallido.
polities.next: Constitutional reform remains unfinished.

polities.gov: Caudillo republics; the Aristocratic Republic; Leguía; military rule 1968 to 1980; Fujimori's autogolpe 1992 to 2000; six presidents since 2016
polities.head: Ramón Castilla; Augusto Leguía; Velasco Alvarado; Alberto Fujimori; Pedro Castillo, removed 2022
polities.rel: Catholic majority
polities.econ: Guano in the 1850s, then copper, gold, fishmeal; the Shining Path war of 1980 to 2000 killed about 70,000; strong growth 2000 to 2015
polities.now: Independent after Ayacucho, Peru lost the War of the Pacific, fought the Shining Path insurgency, elected and then imprisoned Fujimori, and has had a revolving door of presidents removed by Congress since 2016.
polities.how: Guano, the Pacific war, Velasco's reforms, the Shining Path, Fujimori's coup, the 2000s boom.
polities.next: Institutional collapse with a growing economy.

polities.gov: Liberal and Conservative republics; the War of a Thousand Days 1899 to 1902; La Violencia 1948 to 1958; the National Front; insurgency since 1964; the 2016 FARC peace
polities.head: Rafael Núñez; Jorge Eliécer Gaitán, assassinated 1948; Álvaro Uribe; Juan Manuel Santos; Gustavo Petro
polities.rel: Catholic majority
polities.econ: Coffee, oil, coal; cocaine production the largest in the world; Panama lost in 1903 to a US-backed secession
polities.now: A country of two parties whose rivalry produced civil wars, then a sixty-year insurgency fed by cocaine, with the FARC's demobilisation in 2016 only partly ending the violence.
polities.how: Gran Colombia's breakup, the partisan wars, Panama, La Violencia, the cartels, the peace process.
polities.next: Dissident guerrillas and the drug economy persist.

polities.gov: Caudillos and dictators to 1958; a two-party democracy under the Punto Fijo pact; Hugo Chávez's Bolivarian revolution from 1999; Nicolás Maduro's authoritarian rule since 2013
polities.head: José Antonio Páez; Juan Vicente Gómez (1908 to 1935); Rómulo Betancourt; Hugo Chávez; Nicolás Maduro
polities.rel: Catholic majority
polities.pop: About 28 million; nearly 8 million have left since 2014
polities.econ: The world's largest oil reserves; OPEC founder; the economy fell by three-quarters between 2013 and 2020
polities.now: Bolívar's homeland lived on oil from the 1920s, built a democracy from 1958, elected Chávez in 1998, and under Maduro has suffered the largest economic collapse of a country not at war, with a disputed 2024 election.
polities.how: Gómez, the 1958 pact, the 1989 Caracazo, Chávez's rise, the collapse after 2014.
polities.next: Maduro's hold against sanctions and an opposition that won the 2024 vote by its own count.

polities.gov: Caudillo republics; the 1952 revolution; military rule 1964 to 1982; democracy since; Evo Morales 2006 to 2019
polities.head: Andrés de Santa Cruz; Víctor Paz Estenssoro; Hugo Banzer; Evo Morales; Luis Arce
polities.cap: Sucre; La Paz the seat of government
polities.rel: Catholic and Andean traditions
polities.econ: Silver, then tin, then natural gas and lithium; the landlocked poorest state in South America after losing its coast in 1884
polities.now: Named for Bolívar, Bolivia lost its coast to Chile, its rubber lands to Brazil and the Chaco to Paraguay, nationalised tin in the 1952 revolution, and elected its first indigenous president in 2005.
polities.how: The Pacific war, the Chaco war, 1952, the coups, Morales and the 2019 crisis.
polities.next: Lithium and the Morales-Arce split.

polities.gov: Caudillo and oligarchic republics; the Liberal revolution of 1895; military rule in the 1970s; three presidents toppled by protest 1997 to 2005; Correa 2007 to 2017; democracy under cartel violence since
polities.head: Gabriel García Moreno; Eloy Alfaro; José María Velasco Ibarra; Rafael Correa; Daniel Noboa
polities.rel: Catholic majority
polities.econ: Cacao, bananas, oil from 1972; dollarised since 2000; cocaine transit since the 2010s
polities.now: A small republic dollarised after a banking collapse, which has become a cocaine corridor with a murder rate that rose eightfold between 2018 and 2023.
polities.how: The conservative-liberal struggle, oil, the 1999 crisis, Correa, the cartels.
polities.next: The internal armed conflict declared against gangs in 2024.

polities.gov: Francia's closed dictatorship 1814 to 1840; the López dynasty; the war of 1864 to 1870 killed most of the population; Stroessner's dictatorship 1954 to 1989; democracy since under Colorado dominance
polities.head: José Gaspar de Francia; Francisco Solano López; Alfredo Stroessner; Santiago Peña
polities.rel: Catholic; Guaraní and Spanish both official
polities.econ: Soybeans and beef; the Itaipú dam shared with Brazil; contraband
polities.now: A landlocked republic that under Francia sealed itself off, under López fought Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay until most of its men were dead, and under Stroessner endured the hemisphere's longest dictatorship.
polities.how: Francia, the Triple Alliance war, the Chaco war victory of 1935, Stroessner.
polities.next: Colorado Party dominance since 1947, with one interruption.

polities.gov: Colorado and Blanco civil wars in the nineteenth century; Batlle's welfare state from 1903; military dictatorship 1973 to 1985; democracy since
polities.head: José Batlle y Ordóñez; the Tupamaros; the generals; Tabaré Vázquez; José Mujica
polities.rel: The most secular state in Latin America
polities.econ: Beef, wool, soybeans, forestry; the highest income and lowest inequality in the region
polities.now: A buffer state between Argentina and Brazil that built Latin America's first welfare state, suffered a dictatorship, and is now the region's most stable democracy.
polities.how: Independence as a buffer in 1828, Batlle's reforms, the Tupamaro insurgency, the 1973 coup, the 1985 return.
polities.next: An ageing population and a small economy's exposure to its neighbours.

polities.gov: Liberal dictatorships in Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras and Nicaragua; US Marines in Nicaragua 1912 to 1933; Costa Rica's early democracy
polities.head: Justo Rufino Barrios; Manuel Estrada Cabrera; Jorge Ubico; the Somozas from 1936; Augusto Sandino
polities.cap: Guatemala City; Tegucigalpa; San Salvador; Managua; San José
polities.rel: Catholic
polities.pop: About 7 million across the five republics in 1940
polities.econ: Coffee and bananas; the United Fruit Company's plantations, railways and governments
polities.now: Five republics that broke from the federation of 1839 and fell to coffee oligarchies and the United Fruit Company, with the United States intervening by Marines and loans and the Somozas installed in Nicaragua.
polities.how: The federation's collapse, the liberal reforms of the 1870s, banana enclaves, the Sandino war.
polities.next: Guatemala's 1944 revolution; the Cold War arrives with the 1954 CIA coup.

polities.gov: A democratic decade 1944 to 1954 ended by the CIA-backed coup against Árbenz; military rule; a civil war 1960 to 1996 that killed 200,000, mostly Maya; democracy since
polities.head: Jacobo Árbenz; Efraín Ríos Montt; Álvaro Arzú; Bernardo Arévalo
polities.rel: Catholic and evangelical; Maya spirituality
polities.econ: Coffee, sugar, remittances; among the most unequal countries
polities.now: The 1954 coup against Árbenz's land reform began a thirty-six-year war with genocide against the Maya highlands; since the 1996 peace the state has fought a long contest with the 'pact of the corrupt'.
polities.how: The 1944 revolution, the coup, the war, the peace accords, the anti-corruption commission.
polities.next: Arévalo's government against an entrenched elite.

polities.gov: Military rule to 1979; civil war 1980 to 1992 killing 75,000; democracy; Nayib Bukele's one-man rule since 2019 with mass gang incarceration
polities.head: Archbishop Romero, murdered 1980; Alfredo Cristiani; Nayib Bukele
polities.rel: Catholic and evangelical
polities.econ: Coffee, remittances a quarter of GDP; dollarised; bitcoin as legal tender 2021 to 2025
polities.now: The 1932 massacre of 30,000 peasants and the civil war of the 1980s gave way to gang rule by MS-13 until Bukele's state of exception jailed 80,000 people and cut the murder rate to the region's lowest, at the cost of due process.
polities.how: La Matanza, the war, the Chapultepec accords, the gangs, Bukele.
polities.next: A presidency without limits and a prison population among the world's highest.

polities.gov: Military and civilian governments; the 2009 coup; Juan Orlando Hernández, later convicted of drug trafficking in the US; Xiomara Castro since 2022
polities.head: Tiburcio Carías; Manuel Zelaya; Juan Orlando Hernández; Xiomara Castro
polities.rel: Catholic and evangelical
polities.econ: Bananas, coffee, maquilas, remittances; among the poorest and most violent
polities.now: The original banana republic, a US base in the Contra war, and a state whose president ran a cocaine conspiracy, with emigration to the United States its main export.
polities.how: United Fruit, the Contra war, Hurricane Mitch in 1998, the 2009 coup.
polities.next: Violence and migration.

polities.gov: The Somoza dynasty to 1979; the Sandinista revolution and the Contra war; elections 1990 to 2006; Daniel Ortega's dictatorship since 2007
polities.head: Anastasio Somoza García and sons; Daniel Ortega; Violeta Chamorro
polities.rel: Catholic and evangelical; the Church persecuted since 2018
polities.econ: Coffee, beef, gold, remittances
polities.now: The Somozas' forty-three years ended in the Sandinista revolution of 1979, which the US-funded Contras fought through the 1980s; Ortega lost in 1990, returned in 2007, and has since jailed or exiled every opponent and the Church.
polities.how: Sandino, the Somozas, 1979, the Contras, the 1990 election, Ortega's return and the 2018 crackdown.
polities.next: A family dictatorship in all but name.

polities.gov: Democracy since 1949 with the army abolished after the 1948 civil war
polities.head: José Figueres Ferrer; Óscar Arias; Rodrigo Chaves
polities.rel: Catholic established church
polities.econ: Coffee, bananas, ecotourism, medical devices, Intel; the region's richest
polities.now: The exception in Central America: no army since 1948, continuous democracy, and a Nobel peace laureate president who brokered the end of the regional wars.
polities.how: Coffee smallholders, the 1948 war, Figueres's reforms, the Esquipulas accords.
polities.next: Rising cocaine-related violence and inequality.

polities.gov: Republic created by a US-backed secession from Colombia; the Canal Zone under US sovereignty to 1979; Noriega's dictatorship ended by US invasion 1989; democracy since
polities.head: Omar Torrijos; Manuel Noriega; Martín Torrijos; José Raúl Mulino
polities.rel: Catholic
polities.econ: The Canal, transferred in 1999, expanded in 2016; banking; the Panama Papers of 2016; the Darién migration route
polities.now: Carved out for the Canal in 1903, controlled by the United States for most of the century, invaded in 1989 to remove Noriega, and now the richest economy per head in Latin America on canal fees and finance, with US pressure over Chinese port concessions since 2025.
polities.how: The 1903 secession, the 1977 Torrijos-Carter treaties, the 1989 invasion, the 1999 handover.
polities.next: Water for the Canal and the Darién migration crisis.

polities.gov: British, Dutch and French plantation colonies; independent since the 1960s to 1980s as parliamentary democracies; French Guiana a department of France
polities.head: Prime ministers; Eric Williams of Trinidad; Cheddi Jagan and Forbes Burnham of Guyana
polities.cap: Belmopan; Georgetown; Paramaribo; Port of Spain; Bridgetown; Nassau
polities.rel: Christian majority; Hindu and Muslim communities in Guyana, Trinidad and Suriname from Indian indenture
polities.econ: Sugar and slavery, then indentured Indian labour; oil in Trinidad and, since 2019, Guyana's offshore boom, the fastest growth in the world; tourism and finance in the islands
polities.now: Plantation colonies built on African slavery and Indian indenture, independent since the 1960s, among which Guyana's oil discoveries have made it the fastest-growing economy on earth and Venezuela's claim to its Essequibo region a live dispute.
polities.how: The sugar revolution of the 1640s, emancipation, indenture, the West Indies Federation's failure in 1962.
polities.next: Climate exposure and, in Guyana, managing a windfall.

polities.gov: French royal colony from 1663 under a governor and intendant; seigneurial land tenure
polities.head: Champlain; Frontenac; Montcalm
polities.rel: Catholic; Jesuit missions to the Huron
polities.pop: About 70,000 French in 1760 against 1.5 million British colonists
polities.econ: The fur trade with Algonquian and Huron partners; a thin farming settlement along the St Lawrence
polities.now: A fur-trading empire stretching from the St Lawrence to Louisiana on alliances with the indigenous nations, with few settlers and dependent on France, which loses it to Britain at Quebec in 1759.
polities.how: Champlain's founding of Quebec in 1608, the Iroquois wars, the royal takeover of 1663.
polities.next: Ceded to Britain in 1763; the Quebec Act of 1774 protects French law and religion.

polities.gov: Thirteen colonies with elected assemblies under royal or proprietary governors; Parliament's claims to tax them disputed from 1765
polities.head: Colonial governors; the Continental Congress from 1774
polities.cap: None; Boston, Philadelphia, New York, Charleston the main towns
polities.rel: Puritan New England, Anglican south, Quaker Pennsylvania; the Great Awakening of the 1740s
polities.pop: About 250,000 in 1700, 2.5 million in 1775, a fifth enslaved
polities.econ: Tobacco, rice and indigo on slave plantations in the south; shipping, fish and timber in the north; trade within the Navigation Acts
polities.now: Thirteen self-governing colonies grown rich and populous, which fought France alongside Britain and then refused the taxes Britain levied to pay for it, from the Stamp Act of 1765 to the Boston Tea Party of 1773.
polities.how: Jamestown 1607, Plymouth 1620, the slave codes, the Seven Years' War, the imperial crisis.
polities.next: War begins at Lexington in April 1775; independence is declared in July 1776.

polities.gov: Federal republic under the 1787 constitution; a presidency, Congress and Supreme Court; slavery in the south; suffrage widened to most white men by the 1830s
polities.head: Washington, Jefferson, Jackson, Polk, Lincoln elected 1860
polities.rel: Protestant denominations, disestablished; the Second Great Awakening; Catholic immigration from the 1840s
polities.pop: About 4 million in 1790, 31 million in 1860, 4 million enslaved
polities.econ: Cotton the largest export, grown by slaves; the Erie Canal, railways, northern factories; the Louisiana Purchase of 1803 and the Mexican cession of 1848 double the territory
polities.now: A republic that doubled its territory by purchase and conquest, removed the eastern Indian nations across the Mississippi, built a cotton economy on slavery and an industrial one in the north, and could not agree on slavery's extension into the west.
polities.how: The constitution, the Louisiana Purchase, the Missouri Compromise, Jacksonian democracy, the Mexican war, Dred Scott.
polities.next: Lincoln's election; seven states secede; war at Fort Sumter in April 1861.

polities.t: United States, civil war and Gilded Age
polities.gov: Federal republic; the Confederacy's secession defeated; Reconstruction 1865 to 1877 and its abandonment; the Thirteenth, Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendments
polities.head: Lincoln (assassinated 1865), Grant, Hayes, Cleveland
polities.rel: Protestant majority; black churches; Catholic and Jewish immigration
polities.econ: The war's 750,000 dead; emancipation; transcontinental railways, steel, oil, Carnegie and Rockefeller; the US becomes the largest industrial economy by the 1890s
polities.now: The war that ended slavery and the Reconstruction that failed to secure black citizenship; then the conquest of the plains Indians, the railroad and industrial boom, and a politics of trusts and tariffs.
polities.how: Secession, Gettysburg, emancipation, Appomattox, Reconstruction's end in 1877, Wounded Knee in 1890.
polities.next: The 1898 war with Spain makes the United States a Pacific and Caribbean empire.

polities.gov: Federal republic; women's suffrage 1920; the New Deal's expansion of federal power; FDR's four terms
polities.head: McKinley, Theodore Roosevelt, Wilson, Hoover, Franklin Roosevelt (1933 to 1945)
polities.rel: Protestant majority; the Scopes trial; Catholic and Jewish immigration restricted after 1924
polities.econ: The world's largest economy by 1900; mass production; the 1929 crash and 25 per cent unemployment; war production from 1940
polities.now: The country took the Philippines and Cuba in 1898, built the Panama Canal, entered and left the First World War, boomed and crashed, and under Roosevelt built the welfare state and the arsenal of democracy.
polities.how: The Spanish war, Wilson's war and the League's rejection, the twenties, the crash, the New Deal, Pearl Harbor.
polities.next: Victory in 1945 leaves the United States with half the world's industrial output and the atomic bomb.

polities.t: United States in the Cold War
polities.gov: Federal republic; the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and Voting Rights Act of 1965; Watergate
polities.head: Truman, Eisenhower, Kennedy, Johnson, Nixon, Carter, Reagan, Bush
polities.rel: Protestant and Catholic; the evangelical movement in politics from the 1970s
polities.econ: The dollar at the centre of Bretton Woods; postwar boom; the 1970s stagflation; Reagan's tax cuts and deficits
polities.now: The superpower that rebuilt Europe and Japan, contained the Soviet Union, fought to a draw in Korea and lost in Vietnam, ended legal segregation at home, and outspent the Soviet Union into collapse.
polities.how: The Marshall Plan, NATO, Korea, the civil rights movement, Vietnam, Watergate, Reagan.
polities.next: The Soviet Union dissolves in December 1991; the unipolar moment.

polities.gov: Federal republic; polarised two-party politics; the January 2021 attack on the Capitol; Trump's second term from 2025
polities.head: Clinton, George W. Bush, Obama, Trump, Biden, Trump
polities.rel: Christian majority declining; a third unaffiliated
polities.econ: The largest economy; technology, finance, shale oil; the 2008 financial crisis; national debt above 100 per cent of GDP
polities.now: The unipolar power of the 1990s fought two long wars after September 11, suffered the 2008 crash, elected its first black president and then a populist who contested his 2020 defeat, and now faces China as a peer competitor and a politics its institutions strain to contain.
polities.how: The 1990s boom, 9/11, Iraq and Afghanistan, 2008, Obama, Trump, the pandemic, Biden, Trump again.
polities.next: The China rivalry, the debt, and the durability of the constitutional order.

polities.gov: Quebec and the Maritime colonies; Upper and Lower Canada from 1791; responsible government from 1848 after the 1837 rebellions
polities.head: British governors; Louis-Joseph Papineau and William Lyon Mackenzie as rebels; John A. Macdonald
polities.rel: Catholic Quebec, Protestant Ontario
polities.econ: Fur, timber, wheat; the Hudson's Bay Company's west; reciprocity with the United States 1854 to 1866
polities.now: The loyalists' refuge after the American revolution, which repelled the American invasion of 1812, rebelled for self-government in 1837, and moved toward union to resist the United States after its civil war.
polities.how: The Quebec Act, the loyalist migration, the war of 1812, Durham's report, responsible government.
polities.next: Confederation on 1 July 1867 creates the Dominion of Canada.

polities.gov: Federal parliamentary democracy and constitutional monarchy; full sovereignty by the Statute of Westminster 1931 and the patriated constitution of 1982
polities.head: Prime ministers Macdonald, Laurier, Mackenzie King, Pearson, Pierre and Justin Trudeau, Harper, Carney
polities.rel: Christian majority declining; Quebec secularised since the 1960s
polities.econ: Wheat, timber, oil sands, minerals, cars under free trade with the United States since 1989; among the ten largest economies
polities.now: A dominion that bought the west, built a railway to the Pacific, fought in both world wars, treated its indigenous peoples by residential schools it has since apologised for, nearly lost Quebec in the 1995 referendum, and lives beside and depends on the United States.
polities.how: Confederation, the railway, Vimy, the Depression, the Quiet Revolution, the Charter of 1982, NAFTA.
polities.next: Trade and sovereignty pressure from Washington, and housing.

polities.gov: French colony to 1762, Spanish to 1800, French again briefly
polities.head: French and Spanish governors
polities.rel: Catholic
polities.econ: Indigo, sugar, the Mississippi trade
polities.now: The French claim to the Mississippi basin, a thinly settled colony traded between France and Spain, which Napoleon sells to the United States in 1803 for 15 million dollars, doubling the republic.
polities.how: La Salle's claim of 1682, New Orleans, the 1762 cession to Spain, the 1800 retrocession.
polities.next: The Louisiana Purchase of 1803.

polities.gov: Danish colony to 1953, then county; home rule 1979; self-government 2009 with Denmark keeping defence and foreign affairs
polities.head: Premier of Greenland; the Danish monarch
polities.rel: Lutheran
polities.econ: Fishing, Danish subsidy, mineral and rare-earth prospects; the US base at Pituffik
polities.now: The world's largest island, Inuit-settled and Danish-ruled since 1721, moving toward independence while the United States, which tried to buy it in 1946 and 2019 and pressed again in 2025, treats it as strategic ground.
polities.how: Norse settlement, Danish colonisation, the 1941 US defence agreement, home rule.
polities.next: Independence and the American interest.

polities.gov: Confederacies and nations with councils of chiefs; the Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) league of five, then six nations
polities.head: Clan mothers and sachems of the Iroquois; war chiefs
polities.rel: Indigenous religions
polities.pop: Perhaps 2 to 7 million north of Mexico in 1492, falling by 90 per cent within two centuries from disease
polities.econ: Maize, beans and squash agriculture; the fur trade; horses transform the plains from the 1700s
polities.now: Hundreds of nations, among them the Iroquois league that played France and Britain against each other, the Cherokee of the southeast, and the Comanche who built a horse empire on the southern plains, all facing epidemics and settlement.
polities.how: Settlement before 15,000 years ago; the maize revolution; contact and disease from 1492.
polities.next: Removal, treaties and war push the nations west and onto reservations through the nineteenth century.
polities.wk: Native Americans in the United States

polities.gov: Penal colony at Sydney from 1788; six self-governing colonies by 1859 with responsible government
polities.head: Governors Phillip, Macquarie; colonial premiers
polities.cap: Sydney; Melbourne, the richest city in the empire in the 1880s; Adelaide; Brisbane; Perth
polities.rel: Anglican, Catholic Irish, Protestant dissenters
polities.pop: About 3.7 million settlers by 1900; the Aboriginal population fell from perhaps 750,000 to under 100,000
polities.econ: Wool, then the gold rushes of the 1850s, wheat, mining; frontier wars against Aboriginal peoples throughout
polities.now: Britain's convict dumping ground became six wool-and-gold colonies with the world's earliest secret ballot and widest male franchise, built on dispossession of the Aboriginal nations.
polities.how: The First Fleet, the wool boom, the gold rushes, the Eureka stockade, self-government.
polities.next: The colonies federate as the Commonwealth of Australia on 1 January 1901.

polities.gov: Federal parliamentary democracy and constitutional monarchy; the White Australia policy to 1973; a republic referendum defeated in 1999
polities.head: Prime ministers Deakin, Curtin, Menzies, Whitlam, Hawke, Howard, Albanese
polities.rel: Christian plurality; 40 per cent no religion
polities.econ: Wool, wheat, then iron ore, coal and gas to Asia; thirty years without recession to 2020
polities.now: A federation that fought at Gallipoli and in New Guinea, turned from Britain to the United States in 1942, abolished White Australia, apologised to the Stolen Generations in 2008, rejected an indigenous Voice in 2023, and depends on China for exports and the US for defence, with AUKUS submarines on order.
polities.how: Federation, Gallipoli, 1942, postwar immigration, the 1967 referendum, the Asian turn.
polities.next: The China-US balance and housing.

polities.gov: Crown colony under the Treaty of Waitangi; responsible government 1856; dominion 1907; women's suffrage 1893, the first in the world; parliamentary democracy with proportional representation since 1996
polities.head: Prime ministers Seddon, Savage, Muldoon, Lange, Clark, Key, Ardern, Luxon
polities.rel: Christian plurality; half no religion; Māori churches
polities.econ: Wool, dairy and meat for Britain until 1973; deregulation in the 1980s; tourism; dairy to China
polities.now: The treaty of 1840 was followed by the New Zealand Wars and land confiscation; the Waitangi Tribunal since 1975 has settled claims, and the country has been a laboratory for welfare, deregulation and electoral reform.
polities.how: Waitangi, the wars of the 1860s, the welfare state of 1938, Rogernomics, the treaty settlements.
polities.next: Māori rights and the treaty principles are the contested ground.

polities.gov: Kamehameha I's unified monarchy; a constitution from 1840; the Bayonet Constitution of 1887 imposed by American settlers
polities.head: Kamehameha I to V; Kalākaua; Queen Liliuokalani
polities.rel: Hawaiian religion abolished 1819; Congregationalist missions from 1820
polities.econ: Sandalwood, whaling, then sugar plantations owned by American families with Asian labour
polities.now: A kingdom unified by Kamehameha, recognised by the powers, and taken over by American sugar planters who overthrew the queen in 1893 with Marines ashore.
polities.how: Unification, the missionaries, the sugar treaty of 1875, the 1887 constitution, the 1893 coup.
polities.next: Annexed by the United States in 1898; a state in 1959.

polities.gov: Fiji a British colony 1874 to 1970, with four coups since 1987; Samoa a German colony, New Zealand mandate, independent 1962 as the first Pacific state
polities.head: Fiji's Ratu Mara, Sitiveni Rabuka, Frank Bainimarama; Samoa's Malietoa Tanumafili II, Fiamē Naomi Mataʻafa
polities.rel: Methodist and Catholic Christianity; Hindu Indo-Fijians
polities.econ: Sugar, tourism, remittances; Fiji's Indian-Fijian divide the axis of its coups
polities.now: Fiji's indentured Indian population made it a two-community state whose coups in 1987, 2000 and 2006 turned on ethnic politics; Samoa's chiefly system runs a stable parliamentary democracy.
polities.how: Cession in 1874, indenture, the 1987 coups; Samoa's partition and the Mau movement.
polities.next: Climate change and the China-Australia contest for the Pacific.

polities.gov: Mongol khans claiming the Yuan succession; the Oirats dominant in the mid-fifteenth century
polities.head: Esen Taishi (died 1455); Dayan Khan (around 1480 to 1517)
polities.rel: Shamanism; Tibetan Buddhism from the 1570s
polities.econ: Pastoral nomadism; raids and trade with Ming China
polities.now: The Mongols driven from China in 1368 still hold the steppe, and under Esen captured a Ming emperor at Tumu in 1449.
polities.how: The Yuan dynasty's expulsion; the Oirat ascendancy.
polities.next: Dayan Khan reunites the eastern Mongols; Altan Khan brings Tibetan Buddhism in the 1570s; the Manchus absorb them by the 1690s.

polities.gov: Independent merchant city-states under sultans: Kilwa, Mombasa, Malindi, Zanzibar, Pate
polities.head: Sultans of Kilwa and Mombasa
polities.rel: Sunni Islam in a Swahili culture of African and Arab descent
polities.econ: Gold from Mutapa, ivory and slaves traded to Arabia, Persia and India; Chinese porcelain in the ruins
polities.now: A chain of stone towns on the East African coast trading across the Indian Ocean, which Vasco da Gama reached in 1498 and the Portuguese sacked and garrisoned from 1505.
polities.how: Islamised trading settlements from the ninth century; Kilwa's gold monopoly.
polities.next: Portuguese Fort Jesus at Mombasa from 1593; Oman expels the Portuguese in 1698.

polities.gov: The kingdoms of Makuria and Alwa in decline
polities.head: Nubian kings
polities.rel: Coptic Christianity, giving way to Islam
polities.econ: Nile agriculture, trade with Egypt
polities.now: The last Christian kingdoms of the Nile, which held Egypt's armies off for six centuries and are now dissolving under Arab migration and Mamluk pressure.
polities.how: Christian conversion in the sixth century; the baqt treaty with Egypt; Mamluk invasions.
polities.next: The Funj sultanate takes Soba around 1504; Nubia becomes Muslim.

polities.gov: Aymara kingdoms around Lake Titicaca, the Chimú empire on the coast, and many chiefdoms
polities.head: Chimú kings at Chan Chan; Aymara lords
polities.rel: Andean religion; ancestor worship
polities.econ: Irrigated coastal valleys, highland terraces, llama herds
polities.now: The Andes before Inca unification: the Chimú on the coast and the Aymara kingdoms of the altiplano, all conquered by Cusco between the 1440s and 1470s.
polities.how: Tiwanaku and Wari collapsed around 1000; regional states filled the space.
polities.next: Pachacuti's and Topa Inca's conquests absorb them into Tawantinsuyu.

polities.gov: Gadaa age-set system of elected leaders; no central state
polities.head: Gadaa councils
polities.rel: Waaqeffanna; Islam and Christianity adopted in different regions
polities.econ: Cattle pastoralism, then settled agriculture
polities.now: Oromo pastoralists moving north from the southern highlands from the 1530s occupy much of the Ethiopian plateau weakened by the Adal wars, and are absorbed into and transform the Ethiopian state over three centuries.
polities.how: Pressure from the south and the Christian-Muslim wars opened the highlands.
polities.next: Menelik's conquests in the 1880s bring the Oromo lands under Addis Ababa.

polities.t: Sultanates of Darfur, Wadai and Bagirmi
polities.gov: Muslim sultanates of the central Sudan
polities.head: Keira sultans of Darfur; Wadai's kolaks; Ali Dinar (1898 to 1916)
polities.rel: Sunni Islam
polities.econ: Slaves and ivory on the Forty Days Road to Egypt
polities.now: Sultanates between Bornu and the Nile, living on the Saharan slave trade, which outlasted the Mahdist state and fell to France and Britain only in the twentieth century.
polities.how: The Keira dynasty's rise in the seventeenth century; Wadai's independence from Darfur.
polities.next: France takes Wadai in 1909; Britain kills Ali Dinar and annexes Darfur in 1916.

polities.gov: Hindu warrior kingdoms of Mewar, Marwar, Amber and others; Mughal vassals from Akbar's reign
polities.head: Rana Sanga; Rana Pratap of Mewar; Jai Singh of Amber
polities.rel: Hinduism; Rajput honour codes
polities.econ: Arid agriculture, caravan routes, Mughal military service
polities.now: The Rajput clans whose alliances and resistance shaped Mughal India, with Mewar alone refusing submission until 1615.
polities.how: Clan kingdoms from the seventh century; Akbar's marriage alliances.
polities.next: Subsidiary treaties with the Company in 1818 make them princely states.

polities.gov: Tuareg sultanate at Agadez
polities.head: Sultans of Agadez
polities.rel: Sunni Islam
polities.econ: Salt caravans from Bilma, trans-Saharan trade
polities.now: A Tuareg sultanate controlling the salt and caravan routes of the central Sahara.
polities.how: Founded around 1405 by Tuareg confederations.
polities.next: France occupies Agadez in 1906; the Kaocen revolt of 1916 fails.

polities.t: Bunyoro and the Great Lakes kingdoms
polities.gov: Kingdoms of Bunyoro, Nkore, Toro and Rwanda-style monarchies
polities.head: Kabalega of Bunyoro (1869 to 1899)
polities.rel: Traditional religion
polities.econ: Cattle, ivory, salt at Kibiro
polities.now: Buganda's older rival, which Kabalega rebuilt with a standing army and lost to British and Ganda forces in 1894 to 1899.
polities.how: The Bito dynasty's kingdom; Buganda's rise at its expense.
polities.next: Kabalega is captured in 1899 and exiled; Bunyoro loses its 'lost counties' to Buganda.

polities.gov: Nyamwezi chiefs on the caravan route; Mirambo's state 1860s to 1884
polities.head: Mirambo (died 1884)
polities.rel: Traditional religion
polities.econ: Porterage and ivory on the Zanzibar caravan route
polities.now: The Nyamwezi, the porters of East Africa, built a warlord state under Mirambo athwart the caravan route from the coast to the lakes.
